questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Target reached before the plan ends
questions.question: Two of four actions in a software reseller's license-fraud plan are validated, and the re-rated risk already meets the plan's target; the last two cost $120,000. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Complete the last two actions as the agreed plan sets out
options.B: Give the risk owner a fresh cost-benefit of the last two actions
options.C: Close the risk's register entry now that it meets target
options.D: Have each action owner decide whether to finish their own action

questions.key_concept: A plan serves its target risk; once validated actions reach it, the remaining actions need a fresh cost-benefit decision by the risk owner.
questions.pre_read: Compare where the risk stands now with what the plan set out to reach.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan exists to bring the risk to target, and validated actions already have. Whether the last two are still worth $120,000 now depends on how much further they would cut the risk: the analyst prepares a fresh cost-benefit, and the risk owner decides whether to keep, scale back or cancel them. Completing them as planned is the runner-up: plans are normally seen through, but the facts behind these two have changed.

wrong_explanations.A: Completing them as planned treats the plan as the goal; with the risk already at target, $120,000 more needs a fresh cost-benefit case and the owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.C: A risk at its target still exists; it stays in the register and is monitored, and closing it now also skips the decision on the last two actions.
wrong_explanations.D: Action owners deliver their tasks; whether the risk needs further treatment is the risk owner's call, made on the whole plan's cost-benefit.

tips: Eliminate: C closes the risk itself, though a risk at target stays in the register and is monitored, and D lets each action owner choose, though treatment is the risk owner's call.
Final two: B beats A because the risk already meets its target; whether $120,000 more is worth spending is a new cost-benefit decision for the risk owner.
Exam cue: when the facts behind a plan change, even for the better, take the revised cost-benefit to the risk owner before spending or stopping.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Threshold after a volume change
questions.question: A documented merger doubled a commercial lender's business-loan applications; its weekly KRI counting credit-check overrides has been red every week since, though overrides remain 2% of applications. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Re-set the threshold with the risk owner and tolerance approver
options.B: Escalate each further red breach to the lending risk owner
options.C: Find out why overrides rose in each of the red weeks
options.D: Use credit losses against tolerance as the KRI

questions.key_concept: When a documented rise in volume, with the rate unchanged, makes a count-based KRI breach, re-base its threshold with the risk owner and tolerance approver.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the KRI counts with what has actually changed in the business.
questions.correct_explanation: The KRI counts overrides, so doubling applications doubled the count while the override rate held at 2%: the red weeks track the larger loan book, not worse override practice. Re-setting the threshold for the new volume, say as a rate, with the risk owner and whoever approved the tolerance keeps it tied to that tolerance. Escalating each breach is the runner-up: it follows the rule, but sends alarms that teach owners to ignore red.

wrong_explanations.B: Escalation suits real breaches; these track the larger loan book, not worse practice, so repeated escalations would teach the owner to ignore the KRI.
wrong_explanations.C: The cause is already documented: the merger doubled applications and the override rate is unchanged, so investigating each week again only delays the fix.
wrong_explanations.D: Credit losses lag and arrive after the harm; the override KRI still warns early once its threshold fits the new volume.

tips: Eliminate: C re-investigates a cause already documented, and D swaps a leading indicator for lagging loss figures.
Final two: A beats B because the override rate is unchanged, so the red weeks track volume, not worse practice; re-setting the threshold with its approvers fixes the measure.
Exam cue: re-set a threshold only on evidence that volume, not the underlying rate, has changed, and with the risk owner and the tolerance approver.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Agreed trigger reached
questions.question: A PR agency's risk owner agreed that final rules on labeling AI-made content would trigger a funding decision on an analyzed labeling plan; the rules are now final. What is the risk analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Start the analyzed labeling plan under the agreed trigger
options.B: Record the final rules as a new emerging risk entry
options.C: Tell the risk owner the agreed trigger has been reached
options.D: Ask the regulator how strictly it will enforce the rules

questions.key_concept: Agreed triggers turn emerging-risk monitoring into decisions; when one is reached, report it to the risk owner, who decides on the prepared response.
questions.pre_read: Note what was agreed in advance and what has now happened.
questions.correct_explanation: The owner set the trigger so that a decision would follow once it came. It has come, so the analyst reports it to the owner, with the analyzed plan ready, and the owner decides on funding. Starting the plan is the runner-up: the trigger and plan were agreed in advance, but the trigger called for the owner's funding decision, not for the analyst to commit money and staff.

wrong_explanations.A: The agreed trigger calls for the owner's funding decision; starting the plan commits money and effort that only the owner can authorize.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk is already recorded with its trigger; a second entry duplicates it, and the final rules call for a decision, not more recording.
wrong_explanations.D: Enforcement intent may matter later, but the agreed trigger was the rules becoming final; asking first delays a decision the owner planned for.

tips: Eliminate: B records a risk already in the register, and D seeks enforcement intent when the agreed trigger was the rules becoming final.
Final two: C beats A because the trigger was set for the owner's funding decision; starting the plan commits money the owner has not approved.
Exam cue: when an emerging risk's agreed trigger is reached, report it to the risk owner with the prepared options; the owner decides on spending.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Risk held by two directors
questions.question: A mortgage servicer's payoff-error risk is jointly owned by its servicing and finance directors, and last quarter its red KRI went seven weeks without a response. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Set a 48-hour response deadline for red KRI results
options.B: Have both directors approve each response together
options.C: Report the seven-week delay to the risk committee
options.D: Propose one director as owner, the other consulted

questions.key_concept: A risk needs one accountable owner; joint owners can each wait for the other, so name one and keep the other consulted.
questions.pre_read: Look for why nobody acted, not only for how slowly the response came.
questions.correct_explanation: With two joint owners, neither director was clearly accountable, and the red KRI sat for seven weeks. Having senior management name one director as the accountable owner, usually the one whose objectives and budget the risk mainly affects, with the other consulted, removes that cause. A response deadline is the runner-up: it sets a clock, but while two owners still share the risk, each can wait for the other to meet it.

wrong_explanations.A: A deadline sets a clock but names nobody to meet it; with two joint owners, each can still wait for the other.
wrong_explanations.B: Joint approval of each response is the shared ownership that stalled the KRI; it adds a step without making either director accountable.
wrong_explanations.C: Reporting the delay records a past failure; the next red KRI would meet the same two owners waiting on each other.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps the shared ownership behind the seven-week wait, and C reports a past delay without changing who acts next time.
Final two: D beats A because a deadline needs one accountable person to meet it; one named owner removes the wait the two directors created.
Exam cue: when two owners share a risk and nothing happens, propose one accountable owner with the other consulted, before adding deadlines.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Error that reached investors
questions.question: A fund administrator's controls prevent and detect net asset value (NAV) errors, yet one reaching investors took three weeks to correct as staff debated how. Which addition should the risk analyst recommend as MOST important?

options.A: A NAV-error trend report to the fund's risk owner
options.B: A NAV-error correction procedure with a named owner
options.C: A second price review carried out by the NAV control owner
options.D: Insurance cover for losses caused by NAV errors

questions.key_concept: A layered control set needs a corrective function too; when errors that get through take weeks to fix, a set correction procedure fills the gap.
questions.pre_read: Sort the existing controls by what they do, then ask which function failed in the story.
questions.correct_explanation: The stem says prevention and detection exist; what failed was correction, with staff spending three weeks deciding how to fix investors' holdings. A documented correction procedure with an owner is the missing corrective control and cuts the harm from any error that gets through. A second price review is the runner-up: it strengthens a layer already in place, but the next error that slips past it would meet the same three-week debate.

wrong_explanations.A: A trend report shows the risk owner how NAV errors are changing; it does not give staff a way to correct holdings faster.
wrong_explanations.C: Another review adds to prevention and detection, which already exist; errors that still get through would wait just as long to be fixed.
wrong_explanations.D: Insurance can repay part of the cost, but it does not correct investors' holdings or shorten the weeks they wait.

tips: Eliminate: A reports errors without fixing them, and D transfers part of the cost while investors still wait for corrected holdings.
Final two: B beats C because prevention and detection already exist; the three-week debate shows the missing layer is correction.
Exam cue: map existing controls to prevent, detect and correct, then recommend the function the scenario shows is missing, not more of one already there.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. AI services outside the register
questions.question: A credit bureau's board wants an AI risk report next quarter; its register lists five AI tools, but expense records show staff paying for 14 AI services. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: List the AI services in use, each with a business owner
options.B: Report on the five registered tools, noting the gap
options.C: Ask the five tools' business owners to confirm their ratings
options.D: Rate the nine unlisted services as high risk for now

questions.key_concept: An AI risk report is only as complete as its inventory; find each AI service in use, with its owner, before rating or reporting.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the register holds with what is actually in use, and note how much time is left.
questions.correct_explanation: Expense records show 14 AI services in use, but the register holds five, so a report built on it would leave most AI use unrated. With a quarter to go, the first step is a complete inventory, each service with a business owner who can describe its use and data. Reporting the five with the gap noted is the runner-up: stating limits suits a report due now, not one with time to close the gap.

wrong_explanations.B: Noting a gap suits a deadline too close to fill it; here a quarter remains, and nine of 14 services would go unrated.
wrong_explanations.C: Confirming five ratings polishes what is already known; the nine unlisted services, which may handle consumer credit data, stay outside the report.
wrong_explanations.D: Rating services high before anyone knows their use or data is a guess, and it could mislead the board in either direction.

tips: Eliminate: C refines the five known ratings while nine services stay unseen, and D rates services before anyone knows how they are used.
Final two: A beats B because a quarter remains to close the gap; noting limits fits a report due now, not an inventory missing most of its items.
Exam cue: before rating or reporting a risk area, make sure the population is complete; use found in spending or logs goes into the inventory first.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Alerts mostly false
questions.question: Since a coffee roaster switched on a new monitoring tool, 95% of its alerts have proved false, and responders now dismiss most in bulk. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the tool's owner add staff to work through each alert
options.B: Have control owners review the alert backlog at month end
options.C: Have the tool's owner tune its rules against past incidents
options.D: Report the false-alert rate to each risk owner

questions.key_concept: Alerts that are mostly false teach responders to dismiss them; tuning the rules against confirmed incidents restores the signal before more effort is added.
questions.pre_read: Ask why responders stopped reading the alerts, and which option changes that cause.
questions.correct_explanation: With 95% of alerts false, responders have learned to dismiss them, so real alerts are lost in the noise. Having the tool's owner tune the rules against past confirmed incidents cuts the false alerts while keeping the patterns that matter, so each alert is worth reading again. Adding staff is the runner-up: it gets alerts read, but people still wade through mostly false alarms, at higher cost and with the same fatigue.

wrong_explanations.A: More staff can read each alert, but most stay false; cost rises and fatigue returns, because the noise itself is unchanged.
wrong_explanations.B: A month-end backlog review comes weeks after an attack would need a response; monitoring helps only if alerts are handled in time.
wrong_explanations.D: Reporting the false-alert rate describes the problem to risk owners but changes nothing about which alerts responders see.

tips: Eliminate: B reviews alerts weeks late, and D reports the false-alert rate without changing what responders receive.
Final two: C beats A because tuning removes the noise that taught responders to dismiss alerts; more staff still wade through mostly false alarms.
Exam cue: when monitoring output is ignored, fix the signal first; tune the rules so alerts are worth acting on before adding people or reports.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-137 Section 3.6 (Review and Update the Monitoring Program and Strategy: the accuracy of measurements and the usefulness of collected data are reviewed, and collection found not useful is reconsidered); NIST SP 800-137 Section 3.5 (Respond to Findings)

Owner pattern: all four options name an owner (k=4); the key C and the runner-up A both name the tool's owner. Neighbours checked (stems, keys and decoy families): crisc_d3_018 (alerts unread in a shared inbox: route each type to a responder), crisc_d3_078 (600 checks switched on at once: start with the top risks), crisc_d3_126 (share of alerts resolved in time), crisc_d3_167 (vendor drift alerts routed to the agency's owner), crisc_d2_105 (a sample of scanner findings verified); AAIA aaia_d2_197 (drift limits based on past winters so alerts flag unusual change: the closest lesson, in an AI-audit lens), CISA d5_287 (DLP false alerts: a better detection method). questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Which rating meets appetite
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows a title insurer's board whether its cyber risks sit within appetite?

options.A: The count of open actions each risk owner holds
options.B: Each risk's inherent rating set against appetite
options.C: Pass rates from control owners' latest tests
options.D: Each risk's current rating set against appetite

questions.key_concept: Appetite is compared with current risk, which counts the controls working today; inherent ratings overstate exposure wherever controls work.
questions.pre_read: Picture the board's question, then ask what each measure would really answer.
questions.correct_explanation: Whether a risk sits within appetite depends on the exposure the insurer carries today, after the controls already working, which is its current rating. Setting each risk's current rating against appetite shows the board where it stands and where decisions are needed. Inherent ratings against appetite is the runner-up: it looks like the same view, but it leaves out working controls, so most cyber risks would appear above appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: Open actions measure work on treatment plans; a risk with none may still be above appetite, and one with many may be within it.
wrong_explanations.B: Inherent ratings leave out the controls already working, so they overstate today's exposure and would show most risks above appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Test pass rates show whether controls work, but not how much risk remains or how that compares with the board's appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A counts open actions and C reports control test results; neither shows how much risk remains against appetite.
Final two: D beats B because appetite is compared with today's exposure after working controls; inherent ratings leave those controls out.
Exam cue: for 'within appetite', compare current or residual risk, not inherent; inherent risk shows how much work the controls are doing.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Measuring horizon scanning
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows a seed bank's risk analyst that its horizon scanning is working?

options.A: Share of this year's new risks the scan flagged before harm
options.B: Number of news and research items the team screens
options.C: Number of emerging risks added to the register this year
options.D: Hours the risk team spends on horizon scanning

questions.key_concept: Horizon scanning works if it warns before harm, so measure how many new risks it caught early, not how much scanning was done.
questions.pre_read: Separate measures of scanning effort from measures of what the scanning achieved.
questions.correct_explanation: Horizon scanning exists to spot risks before they cause harm, so the telling measure is how many of the year's new risks it flagged ahead of any loss, rather than those first found through incidents. Counting emerging risks added to the register is the runner-up: it shows output, but a long list can hold irrelevant entries while the risks that later struck went unflagged.

wrong_explanations.B: Items screened measure activity; a team can read thousands of articles and still miss the signal that mattered to the seed bank.
wrong_explanations.C: A count of new entries shows output, not accuracy: the list can grow while the risks that actually struck were never on it.
wrong_explanations.D: Hours spent are an input; more time scanning does not show that the scan caught anything before it caused harm.

tips: Eliminate: B counts items read and D counts hours spent; both measure effort, not whether the scan warned in time.
Final two: A beats C because it tests the scan against what really happened; a longer emerging-risk list can still miss the risks that struck.
Exam cue: to show a process works, prefer an outcome measure tied to its purpose over counts of activity, effort or output.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.3.2 (Effectiveness Measures: evaluate how well processes and controls are working and whether they are meeting desired outcomes); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-03 (internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded)

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Reviews after onboarding
questions.question: Which of the following should a debt collector's risk analyst recommend as the BEST addition to its one-time vendor reviews at onboarding?

options.A: A full review of each vendor with its business owner at renewal
options.B: Reviews whenever a vendor's business owner reports a problem
options.C: Recurring reviews scaled to each vendor's criticality and data
options.D: A fresh onboarding questionnaire from each vendor's contract owner

questions.key_concept: Vendor risk changes after signing, so monitoring continues for the life of the contract, with depth and frequency scaled to each vendor's criticality.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option keeps watching vendors over time and puts the most effort where the most is at stake.
questions.correct_explanation: A vendor's risk keeps changing after onboarding, through new services, subcontractors, incidents or weaker controls, so reviews must continue. Scaling their depth and frequency to each vendor's criticality and the data it holds puts the closest watch where failure would hurt most. A review at each renewal is the runner-up: it recurs, but it spends as much on a stationery supplier as on a critical vendor, and can leave years between checks.

wrong_explanations.A: A review at each renewal treats minor and critical vendors alike and can leave years between checks of a vendor whose risk has changed.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for a business owner to report a problem makes reviews reactive; many vendor weaknesses surface only after harm is done.
wrong_explanations.D: Repeating the onboarding questionnaire is another one-time snapshot of self-reported answers, not monitoring over the contract's life.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for a reported problem, and D repeats a one-time questionnaire; neither monitors vendors over the contract's life.
Final two: C beats A because effort should follow each vendor's criticality; a flat renewal cycle under-watches critical vendors and over-reviews minor ones.
Exam cue: vendor risk is managed for the life of the contract, with monitoring depth and frequency scaled to criticality, not checked once at onboarding.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-07 (the risks posed by a supplier, their products and services and other third parties are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to and monitored); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-04 (suppliers are known and prioritized by criticality)

Owner pattern: three options name an owner (A, B, D) and the key is the one without; the runner-up A names one. questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Plans tracked in a project tool
questions.question: A tram operator tracks risk action plans only in a project tool, and five finished in March, yet its risk register still lists them as under way. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have action owners email the risk team as each action closes
options.B: Have action owners log progress in each register entry
options.C: Re-rate the five risks in the register from the project tool
options.D: Ask risk owners to track their plans in the project tool

questions.key_concept: Each action plan is tied to its risk's register entry, so progress, slippage and closure reach the risk picture that reports draw on.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the picture of each risk lives, and whether plan progress ever reaches it.
questions.correct_explanation: The register holds the risk picture, but the plans live only in the project tool, so finished work never reaches it. Having action owners log progress in each risk's register entry keeps plan and risk in one view, ready for the risk team to validate the work and re-rate. Closure emails are the runner-up: they cover the finish line only, leave milestones and slippage outside the register, and depend on someone remembering.

wrong_explanations.A: Closure emails cover only the finish; milestones and slippage stay outside the register, and a forgotten email recreates the gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Re-rating from the project tool's status credits work nobody has validated; finished actions are tested before a risk's rating changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving risk owners into the project tool deepens the split; the register still would not show plan progress.

tips: Eliminate: C re-rates on unvalidated tool status, and D pulls risk owners further into a tool the register never sees.
Final two: B beats A because logging progress in the register entry carries milestones and slippage too; closure emails cover only the finish and depend on memory.
Exam cue: an action plan belongs with its risk's register entry, so progress and closure update the risk picture; ratings change only after validation.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 3 Table 1 (Descriptions of notional cybersecurity risk register template elements); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated)

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. A control that serves several risks
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows an open university's risk analyst the benefit of a control reducing five risks, to weigh against its cost?

options.A: Reduction in each of the five risks' ratings
options.B: Expected loss avoided on the highest-rated of the five risks
options.C: Expected loss avoided, summed across the five risks
options.D: Spending on the same control at peer universities

questions.key_concept: A control's benefit is the expected loss it avoids across every risk it reduces, weighed against its full cost.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a control's benefit is made of before comparing the measures offered.
questions.correct_explanation: A control's benefit is the loss it is expected to avoid, so when one control reduces five risks, its benefit is the reduction summed across all five, weighed against its full cost. The loss avoided on the highest-rated risk is the runner-up: it is only part of the benefit, so judging the control on it understates the case and can reject a control that pays for itself across the five.

wrong_explanations.A: Rating drops show each risk moving, but not a value that can be summed or weighed against the control's cost.
wrong_explanations.B: The highest-rated risk shows only part of the benefit; leaving out the other four understates the control's value and can reject a sound investment.
wrong_explanations.D: Peer spending is a cost benchmark, showing what others paid; it says nothing about the loss this control would avoid at the university.

tips: Eliminate: A shows rating changes with no value to weigh against cost, and D counts peers' spending; neither measures the loss the control would avoid.
Final two: C beats B because a control's benefit is all the loss it avoids; scoring it on one risk understates the case.
Exam cue: in a cost-benefit case, count the risk reduction across every risk a control serves, then weigh it against the control's full cost.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Exceptions approved by IT security
questions.question: A tire maker's IT security team approves every exception to its patching standard, including those for production-line controllers that cannot be patched mid-run. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owners of the affected risks approve exceptions
options.B: Keep IT security as approver, adding a risk review of each
options.C: Send patching exceptions to senior management for approval
options.D: Move exception approval from IT security to the risk team

questions.key_concept: An exception keeps a known weakness in place, so the owner of the affected risk approves it, at a level matching the rating.
questions.pre_read: List the roles named in the options and what each one answers for.
questions.correct_explanation: An exception keeps a known weakness in place, so approving it is a decision to carry risk, and that belongs to the owners of the affected risks, here the managers accountable for the production lines, at a level matching the rating. Keeping IT security as approver with a risk review is the runner-up: the review improves the analysis, but IT still accepts risk it does not own.

wrong_explanations.B: A risk review improves the analysis, but IT security still makes the decision; the managers who own the production risk never decide on it.
wrong_explanations.C: Senior management approves deviations beyond an owner's authority; sending routine exceptions there whatever their rating bypasses the owners and overloads the top.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk team assesses and advises on exceptions; granting them would have the second line accept risk it should only challenge.

tips: Eliminate: C sends routine exceptions to senior management whatever their rating, and D has the risk team grant deviations it should only assess.
Final two: A beats B because approving an exception is a decision to carry risk, which belongs to the risk's owner; a risk review cannot make IT security the right approver.
Exam cue: the owner of the affected risk approves a deviation, at a level matching its rating; IT and the risk team assess and advise.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Survey-based patch indicator
questions.question: A metro operator's patch tool covers its signaling workstations, but their missing-patch KRI comes from a quarterly depot survey; attackers exploit new flaws within days. Which change should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Quarterly figures drawn straight from the patch tool
options.B: Quarterly survey figures checked on sampled workstations
options.C: Weekly figures that depot staff report in a survey
options.D: Weekly figures drawn straight from the patch tool

questions.key_concept: Collect a KRI as often as its risk can change, drawing it from system records where they exist rather than from people's reports.
questions.pre_read: Check two things in each option: how often the figure arrives and where it comes from.
questions.correct_explanation: Flaws are now exploited within days, so a quarterly figure arrives long after exposure has turned into harm; collection must match how fast the risk moves. Weekly figures drawn from the patch tool are complete, consistent and cheap to collect. Weekly depot surveys are the runner-up: the timing fits, but hand-reported answers vary between staff, miss machines and take depot time every week.

wrong_explanations.A: The patch tool gives reliable data, but quarterly figures still arrive months after flaws that attackers exploit within days.
wrong_explanations.B: Checking survey answers on sampled workstations improves accuracy, but the figures still arrive quarterly, far too late for flaws exploited within days.
wrong_explanations.C: Weekly timing fits the threat, but hand-reported survey answers vary between staff and miss machines, while the patch tool already holds the data.

tips: Eliminate: A and B keep a quarterly cycle, far too slow for flaws that attackers exploit within days of release.
Final two: D beats C because the patch tool gives complete, consistent figures without depot effort; weekly surveys fit the timing but stay hand-reported.
Exam cue: collect a KRI as often as its risk can change, and from system records where they exist, rather than from people's reports.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Test cycle under a regulator's rule
questions.question: A land registry's regulator requires a restore test of its title records each quarter; after three clean tests, the control owner wants to move to half-yearly tests. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the risk owner decide the new test cycle
options.B: Keep the restore test on its quarterly cycle
options.C: Move to half-yearly tests with backup integrity checks
options.D: Ask internal audit to approve a half-yearly cycle

questions.key_concept: Control frequency follows risk, but a frequency a law or regulator requires is a floor that risk ratings and owners' decisions cannot lower.
questions.pre_read: Note who or what set the current cycle before judging who may change it.
questions.correct_explanation: Test frequency is normally set by risk, but a regulator's rule sets a floor that no rating or owner's decision can lower, so the quarterly cycle stays. Having the risk owner decide the cycle is the runner-up: risk owners do decide how much control a risk needs above any legal minimum, but none can choose fewer tests than the regulator requires.

wrong_explanations.A: Risk owners decide how much control a risk needs, but only above legal minimums; no owner can choose fewer tests than the regulator requires.
wrong_explanations.C: Integrity checks may help, but half-yearly tests would still break the regulator's quarterly rule; a compensating control cannot replace a required one.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit gives independent assurance; it does not approve management's control changes, and it cannot set aside the regulator's quarterly rule.

tips: Eliminate: C still halves the required test cycle despite the backup checks, and D asks internal audit to approve a control change it only gives assurance on.
Final two: B beats A because the regulator's quarterly rule is a floor; the risk owner decides control levels above it, never below.
Exam cue: set control frequency by risk, but never below a legal or regulatory minimum; the rule sets the floor, and risk decides anything above it.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Human checks of AI translations
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows a risk analyst that a refugee charity's caseworker checks of AI translations work?

options.A: Caseworkers' accounts of how they check each one
options.B: The vendor's published accuracy rates per language
options.C: The tool's record of each translation a caseworker approved
options.D: A linguist's re-check of sampled approved translations

questions.key_concept: Reperforming a human review of AI output on a sample shows whether it catches errors; approval records show only that it ran.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the test must show about the caseworkers' checks before ranking the evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: The question is whether the checks catch errors, so the strongest evidence is reperformance: a qualified linguist re-checks a sample of translations caseworkers approved and sees whether mistakes got through. The tool's approval record is the runner-up: it proves a check was recorded for each translation, but an approval clicked in seconds leaves the same record as a careful one.

wrong_explanations.A: Caseworkers' own accounts are inquiry, the weakest evidence; people describe the check as intended, not how carefully they perform it.
wrong_explanations.B: Vendor accuracy rates describe the tool on the vendor's test data; they say nothing about whether caseworkers catch the errors it makes.
wrong_explanations.C: Approval records show a check was recorded for each translation, not that it was careful; a habitual approval leaves the same record as a real one.

tips: Eliminate: A rests on caseworkers' own accounts, and B describes the tool rather than the human check that controls it.
Final two: D beats C because re-checking approved work shows whether errors get through; approval records prove only that a check was recorded.
Exam cue: to show a review control works, reperform it on a sample; sign-offs and logs show it ran, not that it caught anything.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for pediatric dosing errors
questions.question: Which of the following should a children's hospital's risk analyst propose as the BEST KRI for weight-based dosing errors?

options.A: Share of dose orders placed without a current weight
options.B: Dosing errors that staff report through incident forms
options.C: Share of nurses trained in weight-based dosing
options.D: Average time pharmacists take to verify an order

questions.key_concept: A good KRI tracks a driver of the risk that moves before harm occurs, such as dose orders placed without a current weight.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each measure counts and when it would change.
questions.correct_explanation: Weight-based doses are only as accurate as the weight they use, so orders placed without a current weight are a direct driver of the scenario and rise before any harm, which makes them a leading KRI. Dosing errors that staff report are the runner-up: they relate to the same risk, but they count errors already made, and under-reporting hides many of them.

wrong_explanations.B: Reported errors are lagging: they count harm or near harm already done, and depend on staff choosing to report them.
wrong_explanations.C: Training completion measures a program's delivery; trained staff can still order from an outdated weight, so it does not track the risk's driver.
wrong_explanations.D: Verification time is a KPI for pharmacy workflow; faster or slower checks say little about whether doses rest on accurate weights.

tips: Eliminate: C counts training completed and D times the pharmacy's checks; both measure activity or performance, not the dosing risk.
Final two: A beats B because orders without a current weight rise before an error occurs; reported errors are lagging and count harm already done.
Exam cue: the best KRI tracks a driver of the risk scenario that moves before the loss, not a count of the losses themselves.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Committee unable to see the stakes
questions.question: A chemical plant's report to its executive committee lists control-system vulnerabilities by count and CVSS score, and members say they cannot tell what is at stake. What is the risk analyst's BEST change?

options.A: Send the report to the plant's risk owners instead
options.B: State each risk's possible effect on safety and output
options.C: Show each count against its threshold and trend
options.D: Have control owners explain the scores at meetings

questions.key_concept: Leaders decide on consequences, so report technical risk as its possible effect on objectives such as safety and production.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the audience needs in order to decide, and whether the measures shown speak to it.
questions.correct_explanation: Vulnerability counts and CVSS scores describe technical severity, not consequences, so members cannot weigh them. Stating each risk's possible effect on safety and production ties it to the plant's objectives, which is what an executive committee decides on. Showing counts against thresholds and trend is the runner-up: it adds limits and direction, but the measures stay technical, so members still cannot see what is at stake.

wrong_explanations.A: Risk owners need their own reports, but the committee still decides on priorities and funding and still cannot judge what is at stake.
wrong_explanations.C: Thresholds and trend add context, but they are still vulnerability counts; the committee still cannot see the effect on safety or production.
wrong_explanations.D: Explaining the scoring teaches the scale, not the stakes; a CVSS score rates a flaw's technical severity, not its effect on this plant.

tips: Eliminate: A moves the report away from the committee that must decide, and D explains the scores instead of what they mean for the plant.
Final two: B beats C because the committee asked what is at stake; thresholds and trend add context, but technical counts still hide the effect on safety and output.
Exam cue: report risk to leaders in business terms, such as the effect on safety, output or objectives, not in technical severity scores.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Final law narrower than the draft
questions.question: A dental chain's emerging-risk entry covers a draft law on where patient X-rays are stored; the final law applies only above 500 staff, and the chain has 120. What is the risk analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Rate the risk as a range until the law takes effect
options.B: Ask the risk owner to keep the entry open for amendments
options.C: Ask the risk owner to close the entry, noting the law's scope
options.D: Move the risk into the main profile at a low rating

questions.key_concept: Emerging risks are refined as evidence grows; when the facts show one does not apply, its owner closes the entry with the reason recorded.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the newest fact in the stem does to the uncertainty the entry was created to watch.
questions.correct_explanation: An emerging-risk entry exists to watch an uncertain threat; the final law settles that the rule does not reach a chain of 120 staff, so there is no risk left to track. The risk owner closes the entry with the reason recorded. Keeping it open for amendments is the runner-up: it feels prudent, but horizon scanning would catch any later change as a new signal, and stale entries blur the register.

wrong_explanations.A: A rating range expresses uncertainty about a live risk; the final law removes that uncertainty and shows the chain is outside its scope.
wrong_explanations.B: Holding the entry open for possible amendments keeps a risk that does not apply; horizon scanning would flag any later change as a new signal.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving it into the main profile treats it as a real, understood risk; the final law shows it does not apply to the chain.

tips: Eliminate: A rates a range for uncertainty the final law has removed, and D moves into the profile a risk that does not apply.
Final two: C beats B because the facts now show the risk does not apply; scanning catches later amendments, so an open entry only clutters the register.
Exam cue: an emerging risk is refined as evidence arrives, and that includes closing it, with the reason recorded, when evidence shows it does not apply.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Owner of a review of approvals
questions.question: At a construction contractor, the site manager who approves subcontractor invoices has been named owner of the control that reviews those approvals. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Move the review of invoice approvals to internal audit
options.B: Name the site manager's deputy as the review's control owner
options.C: Keep the site manager as owner, with the director countersigning
options.D: Make the finance controller the review's control owner

questions.key_concept: A control owner answers for a check working, so they must not own a check on their own work, and need authority to run it.
questions.pre_read: Read who does the work, who checks it, and what each person named in the options controls.
questions.correct_explanation: The review exists to catch wrong invoice approvals, so its owner must answer for it independently; a site manager cannot be accountable for checking their own approvals. A finance controller normally sits outside site operations and controls payment, so can own the review independently. Keeping the site manager with the director countersigning is the runner-up: it adds a second look, but the accountable owner is still the person whose work is checked.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit gives independent assurance; running a management control would have it audit its own work and leave the business with no owner.
wrong_explanations.B: The deputy reports to the site manager, so the review still sits inside the approving line it is meant to check.
wrong_explanations.C: A countersignature adds a second look, but the owner accountable for the review is still the manager whose approvals it checks.

tips: Eliminate: A hands a management control to internal audit, which must stay independent, and B leaves the review under the manager it checks, through a deputy.
Final two: D beats C because a countersignature adds oversight but leaves the conflicted manager accountable; a finance controller normally sits outside site operations and controls payment.
Exam cue: no one should own a check on their own work; an approver never owns the review of their own approvals, however many others sign.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Settings an AI tool applies itself
questions.question: A chip fabrication plant's AI tool adjusts etch-tool settings automatically between runs. Which control should the risk analyst recommend as BEST to stop a faulty adjustment from scrapping wafers?

options.A: Automatic rejection of settings outside engineering limits
options.B: Alerts to process engineers when wafer yield drops after a change
options.C: A log of each AI change for its control owner's review
options.D: Insurance the risk owner buys against scrapped wafers

questions.key_concept: To stop harm from an AI or automated output, validate the output before it acts; detective controls only find the damage afterward.
questions.pre_read: Note what the question asks the control to do, then sort each option by what it actually does.
questions.correct_explanation: The tool applies its settings with no person in between, so only a control that acts before a setting is used can stop a faulty one. Automatically rejecting settings outside engineering limits validates the output first, a preventive control. Yield alerts are the runner-up: they are fast detective controls, but by the time yield drops, wafers from that run are already scrapped, so they limit the loss rather than stop it.

wrong_explanations.B: Yield alerts detect a bad setting after wafers are processed; they limit how many lots are lost but cannot stop the first loss.
wrong_explanations.C: A log reviewed later is detective and slower still; the faulty setting has already run on the tools before anyone reads the entry.
wrong_explanations.D: Insurance transfers part of the financial loss; the wafers are still scrapped and faulty settings still reach the tools.

tips: Eliminate: C reviews a log after the setting has run, and D insures the loss instead of stopping it; neither acts before wafers are processed.
Final two: A beats B because the question asks to stop the loss; yield alerts are detective, so the wafers are already scrapped when they fire.
Exam cue: when an AI or automated output acts with no one in between, validate it against set limits before it is used; that check is preventive.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Alerts stop after a network change
questions.question: Since a network change last month, an airline maintenance shop's monitoring tool has logged no access alerts from one hangar that used to raise 40 a week. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Report the drop as an improvement in the hangar's controls
options.B: Compare the hangar's alerts with the same weeks last year
options.C: Have the control owner confirm the hangar's log feed works
options.D: Lower the hangar's alert thresholds to restore the usual volume

questions.key_concept: A sudden silence in monitoring data, especially after a change, is first checked as a possible data failure before it is read as good news.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else could explain the numbers before deciding what they say about the controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Alerts falling from 40 a week to none, right after a network change, more likely mean the hangar's logs stopped arriving than that its controls improved. Monitoring results count only once the data behind them is confirmed, so the first step is for the control owner to check the feed. Comparing with the same weeks last year is the runner-up: seasonal patterns move volumes, but they do not drop them to zero overnight.

wrong_explanations.A: Reporting the silence as an improvement credits the controls before anyone confirms the logs still arrive; a broken feed would look exactly the same.
wrong_explanations.B: A seasonal comparison explains gradual or recurring shifts; an abrupt fall to zero right after a network change points to the data, which is checked first.
wrong_explanations.D: Lowering thresholds tunes the rules to produce alerts again without knowing why they stopped; if no logs arrive, no threshold will fire.

tips: Eliminate: A treats silence as good news without checking the data, and D retunes alert rules before anyone knows why the alerts stopped.
Final two: C beats B because a drop to zero right after a network change points to a broken feed; seasonality does not empty a data source overnight.
Exam cue: when a monitoring measure suddenly goes quiet, confirm the data is still flowing and complete before reading the result as a change in risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-137 Section 3.6 (Review and Update the Monitoring Program and Strategy: the accuracy of measurements and the usefulness of collected data are reviewed, and collection found not useful is reconsidered); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.4 (Data Quality: a validation process checks the integrity, accuracy and structure of data before any analysis is done)

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Critical vendor in financial trouble
questions.question: A hotel group's reservations vendor, rated critical, has reported two years of losses and cut a third of its staff. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Get the contract owner to add service credits for outages
options.B: Have the service's business owner prepare an exit plan
options.C: Begin replacing the vendor, led by the service's business owner
options.D: Run a full on-site security review of the vendor's systems

questions.key_concept: When a critical vendor may fail, plan how the service would move or continue, in proportion to the dependence, before failure forces it.
questions.pre_read: Ask which risk the new facts raise, and which response fits its size and its timing.
questions.correct_explanation: Losses and deep staff cuts raise the chance that a critical vendor fails, and the group's exposure is how long reservations would stop. An exit plan, owned by the service's business owner, sets out data return, an alternative and the steps to move, so the group can act quickly if needed. Replacing the vendor now is the runner-up: it removes the dependence, but at full cost and disruption before the vendor has failed.

wrong_explanations.A: Service credits refund fees for missed service; a vendor that fails cannot pay them, and they do not keep reservations running.
wrong_explanations.C: Replacing a critical platform is costly and risky in itself; doing it before any failure is a large response to a risk an exit plan can contain.
wrong_explanations.D: A security review tests the vendor's controls, not its financial health or the group's ability to move the service if the vendor fails.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on credits a failing vendor cannot pay, and D reviews security when the new risk is the vendor's survival.
Final two: B beats C because an exit plan contains the risk at a fraction of the cost; replacing the vendor now pays the full price before any failure.
Exam cue: signs that a critical vendor may fail call for a ready exit or contingency plan, scaled to the dependence, rather than an immediate switch.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Actions scheduled easiest first
questions.question: A life insurer's ten actions against a data risk above appetite run easiest first, so claims database encryption, the biggest risk cut and dependent on nothing, comes last. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Track each action owner's progress against its due date
options.B: Replace the action owners with a single project manager
options.C: Add interim monitoring of the database by its control owner
options.D: Reorder the actions so the largest reductions come first

questions.key_concept: Bring a plan's largest risk reductions forward, subject to dependencies and resources, so exposure above appetite falls as early as possible.
questions.pre_read: Ask how long the exposure stays above appetite under this plan, and what keeps it there.
questions.correct_explanation: While the risk sits above appetite, every month the biggest cut waits is exposure the insurer need not carry; encryption depends on nothing, so it can start now. Reordering the actions by the risk each removes brings the risk down soonest. Interim monitoring is the runner-up: it helps when a long action cannot start sooner, but here it would watch a delay the plan itself created instead of removing it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tracking dates shows whether the plan keeps to schedule; a plan on schedule still leaves the largest exposure open until its final action.
wrong_explanations.B: Each action needs a named owner who can deliver it; one project manager in their place weakens accountability and still leaves encryption last.
wrong_explanations.C: Interim monitoring watches the database while encryption waits; when nothing blocks encryption, moving it forward reduces the exposure itself.

tips: Eliminate: A tracks dates in a badly ordered plan, and B swaps named action owners for one manager; neither changes when the biggest risk cut lands.
Final two: D beats C because encryption depends on nothing, so it can start now; interim monitoring only watches an exposure the plan's order prolongs.
Exam cue: in a risk action plan, check the order as well as the owners and dates; the biggest risk reductions go first unless a dependency or resource limit blocks them.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Insurance that excludes two plants
questions.question: A frozen food processor's ransomware risk at two plants, re-rated after its insurer excluded them over single-factor remote access, now exceeds appetite. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add multifactor remote access at the two plants
options.B: Buy a separate cyber policy for the two plants
options.C: Seek the risk owner's acceptance of the uninsured loss
options.D: Raise the insurance limit to take in the two plants

questions.key_concept: When a missing control both raises a risk and voids its insurance, treating that cause beats replacement cover that leaves likelihood unchanged.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each response would change: the chance of an attack, the money lost or neither.
questions.correct_explanation: Single-factor remote access causes both problems: it makes a successful ransomware attack on the two plants more likely, and it is why the insurer excluded them. Recommending multifactor remote access treats that cause: it lowers likelihood and may restore cover once the insurer confirms; the risk owner approves the response. A separate policy is the runner-up: it could shift part of the money lost, but it leaves the plants as easy to breach.

wrong_explanations.B: A separate policy, if any insurer offers one without multifactor access, shifts part of the money lost; the plants stay as easy to breach, and an attack could halt production.
wrong_explanations.C: The re-rated risk exceeds appetite, so it calls for treatment; accepting it instead would need the approval of whoever set appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: A higher limit raises the cover for insured losses; it does not override an exclusion, so the two plants stay uninsured.

tips: Eliminate: C seeks acceptance of a risk the re-rating put above appetite, and D raises a limit that cannot override the policy's exclusion.
Final two: A beats B because the missing control causes both the exposure and the exclusion; a new policy, if offered, pays only after an attack and leaves the plants easy to breach.
Exam cue: when one missing control both raises a risk and voids its cover, treating that cause beats buying replacement insurance.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Review that works from a system report
questions.question: Testing a card payments processor's chargeback review, the risk analyst found all 25 sampled cases properly reviewed; reviewers work only from a system-generated exception report. What should the analyst do FIRST before crediting the control?

options.A: Observe a reviewer working through today's exception report
options.B: Test the report's completeness against the chargeback records
options.C: Reperform the review for a sample of the listed cases
options.D: Ask the control owner how the report's rules were set

questions.key_concept: When a control works from a system report, test the report's completeness and accuracy; a perfect review of an incomplete list still misses cases.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the sample could not show about the control, given where the reviewers' work comes from.
questions.correct_explanation: The sample shows reviewers handled the cases the report listed, but the review can be no better than the report: cases its rules miss are never reviewed at all. Testing the report's completeness against the chargeback records closes that gap before the control is credited. Reperforming sampled reviews is the runner-up: it is strong evidence that listed cases were judged correctly, but it cannot reveal cases the report left out.

wrong_explanations.A: Observing one session shows how a reviewer works that day; like the sample, it starts from the report and cannot show what the report misses.
wrong_explanations.C: Reperformance checks the reviewers' decisions on listed cases; it is strong evidence of their quality, but it never reaches cases the report omits.
wrong_explanations.D: The owner's account of the rules is inquiry, the weakest evidence; it describes the report's design without showing that it captures every case.

tips: Eliminate: D relies on the owner's account, which is inquiry only, and A observes one session that starts from the same report.
Final two: B beats C because reperformance re-checks listed cases only; testing the report's completeness finds cases the review never sees.
Exam cue: when a control relies on system-generated information, test that information's completeness and accuracy as part of testing the control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5 Section 2.4.2 (Assessment Methods: examine, interview and test, with depth and coverage); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2 (Control Assessments)

Owner pattern: one option names an owner and it is an easy distractor (D: inquiry of the control owner), round 15 lone-owner ask. Neighbours checked (stems, keys and decoy families): crisc_d3_102 (population list supplied by the owner: check it against the deployment log; the closest lesson, but about the test population, not the control's own input; its decoy has the owner sign the list, ours asks how the rules were set), crisc_d3_149 (recalculate sampled discounts), crisc_d3_122 (reconciliation against a copy of itself), crisc_d3_134 (records made after the fact), crisc_d3_173 (rule with no cases), CISA d1_118 (sign-off on a daily exception report) and d1_152 (testing billing independently of system reports). questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Report limited to risks under treatment
questions.question: A city bus operator's board risk report lists only risks under treatment, so 14 risks their owners accepted never appear, three of them now near tolerance. What is the risk analyst's BEST change?

options.A: Have owners re-confirm their acceptances before each report
options.B: Report accepted risks when they breach tolerance
options.C: Add accepted risks to the report, showing each one's owner
options.D: Route each acceptance to the board for its approval

questions.key_concept: Accepting a risk does not take it out of view; leaders need accepted risks in the profile they oversee, especially those near tolerance.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the board can and cannot see from this report, and why that matters.
questions.correct_explanation: Acceptance keeps a risk, so it stays part of the profile the board oversees against appetite; three accepted risks near tolerance are exactly what leaders need to see before they breach. Adding accepted risks to the report, each with its owner, gives the board the whole picture. Having owners re-confirm acceptances is the runner-up: it keeps decisions current, but the board still never sees them.

wrong_explanations.A: Re-confirming keeps each acceptance current with its owner; the board's report still leaves out the 14 risks and the three near tolerance.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for a breach removes the warning; the board would learn of three risks near tolerance only after they cross it.
wrong_explanations.D: Owners may accept risks within their authority; sending every acceptance to the board overloads it and still does not show the profile.

tips: Eliminate: B reports accepted risks only after a breach, losing the warning, and D moves acceptances within owners' authority up to the board.
Final two: C beats A because the problem is what the board sees; re-confirmed acceptances that never reach the report still leave it blind.
Exam cue: accepted risk is still risk; keep it in monitoring and reporting, with its owner, so leaders see the full profile against appetite.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3 (Selection of Risk Response Types: senior leaders can be unaware of serious risks accepted by lower levels of management, so response decisions and trends are reported); NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Acceptance: exposure within risk tolerance is still reported, monitored and managed); ISACA Glossary (risk acceptance)

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Chief executive named on every risk
questions.question: A toy importer's register names its chief executive as owner of all 38 risks, including 30 low-rated departmental ones; none has had a decision in a year. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Set a review date for each risk with the chief executive
options.B: Give the risk team charge of the 30 low-rated risks
options.C: Make the leadership team jointly accountable for the 38
options.D: Move the 30 low-rated risks to their process owners

questions.key_concept: Risk ownership sits at the level that matches a risk's reach and rating; an owner too remote to decide leaves the risk unmanaged.
questions.pre_read: Count how many risks one person holds, and read what the record says about their decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: Ownership works only where someone decides, and one person holding 38 risks has decided none in a year. Low-rated risks confined to one department fall within its process owners' authority and budget, so moving them there puts decisions with the people running the work; the chief executive keeps the other eight and agrees the move. Review dates are the runner-up: they prompt the chief executive but leave all 38 with one remote owner.

wrong_explanations.A: Review dates prompt action, but all 38 risks still rest with one person who has decided none in a year and is far from the departments' work.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk team monitors and challenges risk; taking charge of business risks would leave it deciding responses it has no authority or budget to fund.
wrong_explanations.C: Joint accountability spreads ownership so thin that each member can wait for another; every risk needs one named person who answers for it.

tips: Eliminate: B hands business risks to the risk team, which monitors but cannot own them, and C makes a whole team jointly accountable, so no one person acts.
Final two: D beats A because the problem is ownership at the wrong level; review dates prompt one overloaded executive, while departmental risks belong with the managers who run that work.
Exam cue: match each risk owner to the risk's reach and rating; enterprise risks sit high, and a department's low-rated risks sit with the owner of the process they affect.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Different fix from the one agreed
questions.question: Facilities at a property management company want to close a logged issue on ex-tenants' live access fobs, using a manual purge in place of the agreed automatic deactivation. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Evaluate the risk the manual purge still leaves
options.B: Test the purge at the next scheduled control test
options.C: Close the issue on the action owner's report
options.D: Reject the manual purge on the risk owner's behalf

questions.key_concept: When a different fix replaces the agreed action, evaluate the risk it leaves before closing; the agreed action was a means, not the goal.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the original action was meant to achieve, and what each option would check before the issue closes.
questions.correct_explanation: The agreed action was a means to an end: stopping ex-tenants' fobs from opening doors. A manual purge may do that, but it relies on staff and leaves fobs live until each purge, so the analyst first evaluates the risk it leaves; the risk owner then decides on the changed action. Testing at the next scheduled control test is the runner-up: it shows later that the purge runs, while closure is sought now.

wrong_explanations.B: A later test may show the purge runs, but closure is sought now, and a run that works can still leave live fobs between lease end and purge.
wrong_explanations.C: An action owner's report is a claim, not evidence; closing on it skips any check that the substitute treats the issue's risk.
wrong_explanations.D: The analyst advises and the risk owner decides; rejecting the purge for the owner, before its risk is known, could also discard a workable fix.

tips: Eliminate: C closes the issue on the action owner's word, and D has the analyst reject the substitute for the risk owner before its risk is known.
Final two: A beats B because closure is requested now; a later test shows the purge runs, not whether a manual purge treats the risk enough.
Exam cue: when a fix differs from the agreed action, judge the substitute against the issue's risk before closing; the agreed action is a means, not the goal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-5 (Plan of Action and Milestones); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk: compliance, response effectiveness and risk-impacting changes)

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Tailoring COBIT 2019
questions.question: A regional blood service's risk analyst is helping tailor COBIT 2019 to the service. Which of the following is the PRIMARY input COBIT 2019 uses to set which objectives get priority?

options.A: Capability levels assessed for each current process
options.B: Baselines chosen from each system's impact level
options.C: Design factors such as strategy and threat landscape
options.D: CSF Tiers matched to current risk practices

questions.key_concept: COBIT 2019 is tailored through design factors, such as enterprise strategy and the threat landscape, which set objective priorities and target capability levels.
questions.pre_read: Place each option in the framework it comes from, then ask which one describes the enterprise itself.
questions.correct_explanation: COBIT 2019 is generic, so each enterprise tailors it: design factors describing its context, such as strategy, size, regulation and the threat landscape, set which of the 40 objectives get priority and what capability each should reach. Assessing current capability is the runner-up: COBIT uses it to measure how well processes perform and to find gaps once targets are set, but it does not decide which objectives matter.

wrong_explanations.A: Capability assessment measures how well processes perform today; it shows gaps against targets once priorities are set, not which objectives matter to this service.
wrong_explanations.B: Impact-level baselines come from NIST SP 800-53B, for selecting each system's security controls; they are not how COBIT is tailored.
wrong_explanations.D: Tiers belong to NIST CSF 2.0 and describe the rigor of cybersecurity risk practices; COBIT 2019 does not use them to tailor its objectives.

tips: Eliminate: B and D come from other frameworks: impact-level baselines are NIST SP 800-53B, and Tiers are NIST CSF 2.0.
Final two: C beats A because capability levels measure how well processes run; design factors describe the enterprise, and that context sets which objectives get priority.
Exam cue: frameworks are tailored to the enterprise, not adopted whole; in COBIT 2019 the tailoring inputs are the design factors.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Two checks on tax tables
questions.question: A payroll software vendor's tax tables pass an automated plausible-range check, then specialists compare each rate with the published one; the control owner proposes dropping that step. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Drop the manual step and rely on the automated range check
options.B: Keep the manual step after the automated range check
options.C: Narrow the automated ranges, then drop the step
options.D: Have internal audit decide whether to drop the step

questions.key_concept: Before dropping a control as a duplicate, compare what each one catches; checks that look alike often stop different errors.
questions.pre_read: For each check, ask which kind of wrong rate it would let through.
questions.correct_explanation: The two checks catch different errors: the range check stops implausible values, but a wrong rate that still looks plausible passes it, while the specialists' comparison with the published rate catches exactly that. They are layers, not duplicates, so the analyst advises keeping the comparison. Narrowing the ranges is the runner-up: tighter bands catch more slips, but a wrong rate inside the band still passes, and genuine rate changes would start failing the check.

wrong_explanations.A: The range check passes any wrong rate that still looks plausible; without the comparison, such errors reach every customer's payroll.
wrong_explanations.C: Tighter ranges catch more slips but still pass a wrong rate inside the band, and they would reject genuine changes when rates are revised.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit gives independent assurance and does not own this check; dropping it weakens the control, so the decision goes to the risk owner, informed by the analyst's comparison.

tips: Eliminate: A drops the only check that compares rates with the source, and D hands a control decision to internal audit, which gives assurance but does not own the check.
Final two: B beats C because tighter ranges still pass a wrong rate that looks plausible; only comparison with the published rate catches it.
Exam cue: before cutting a control as duplication, compare what each control catches; layers that look alike often stop different errors.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Damage recorded in two places
questions.question: A car rental firm's loss report adds branch repair records to the claims team's insurance files; the risk analyst finds 40% of repairs appear in both. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Report the totals to the risk owner, noting the overlap
options.B: Confirm each branch's repair records with the branch
options.C: Base the total on the claims team's insurance files
options.D: Match the two sources' records to single damage events

questions.key_concept: Fix fixable data flaws before the decision, such as a loss logged twice; state as limitations only gaps that cannot be closed in time.
questions.pre_read: Picture one damaged car and follow it through both sources into the total.
questions.correct_explanation: Adding the two sources counts every repair that also became a claim twice, so the report overstates damage losses and could steer spending toward the wrong risk. Matching the records to single damage events before totaling counts each loss once. Reporting the totals to the risk owner with the overlap noted is the runner-up: stating a limitation suits data that cannot be fixed in time, but these duplicates can be removed before anyone decides.

wrong_explanations.A: Stating a limitation fits gaps that cannot be closed in time; these duplicates can be matched now, so the risk owner would otherwise decide on an inflated figure.
wrong_explanations.B: Each branch's records may be right on their own; confirming them leaves the same repairs counted again through the claims files.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance files hold only damage that became a claim; dropping branch records loses repairs paid without one and understates the losses.

tips: Eliminate: B confirms branch records that are each right but still overlap the claims files, and C drops every repair that never became a claim.
Final two: D beats A because the duplicates can be removed now; a note on the overlap still leaves the risk owner reading an inflated total.
Exam cue: fix a data flaw before reporting when it can be fixed, such as one loss logged twice; a note on a limitation is for gaps that cannot be closed in time.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for an AI voice agent
questions.question: A call center outsourcer's AI voice agent can give callers wrong answers; operations propose the share of calls it closes without a human as the KRI. Which KRI should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Share of agent-handled issues raised a second time
options.B: Share of calls the agent closes without a human
options.C: Error rate found in the vendor's pre-launch tests
options.D: Number of complaints clients escalate about the agent

questions.key_concept: A KRI for an AI agent's wrong answers tracks an early live sign, such as issues raised a second time, not efficiency or complaints.
questions.pre_read: For each measure, ask whether it would move before clients feel the harm, and whether it tracks wrong answers at all.
questions.correct_explanation: A KRI should move before the harm lands. A caller who raises the same issue again is an early sign that the agent's answer failed, visible before complaints or client penalties, and it comes from the outsourcer's own call records. Escalated complaints are the runner-up: they relate directly to wrong answers, but they lag, arriving after clients are already unhappy, and many callers given a wrong answer never complain.

wrong_explanations.B: Closing calls without a human is a performance measure; it can rise while the agent keeps callers it answers wrongly, so it does not warn of the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: A pre-launch error rate is one past figure from the vendor's tests; it cannot show how the agent is answering live calls now.
wrong_explanations.D: Escalated complaints show real harm but arrive late, after clients are unhappy, and many callers given a wrong answer never complain.

tips: Eliminate: B is a performance measure that can rise while wrong answers grow, and C is a one-off vendor figure from before launch, not live monitoring.
Final two: A beats D because callers raise a failed answer again soon after, while escalated complaints arrive after the harm, and only some callers complain.
Exam cue: for an AI agent's error risk, prefer a live signal in your own records that moves before harm builds, over efficiency rates, vendor test scores or complaint counts.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Larger server plan with the same host
questions.question: A brewery is moving its online order system to a larger server plan with the same host; the change record shows none of the policy's reassessment triggers met. What is the risk analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Reassess the risk with its owner before the move closes
options.B: Note the change for the risk owner's next scheduled review
options.C: Increase the likelihood rating for the order system
options.D: Open a separate register entry for the move to a larger plan

questions.key_concept: Reassessment triggers set which changes need prompt review; a change that meets none is noted and covered at the next scheduled review.
questions.pre_read: Check what the stem says about the policy's triggers before deciding how much the change calls for.
questions.correct_explanation: Policy triggers mark the changes material enough to reassess at once; a like-for-like move to a larger plan with the same host meets none, so the risk keeps its rating and the change is noted for the risk owner's next scheduled review, the backstop. Reassessing with the owner before the move closes is the runner-up: it looks careful, but it spends effort on a change the policy's own criteria treat as immaterial.

wrong_explanations.A: Prompt reassessment is for changes that meet a trigger; this move meets none, so reassessing now, even with the owner, spends effort the policy reserves for material change.
wrong_explanations.C: No trigger is met and the host is the same, so nothing shows likelihood rising; a higher rating would record exposure with no evidence behind it.
wrong_explanations.D: A larger plan with the same host is a change to an existing system, not a new risk; a separate entry would log a routine change as a new risk.

tips: Eliminate: C raises a rating with no evidence the move changed the risk, and D records a routine server move as if it were a new risk.
Final two: B beats A because the policy's triggers define what needs reassessing now; a change that meets none waits for the scheduled review, the backstop.
Exam cue: not every change triggers reassessment; when a change meets none of the policy's triggers, note it for the next scheduled review.
