questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. How far ahead to scan
questions.question: Which of the following should MOST guide how far ahead the risk analyst sets a timber mill's horizon scanning to look?

options.A: The time frame used to rate the register's risks
options.B: The look-ahead that peer timber firms use
options.C: The life of the assets and plans it informs
options.D: The review cycle each risk owner prefers

questions.key_concept: Horizon scanning should look as far ahead as the investments and plans it informs, beyond the time frame used to rate known risks.
questions.pre_read: Ask what horizon scanning is for, and whose decisions need its warnings in time.
questions.correct_explanation: Horizon scanning exists to warn decisions in time, so it should look as far ahead as the commitments it informs; a mill's equipment, sites and timber supply plans run for decades, and changes such as new forestry rules or shifting fire seasons can arrive within that life. The time frame for rating register risks is the runner-up: it suits risks already known, but scanning that stops there misses the changes that later commitments will meet.

wrong_explanations.A: Ratings use a set time frame for known risks; scanning only that far misses changes that would arrive within the life of long-term commitments.
wrong_explanations.B: Peers' look-ahead reflects their own plans and assets; the mill's scan should match its own commitments rather than copy another firm's choice.
wrong_explanations.D: Owners' preferred review cycles set how often they meet, not how far ahead the scan must look to warn their decisions in time.

tips: Eliminate: B copies peers' look-ahead instead of the mill's own commitments, and D mixes up how often owners meet with how far the scan must reach.
Final two: C beats A because the rating time frame covers known risks; scanning must reach as far as the plans and assets that today's decisions commit to.
Exam cue: set a scan's reach by the life of the decisions it informs; long-lived assets and plans need a long view.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Pay grades nobody can explain
questions.question: A tea exporter's vendor-supplied AI grades leaf photos to set growers' pay and speed peak buying, but no one can explain a grower's grade; the risk exceeds appetite. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Publish a plain summary of how the model sets grades
options.B: Make the vendor liable for the business owner's dispute losses
options.C: Stop using AI grading and return to manual grading
options.D: Have human graders review disputed grades and give reasons

questions.key_concept: If an AI decision cannot be explained to those it affects, human review giving reasons on challenge treats the risk and keeps the benefit.
questions.pre_read: Note what the affected growers cannot get today, and what the business would give up under each response.
questions.correct_explanation: Human graders re-checking disputed lots keep the AI's speed for most purchases while giving each grower who disputes a grade a reason they can question, which is exactly what an unexplained decision lacks. A plain summary of the model is the runner-up: it tells growers how grading works in general, but not why their own lot received its grade, so disputes stay unresolved.

wrong_explanations.A: A general description says how the model works, not why one lot got its grade, so a grower disputing their pay still has no answer.
wrong_explanations.B: A liability clause may cover some costs, but the growers' grievance and the exporter's accountability for paying them fairly stay with the business.
wrong_explanations.C: Dropping AI grading gives up the faster peak buying the business relies on, when a targeted control can treat the harm.

tips: Eliminate: B shifts some cost but leaves accountability and the unexplained grades with the exporter, and C gives up the peak-season speed the business needs when a control can treat the harm.
Final two: D beats A because a disputed grade needs a reason for that decision; a model summary explains how grading works, not why this lot got its grade.
Exam cue: when people cannot get an AI decision explained, prefer a human route that gives reasons for individual decisions over general model descriptions, contracts or dropping the tool.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Two vendors on one host
questions.question: An airport ground handler chose separate vendors for baggage reconciliation and load planning to avoid one failure stopping both; due diligence finds both run in one cloud region. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Re-rate each vendor's outage scenario with the shared region noted
options.B: Rate a regional outage halting both services as one scenario
options.C: Record both vendors as owners of the shared hosting risk
options.D: Require the load-planning vendor to move to another region

questions.key_concept: Services that share a hidden host can fail together, so the practitioner first rates their joint outage as one scenario before treatments are weighed.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the shared region does to the reason the two vendors were chosen, and what must be known before any fix.
questions.correct_explanation: The services were split so one failure would not stop both, and the shared region undoes that: one regional outage would halt baggage checks and load planning together, delaying departures. Rating that joint event as one scenario shows the real exposure before the owner weighs any treatment. Re-rating each vendor is the runner-up: it notes the region, but two separate ratings still understate an outage that strikes both services at once.

wrong_explanations.A: Two separate ratings each count one service lost; they miss the larger impact when one regional outage stops both services at the same time.
wrong_explanations.C: Vendors run the services, but the risk stays with the ground handler's business owner; outsourcing the hosting does not hand over ownership of the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving a vendor is a treatment chosen before the joint exposure is rated; it may cost more than the risk warrants, and the owner decides.

tips: Eliminate: C hands ownership to vendors, though outsourcing keeps the risk with the business, and D picks a treatment before the shared exposure is rated.
Final two: B beats A because concentration is about failing together; one joint scenario shows the combined impact that two separate vendor ratings understate.
Exam cue: vendors chosen for diversity can share a fourth party, such as a cloud provider in one region; when due diligence finds it, first rate their joint failure as one concentration scenario.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Exemption claimed for new panels
questions.question: A grower's risk owner exempted greenhouse climate panels, which cannot hold accounts, from the sign-in standard after a risk assessment; irrigation staff claim it covers new fertilizer-dosing panels. What is the risk analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Have the fertilizer panels' owner raise their own request
options.B: Check the new panels against the exemption's stated reason
options.C: Add the new panels to the existing exemption's asset list
options.D: Log the new panels as non-compliant in the issues tracker

questions.key_concept: An exemption covers only the assets whose risk was assessed; a new asset needs its own request, even when the reason is the same.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the exemption's approval rested on, and whether anyone assessed that for the new panels.
questions.correct_explanation: An exemption covers the assets whose risk was assessed and approved. Dosing panels do a different job from climate panels, so their risk without sign-in differs, and their owner should raise a request that the analyst can assess and the appropriate risk owner can decide. Checking the panels against the stated reason is the runner-up: the same reason can apply while the risk it leaves is quite different.

wrong_explanations.B: Sharing the reason shows the panels might qualify, but the exemption rests on the climate panels' assessed risk; dosing panels need their own assessment and owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Listing the panels under the old exemption extends an approval to assets nobody assessed, with no decision from the owner of their risk.
wrong_explanations.D: A shortfall the business wants to keep is a deviation to assess and decide through a request, not an issue to log and chase.

tips: Eliminate: C extends an approval to assets no one assessed, and D logs a wanted deviation as an issue instead of sending it through the request process.
Final two: A beats B because an exemption follows the assessed risk, not only the stated reason; dosing panels need their own assessment and decision.
Exam cue: a deviation covers only the scope that was assessed; new assets, even with the same reason, go through their own request.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Seals on card readers
questions.question: How should a parking operator's risk analyst BEST classify the tamper-evident seals its collection staff check on pay-machine card readers?

options.A: A preventive control that stops a reader being opened
options.B: A deterrent control that discourages tampering with a reader
options.C: A corrective control that restores a tampered reader
options.D: A detective control that reveals a reader was opened

questions.key_concept: Tamper-evident seals are detective: they do not stop tampering but reveal it when staff inspect them.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the seal does at the moment someone opens a reader, and what the staff checks add.
questions.correct_explanation: A tamper-evident seal does not stop anyone opening a reader; it breaks when the reader is opened, and staff checking it at collection find the break. Its value comes from that discovery, so it is detective, and it reduces harm only if staff act on a broken seal. Deterrent is the runner-up: a visible seal may discourage some attempts, but discouragement is not why staff are told to check it.

wrong_explanations.A: A seal is easily broken and does not block access to the reader; it shows afterward that someone opened it.
wrong_explanations.B: A visible seal may put some people off, but the control works through staff finding broken seals, which is detection, not deterrence.
wrong_explanations.C: Corrective controls restore or repair after an event, such as replacing a reader; a seal only shows that tampering happened.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an easily broken seal as a barrier, and C confuses showing that tampering happened with repairing a tampered reader.
Final two: D beats B because the seal works through staff finding a break at each check; any discouragement is a side effect.
Exam cue: classify a control by how it acts on the event; 'tamper-evident' means it reveals tampering after it happens, so it detects rather than prevents.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Review run at three warehouses
questions.question: A cold-storage firm's risk ratings credit its manual daily review of freezer alarm logs at three warehouses, but the risk analyst tested it only at the largest. What is the analyst's BEST next step?

options.A: Extend the largest warehouse's result to the other two
options.B: Confirm the other warehouses use the same review procedure
options.C: Test a sample of the review at the other two warehouses
options.D: Rely on each site control owner's own test of the review

questions.key_concept: A manual control's operating test at one site does not show it works at others, where different people run it.
questions.pre_read: Note who performs the review at each site, and what a test at one site can and cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: A manual review depends on the people at each site, so a clean result at the largest warehouse says little about how staff at the other two perform it. Testing a sample at each of the other warehouses gives evidence for the ratings that credit the review there. Confirming the same procedure is the runner-up: it shows the review is designed alike at each site, not that it operates there.

wrong_explanations.A: One site's result shows how that site's staff run the review; manual controls vary with people and workload, so it does not carry to other sites.
wrong_explanations.B: A shared procedure shows the review is designed the same way everywhere, but design is not operation; staff at each site may still skip or rush it.
wrong_explanations.D: Owners testing their own control give self-assessment, useful for monitoring but weaker than the ratings need; they rely on testing by someone who does not run the control.

tips: Eliminate: A carries one site's result to sites where different people run the review, and D relies on owners testing their own control.
Final two: C beats B because a common procedure shows the same design, while only a sample at each site shows the review operates there.
Exam cue: a manual control is only as reliable as the people running it at each location; one site's test does not show it operates at the others the ratings credit.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Measuring a plan's progress
questions.question: Eight of ten actions in a print works' ransomware action plan are done; the two left are expected to cut most of the exposure. Which progress measure should the risk analyst report as BEST?

options.A: Risk reduced so far against the risk owner's target
options.B: Share of actions the action owners have marked complete
options.C: Number of ransomware incidents since the plan began
options.D: Effort each action owner has logged against the plan

questions.key_concept: A risk action plan's progress is the risk reduced toward its target, not the share of actions complete.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each measure would tell the risk owner about the exposure still left.
questions.correct_explanation: Progress on a risk action plan is how far the risk has fallen toward the target set for it, based on validated actions. Here 80% of actions are done, but the two left carry most of the reduction, so the risk is still well above target. The share of actions completed is the runner-up: easy to count, but it would tell the owner the plan is nearly done while most of the exposure remains.

wrong_explanations.B: Counting completed actions treats each as equal; with the two biggest left, 80% complete would hide that most of the exposure remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Few incidents during the plan may be luck; a lagging count does not show how far the planned controls have cut the exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: Logged effort measures what the plan has consumed, not what it has achieved; much effort can leave the risk barely lower.

tips: Eliminate: C is a lagging count that a quiet period can flatter, and D measures effort spent rather than what the plan achieved.
Final two: A beats B because action counts weigh every task alike; risk reduced against the target shows that the biggest cuts are still to come.
Exam cue: report a plan's progress in risk terms, the reduction achieved against its target, not in tasks done, effort spent or quiet periods.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Rating scale changed between reports
questions.question: An engineering consultancy changed its likelihood scale this quarter, moving six risks down a band with no change in exposure; its board dashboard now shows them improving. What is the risk analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Add each risk owner's note that the exposure is unchanged
options.B: Remove the trend arrows from the six rescaled risks
options.C: Restate the risks' earlier ratings on the new scale
options.D: Report each risk on the scale its owner prefers

questions.key_concept: Readers act on a dashboard's visuals; when a scale change creates a false trend, put the data on one basis, not only annotate it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a board member scanning the dashboard would conclude, and which option changes that conclusion.
questions.correct_explanation: A trend means something only when every period is rated on the same scale. Re-rating the earlier quarters on the new scale shows the six risks as flat, which is the truth, and keeps the dashboard comparable from now on. Owners' notes are the runner-up: they flag the problem, but the arrows and colors still show an improvement that never happened, and board members act on the visuals.

wrong_explanations.A: A note admits the change, yet the dashboard's arrows and colors still show six risks improving; readers scanning the visuals take the false trend.
wrong_explanations.B: Removing the arrows takes trend away instead of correcting it; the board loses the history it needs to see risks moving.
wrong_explanations.D: Ratings on different scales cannot be compared or combined; one approved scale applies across the register and the report.

tips: Eliminate: B removes trend instead of correcting it, and D lets owners choose scales, so ratings can no longer be compared.
Final two: C beats A because restating puts every period on one scale, so the trend is true; a note leaves a false improvement on the chart.
Exam cue: when a dashboard shows a false trend, change what is plotted, such as restating earlier periods on one scale; a note beside the chart leaves readers acting on the picture.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Which signal is emerging
questions.question: Which of the following is BEST recorded by a desalination plant's risk analyst as an emerging risk, rather than rated on the usual scale?

options.A: A vendor patch for a flaw in the plant's control software
options.B: Lab research on a new way to spoof membrane-pressure sensors
options.C: A final water-quality reporting rule the plant must meet
options.D: A carrier's set date for closing the 3G network its sensors use

questions.key_concept: A risk is emerging when its likelihood and effect are not yet understood, not merely because it lies in the future.
questions.pre_read: For each item, ask how much is already known about whether and how it would affect the plant.
questions.correct_explanation: An emerging risk is one whose likelihood and effect are not yet understood well enough to rate normally. A new lab technique for spoofing pressure sensors may or may not work against the plant's equipment, so it is recorded with stated uncertainty, an owner and a short review date. The 3G closure is the runner-up: it lies ahead, but its date and the affected sensors are known, so it is rated and treated now.

wrong_explanations.A: A released patch addresses a known flaw in software the plant runs; it is a current risk to rate and fix, not an uncertain new one.
wrong_explanations.C: A final rule is a known requirement with a known date; the plant rates its compliance risk now on the usual scale.
wrong_explanations.D: The closure lies in the future, but its date and the affected sensors are known, so its impact can be rated and planned for now.

tips: Eliminate: A is a known flaw with a patch already out, and C is a settled requirement; both can be rated now on the usual scale.
Final two: B beats D because a risk is emerging when its effect is still uncertain, not merely because it lies ahead; the 3G date and its effect are known.
Exam cue: uncertainty, not distance in time, marks an emerging risk; a dated, well-understood change is a known risk to rate and treat now.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286A Rev. 1 Section 2.2.5 (Recording Identified Risks: developing or emerging risks are yet to be fully defined but might disrupt enterprise objectives in the future); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: uncertainty can be communicated by giving ranges of values rather than single values)

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Credited review nobody runs
questions.question: A pallet maker's kiln-tampering risk rating credits a remote-access review whose named owner, the IT manager, never knew of it; no review has run. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Confirm the IT manager as the review's control owner
options.B: Run the review within the risk team until one is named
options.C: Remove the review and its owner from the register
options.D: Report to the risk owner that the review never ran

questions.key_concept: A credited control that never ran leaves current risk above its rating; the owner of that risk hears first, before the control's ownership is fixed.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the register says from what has actually happened, and ask who relied on the difference.
questions.correct_explanation: The kiln risk's rating counts a review that has never operated, so today's exposure is higher than the rating shows. The risk owner relies on that rating and must decide the interim response and see that the review gets a willing owner. Confirming the IT manager is the runner-up: an owner who never knew of the control cannot simply be confirmed, and the risk owner would still not know the rating was wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: The review does need an owner, but naming someone who never agreed fixes the record, not the gap, and the risk owner still does not know the rating is overstated.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk team oversees and challenges controls; running a first-line review would leave it checking its own work and still unowned by the business.
wrong_explanations.C: Deleting the entry hides that a credited control never ran; the risk it was meant to reduce is unchanged and the risk's owner is still unaware.

tips: Eliminate: B has the risk team run a first-line control, which is not its role, and C deletes the record of a credited control while the exposure it was meant to cut stays.
Final two: D beats A because the risk owner relies on a rating that counts this review; they must learn it never ran before the owner gap is filled.
Exam cue: when validation finds a credited control that never ran, the owner of the risk it protects learns the rating is overstated before anyone settles who owns the control.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Exception sought for a past deviation
questions.question: A medical laundry's standard requires locked wash-cycle records; line 4's have been editable since spring, and its risk owner asks for an exception dated from then. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Log the past gap as an issue, apart from the owner's request
options.B: Make the exception effective from spring, with compensating checks
options.C: Report the risk owner's breach of the standard to the board
options.D: Rate the past months as low risk, since no harm is known

questions.key_concept: An exception approves a deviation before it happens; a deviation already run without approval is logged as an issue, not covered by a backdated exception.
questions.pre_read: Note when the deviation began and when approval is being sought.
questions.correct_explanation: An exception approves a deviation before it happens; months already run with editable records were an unapproved gap. Logging that gap as an issue keeps it visible and prompts a check of whether cycle records from then were changed, while the owner's request is assessed for the time ahead. Making the exception effective from spring is the runner-up: compensating checks help from now on, but dating it back hides the past gap.

wrong_explanations.B: Compensating checks cut risk from now on, but dating the exception back makes months of unapproved editing look approved and hides whether past cycle records were changed.
wrong_explanations.C: A deviation is logged, assessed and fixed through the issue process; nothing in the stem calls for the board, and blaming the owner shows nothing about what the gap exposed.
wrong_explanations.D: No known harm is not evidence of low risk; the stem shows no check of whether wash records from those months were changed, which the logged issue would track.

tips: Eliminate: C takes the gap to the board as a personal breach with no basis for escalating, and D rates the months low because no harm is known, without checking the records.
Final two: A beats B because an exception approves a deviation in advance; months already run stay on record as an issue, and the request covers the time ahead.
Exam cue: an exception looks forward; a deviation found already running is logged as an issue, even when an exception will cover it from now on.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Paper approvals moving to a workflow
questions.question: An industrial bakery will move recipe approvals from paper batch sheets, checked by hand at several steps, to a new workflow its control owner approved for next month. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Test the new workflow's approvals once it has gone live
options.B: Rely on the control owner's approval of the new design
options.C: Trace the checks in the paper process into the workflow
options.D: Keep the paper checks running beside the new workflow

questions.key_concept: When a manual process moves into a system, checks done by hand can quietly drop out; trace each into the new design before go-live.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the paper process did that nobody may have written down, and when a missing check is cheapest to find.
questions.correct_explanation: Paper processes hold checks that live in people's habits, and a new workflow can drop them unnoticed. Tracing each paper check into the workflow before go-live shows which are kept, changed or lost, so gaps are fixed in the design, not after a bad batch. Relying on the control owner's approval is the runner-up: the owner is accountable for the control, but an approval given without that trace can cover a design missing a check.

wrong_explanations.A: Testing after go-live finds a dropped check only once batches have run without it; the gap is cheaper to find in the design.
wrong_explanations.B: The owner's approval matters, but it is only as good as what was compared; without tracing the old checks it can approve a workflow that silently drops one.
wrong_explanations.D: A parallel run can surface differences, but only after batches run; it adds complexity and does not show which paper checks the design omits.

tips: Eliminate: A waits until after go-live to find a missing check, and D surfaces differences only once batches run, without showing which checks the design omits.
Final two: C beats B because the owner's approval is only as good as the design it covered; trace the old checks first so nothing is lost unnoticed.
Exam cue: when a manual process is automated, first trace each manual check into the new design; controls that lived in people's habits are the first to disappear.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-4 (Impact Analyses); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-8(7) (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles | Reduced Complexity: running older and newer technologies side by side during a transition temporarily increases system complexity)

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Independent tests a regulator requires
questions.question: A sugar refinery's regulator now requires independent assurance that its batch-traceability control works; the second-line risk team, which advised on the control's design, has tested it so far. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep the testing in the risk team, apart from operations
options.B: Ask internal audit to include the control in its testing
options.C: Rely on the control owner's signed statement that it works
options.D: Rely on the vendor's SOC 2 report held by the system owner

questions.key_concept: Independent assurance comes from testers with no part in a control's design or operation, usually internal audit; second-line testing is objective, not independent.
questions.pre_read: Note what independence asks of a tester, and what part each candidate has already played in the control.
questions.correct_explanation: Independent assurance needs testers outside management with no part in designing or running the control. Internal audit gives that assurance and sets its own plan, so the analyst asks it to cover the control. Continued testing by the risk team is the runner-up: second-line testing is objective but sits within management, and this team also advised on the design, so it would partly be judging its own advice.

wrong_explanations.A: Apart from operations, the risk team is objective, but it sits within management and advised on the design, so its tests are not independent.
wrong_explanations.C: A control owner's statement is self-assessment by the person accountable for the control; it is not a test, let alone an independent one.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor's SOC 2 report covers the vendor's controls over its service, not whether the refinery's traceability control works as the refinery runs it.

tips: Eliminate: C is the owner vouching for their own control, and D covers the vendor's service rather than how the refinery's own control works.
Final two: B beats A because second-line testing is objective but not independent, and this team advised on the design; internal audit is the independent line.

Exam cue: when a requirement says independent, look past objectivity to where the tester sits and what it helped design; second-line testing sits within management, and design advice adds self-review.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2(1) (Control Assessments | Independent Assessors: assessors are free of conflicts over the development, operation or management of what they assess and do not assess their own work); NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 3.1.1 (Notional Risk Management Roles: the auditor provides independent and formal verification of the achievement of enterprise objectives and the application of ERM processes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B3.2 (Design and Operating Effectiveness Testing: owner-only tests are self-assessment; for independent assurance, internal audit tests, as the second line is objective, not independent). Round 18, 12 Nov 2026: original scenario (a sugar refinery whose regulator now requires independent assurance over a batch-traceability control the second line has been testing), written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Rare on one barge, fleet of 60
questions.question: An inland barge operator rates a grounding from a navigation-system fault as rare, about 2% a year, on each of its 60 barges. How should the risk analyst BEST rate the fleet-wide risk?

options.A: Rate it on the chance that at least one barge grounds
options.B: Carry each barge's rare rating into the fleet view
options.C: Add the 60 barges' scores into one total for the risk owner
options.D: List the 60 barge risks separately, each with its owner

questions.key_concept: When an event can happen at many units, the chance it happens at one or more is far higher than at any single unit.
questions.pre_read: Think about how a small chance at one barge behaves across the whole fleet over a year.
questions.correct_explanation: Each barge's 2% chance is small, but across 60 barges the chance that at least one grounds in a year is about 70% if faults strike independently (1 minus 0.98 to the 60th power), so the fleet should expect a grounding most years. Rating the fleet risk on that combined chance shows the real exposure. Carrying the rare rating over is the runner-up: it is right for any one barge but understates the fleet's exposure.

wrong_explanations.B: Rare is right for one barge, but the fleet view must show how 60 small chances combine into a grounding in most years.
wrong_explanations.C: Ratings are ordinal labels, so totaling them gives a number with no meaning; 60 rare scores added together do not express a likelihood.
wrong_explanations.D: Sixty separate rare lines each look minor, so the fleet view hides that a grounding somewhere in the fleet is likely in most years.

tips: Eliminate: C totals ordinal scores, which gives a meaningless number, and D splits the risk into 60 minor lines, so the combined exposure never shows.
Final two: A beats B because many small independent chances combine; the fleet's chance of at least one grounding is far higher than one barge's.
Exam cue: when one rare event can happen at many units, rate the combined risk on the chance it happens somewhere, not on one unit's rating.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for allowlisting on plant PCs
questions.question: Which of the following should a salt producer's risk analyst propose as the BEST key control indicator for the application allowlisting on its plant PCs?

options.A: Share of launches the tool has blocked
options.B: Ransomware incidents on plant PCs since the tool went live
options.C: The control owner's own score for the tool's health
options.D: Share of plant PCs with the tool set to block

questions.key_concept: A KCI tracks a control's own health, such as the share of assets where it is fully in force, not the activity it records.
questions.pre_read: For each measure, ask whether it would move if the control itself weakened.
questions.correct_explanation: A KCI shows whether a control is in place and working where it is relied on. Allowlisting protects a PC only while it is set to block; switched to log-only, perhaps after it stops a needed program, it records but stops nothing. The share of PCs set to block shows that weakening directly. The share of launches blocked is the runner-up: it tracks activity, so a fall could mean fewer attempts or fewer PCs blocking.

wrong_explanations.A: Blocked launches track activity, not health: a fall could mean fewer attempts or more PCs switched to log-only, so the share cannot show the control weakening.
wrong_explanations.B: Incidents show a failure after the harm is done; a KCI should show the control weakening before an incident happens.
wrong_explanations.C: An owner's own score is self-assessment that may rest on opinion; a KCI needs measured data that shows the control's state.

tips: Eliminate: B counts incidents after the harm, and C rests on the owner's own opinion rather than measured data about the control.
Final two: D beats A because the setting shows where the control is in force, while blocks rise and fall with attempts as well as with the tool's health.
Exam cue: for a KCI, pick a measure that falls when the control weakens, such as coverage or the share set to enforce, not one that tracks the activity it meets.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Licenses suspended before expiry
questions.question: A security guarding company's automated check flags guards whose licenses have expired, using dates in its HR system; the licensing authority can also suspend licenses before expiry. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Run the expiry check more often against HR dates
options.B: Have the control owner add the authority's suspension data
options.C: Require guards to report any suspension to their branch
options.D: Present the check's clean results as evidence of license compliance

questions.key_concept: Automated monitoring sees only the data it reads; when an event never reaches that data, feed the check the authoritative source for it.
questions.pre_read: Ask which events the check can see from the data it reads, and which never reach it.
questions.correct_explanation: The check reads only expiry dates held by HR, so a guard the licensing authority suspends still passes and can be deployed. Adding the authority's suspension data lets the check see the event it now misses, and the control owner, accountable for the check, makes that change. Requiring guards to report suspensions is the runner-up: it helps, but it relies on people who lose shifts by reporting, so suspensions can still go unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Running the same check more often still reads only HR expiry dates, so a suspended guard passes however often it runs.
wrong_explanations.C: Self-reporting helps, but it relies on guards who would lose shifts by reporting; the check still cannot see a suspension nobody reports.
wrong_explanations.D: Clean results mean no expired dates in HR records; they say nothing about suspensions, so presenting them as compliance overstates the control.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats a check that cannot see suspensions, and D presents results that never covered suspensions as evidence of compliance.
Final two: B beats C because monitoring should read the authoritative source for the event it must catch; self-reports depend on people with a reason to stay silent.
Exam cue: when a monitoring check misses a type of event, feed it the authoritative source for that event rather than relying on self-reports or running it more often.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. AI screener reported in model scores
questions.question: A hearing-aid clinic chain's board report on its AI hearing-test screener shows accuracy, AUC and drift scores, and directors ask whether patient harm is within appetite. What is the risk analyst's BEST change?

options.A: Explain each model score in plain words for directors
options.B: Add the vendor's published scores for this model
options.C: Show the referrals the screener misses against appetite
options.D: Add the business owner's view that it is within appetite

questions.key_concept: To judge AI harm against appetite, directors need it measured in the appetite's terms, such as patients missed; clearer model scores cannot supply that.
questions.pre_read: Ask what directors need to judge against appetite, and whether each change gives it to them.
questions.correct_explanation: Directors judge risk by its effect on objectives, so AI risk goes to the board in business terms: here, people with hearing loss whom the screener fails to refer, the patient harm the appetite speaks to. Model scores describe the tool, not that harm. Explaining each score in plain words is the runner-up: directors would understand the scores, but an AUC or drift value still does not say how many people the screener misses.

wrong_explanations.A: Plain words help directors read the scores, but the scores still describe the model; they do not show how many people the screener misses.
wrong_explanations.B: Vendor scores are more model metrics, from the vendor's tests rather than this chain's patients; they still do not show harm against appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: An owner's opinion is not evidence of harm; directors need the measured effect on patients set against appetite, not reassurance.

tips: Eliminate: B adds more model metrics from the vendor's own tests, and D swaps measured results for the business owner's opinion.
Final two: C beats A because directors judge risk by its effect on people and objectives; explained model scores still describe the tool, while missed referrals show the harm.

Exam cue: when directors ask whether an AI system's harm is within appetite, give them the harm in the terms the appetite uses; explaining model scores more clearly still leaves that comparison undone.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. One budget, two risks
questions.question: An iron foundry's operations director, owner of two risks, plans to spend the $80,000 budget on the casting-scrap risk, within appetite, not the furnace-outage risk above appetite. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Direct the budget to the furnace-outage risk first
options.B: Fund the casting-scrap control the risk owner chose
options.C: Split the budget evenly across scrap and furnace-outage risks
options.D: Reassess both risks before spending any of the budget

questions.key_concept: Treatment money goes first to risks above appetite; a risk already within appetite is normally accepted and monitored rather than given new spending.
questions.pre_read: Place each risk against appetite before weighing what the money should buy.
questions.correct_explanation: Responses follow from comparing each risk with appetite. The furnace-outage risk is above appetite and needs treatment; the casting-scrap risk is already within it, so the director can accept and monitor it rather than fund a new control. Funding the casting-scrap control is the runner-up: the risk owner does choose responses, but the analyst's advice should show that this choice leaves the risk above appetite unfunded.

wrong_explanations.B: The director decides, but advice that backs spending on a risk within appetite leaves the furnace-outage risk above appetite untreated.
wrong_explanations.C: An even split diverts money to a risk already within appetite and may leave the furnace-outage risk short of what brings it within appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Both risks are already rated against appetite; reassessing without new facts delays the decision without changing where the money should go.

tips: Eliminate: C diverts part of the money to a risk already within appetite, and D reassesses risks already rated, delaying the decision with no new facts.
Final two: A beats B because a risk within appetite is normally accepted and monitored; the analyst advises funding the risk above appetite, and the director still decides.
Exam cue: when one budget must cover several risks, rank them by how far they sit above appetite; a risk within appetite usually needs monitoring rather than new spending.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Drift checks on a vendor model
questions.question: A data broker's data science team runs drift checks on a vendor's identity-matching model; the sales director owns its risk. Which of the following should the risk analyst propose as the checks' MOST appropriate owner?

options.A: The vendor, as the supplier of the matching model
options.B: The sales director, as owner of the matching risk
options.C: The data science manager, as head of that team
options.D: The risk team, as overseer of risk monitoring

questions.key_concept: A vendor builds the model, but checks on it are owned inside, usually by the manager whose team runs them; the business keeps the risk.
questions.pre_read: Separate who owns the risk from who answers for the check working, and notice whose team does the work.
questions.correct_explanation: A control owner is accountable for a control working, usually the manager whose team runs it. The data science team runs the drift checks, so its manager answers for them and gives results to the sales director. The sales director is the runner-up: they own the matching risk and rely on the checks, but owning a risk does not make them the owner of a check another team runs.

wrong_explanations.A: The vendor built the model but does not run these checks; the broker relies on the model, so it owns the checks with a manager it can hold to account.
wrong_explanations.B: The sales director keeps the risk and receives the results, but cannot answer for checks that another team runs and directs.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk team oversees and challenges monitoring; owning a first-line check would leave it overseeing its own work.

tips: Eliminate: A hands the broker's own check to the outside vendor whose model it watches, and D gives a first-line check to the risk team that oversees it.
Final two: C beats B because an AI check is owned like any control, by the manager who directs it; the sales director keeps the risk and acts on the results.
Exam cue: an AI model's drift checks are a control like any other: owned inside the enterprise, whoever built the model, while the business owner of the risk acts on their results.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Parts from an unauthorized reseller
questions.question: A dental laboratory plans to buy controller boards for its milling machines from an online reseller the maker does not authorize, at 40% below the maker's price. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Take the reseller's warranty as cover for the asset owner
options.B: Test each board against the maker's specifications on arrival
options.C: Have the risk owner insure the machines against board faults
options.D: Buy the boards through the sales channels the maker approves

questions.key_concept: For hardware, buying through channels the maker authorizes keeps counterfeit or altered parts out; tests, warranties and insurance only back that up.
questions.pre_read: Ask where a bad part would enter the lab, and which option stops it there rather than after.
questions.correct_explanation: Boards from a reseller the maker does not authorize may be counterfeit, used or altered, and a bad controller can spoil restorations or open a path into the lab's network. Buying through authorized channels, a trusted distribution route, keeps such parts out at the source. Testing each board on arrival is the runner-up: it catches boards that fail, but a counterfeit or altered board can work normally and pass a functional test.

wrong_explanations.A: A warranty replaces boards that fail; it does nothing to keep a counterfeit or altered board out of the machines.
wrong_explanations.B: Testing helps, but a counterfeit or altered board can pass a functional check; trusted channels keep such parts out at the source.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance pays for some losses; it does not stop an altered board reaching the machines, and the lab still answers for the restorations it ships.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a warranty that only replaces failed boards, and C insures losses, which moves cost while the counterfeit risk stays.
Final two: D beats B because trusted distribution keeps counterfeit parts out at the source; arrival tests can miss an altered board that works normally.
Exam cue: for hardware supply chain risk, buy through channels the maker authorizes; inspection, warranties and insurance back that up but do not replace it.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Relying on a shared control
questions.question: A home care agency's new care-records app will rely on head office's shared access-review control, set for office staff; carers using the app join and leave every week. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Record the shared review as inherited by the app
options.B: Compare the shared review's settings with the app's access risk
options.C: Build a separate access review for the app, run by its owner
options.D: Scope access review out of the app's control baseline

questions.key_concept: A shared or inherited control counts for a new system only once its settings are shown to fit that system's risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether a control built for one group of users does the same job for another.
questions.correct_explanation: A shared control protects a new system only if its settings fit that system's risk. A review set for office staff may run too rarely to catch carers who leave each week, so the analyst first compares its settings with the app's access risk. Recording it as inherited is the runner-up: sharing a control is sound and saves cost, but only once it is shown to fit.

wrong_explanations.A: Sharing controls saves cost, but recording the review as inherited before checking its settings credits protection the app may not get.
wrong_explanations.C: Comparing first may show the shared review only needs a setting changed for the app's users; building a separate one now duplicates effort.
wrong_explanations.D: Access review still applies to the app; scoping out a needed control removes protection rather than tailoring it.

tips: Eliminate: C builds a duplicate review before checking whether the shared one can be adjusted, and D scopes out a control the app still needs.
Final two: B beats A because a shared control counts for a new system only when its settings fit that system's risk; check the fit before recording the inheritance.
Exam cue: when a system relies on a shared or inherited control, check the control's settings against that system's risk before crediting it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Section 2.3 (Control Implementation Approaches: an inheriting entity examines a common control's parameters before assuming it mitigates system-specific risk); NIST SP 800-53B Section 2.4 (Tailoring Control Baselines: align the baseline with organizational risk and record a risk-based justification for each decision)

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Diverted packs put back
questions.question: A poultry processor's line system diverts packs whose label does not match the product, but any line worker can return diverted packs to the line unrecorded. Which change should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have a supervisor sign off each diverted pack's return
options.B: Test the label check with deliberately mislabeled packs
options.C: Retrain line workers on handling diverted packs
options.D: Send counts of diverted packs to the line's control owner

questions.key_concept: Analyze what happens after a control fires: an override or return path with no approval or record can undo a check that works.
questions.pre_read: Follow a mislabeled pack from the moment it is diverted, and find where it could still reach a customer.
questions.correct_explanation: The label check works, but its exception path does not: anyone can put a diverted pack back unrecorded, so a mislabeled pack can still ship. Requiring a supervisor's sign-off before a diverted pack returns closes that path and leaves a record. Testing with mislabeled packs is the runner-up: it proves the check diverts them, but the failure comes after diversion, which such tests never exercise.

wrong_explanations.B: Test packs prove the check diverts mislabeled packs; they say nothing about packs pushed back afterward, which is where this control fails.
wrong_explanations.C: Training tells workers the rule, but the return path stays open to anyone, unrecorded, so one mistake or shortcut still ships a mislabeled pack.
wrong_explanations.D: Counts of diverted packs show the check firing, not which packs went back; returns are unrecorded, so the counts cannot show them.

tips: Eliminate: C trains workers while the unrecorded return path stays open, and D reports diversions, which cannot show the unrecorded returns.
Final two: A beats B because the weakness is in how diverted packs are handled; test packs prove detection, which already works.
Exam cue: when analyzing a control, follow what happens after it fires; an override or return path with no approval or record can undo a check that works.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Plan that cannot reach its target
questions.question: A coworking operator's draft plan for its above-appetite risk of members reaching each other's laptops over Wi-Fi lists one action: reminding members to enable firewalls. What should the risk analyst add as MOST important?

options.A: Proof that the reminder reached each member
options.B: Alerts on traffic passing between members' laptops
options.C: A members' agreement clause on laptop security, set by the risk owner
options.D: Isolation of members' devices from one another on the network

questions.key_concept: Before a plan is signed, check that its actions can bring the risk to target; a reminder cannot remove a network exposure.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the plan, carried out in full, would leave the risk where it needs to be.
questions.correct_explanation: A plan must be able to bring its risk to target. A reminder depends on every member acting and cannot stop one laptop reaching another, so the plan as drafted would end with the risk still above appetite. An action isolating members' devices removes the exposure itself. Traffic alerts are the runner-up: they reveal attacks between members, but only once they start, and the network still lets laptops reach each other.

wrong_explanations.A: Proof the reminder reached members validates the one action, but that action cannot bring the risk within appetite, so proving it moves nothing toward target.
wrong_explanations.B: Alerts detect attacks between members after they begin; laptops can still reach each other, so the exposure stays above appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: A clause shifts blame to members, not the exposure; the operator still runs the network and keeps the risk.

tips: Eliminate: A proves an action was done that cannot reach the target anyway, and C shifts responsibility to members while the operator keeps the risk.
Final two: D beats B because a plan needs an action that brings the risk to target; isolation removes the exposure, while alerts only spot attacks once begun.
Exam cue: before a plan is signed, ask whether its actions, done in full, bring the risk to target; reminders and alerts do not remove a technical exposure.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Scans entered late
questions.question: A florist wholesaler's KRI for time flowers spend out of cold storage uses warehouse scan times, but 30% of scans are entered hours after the boxes move. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Correct the late scan times by hand before each KRI report
options.B: Have the scan data's owner make staff scan as boxes move
options.C: Flag the scan delays to the risk owner in each report
options.D: Suspend the KRI until every scan time is accurate

questions.key_concept: A recurring data flaw is fixed where the data is captured, by the data's owner; correcting each report by hand treats the symptom.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the bad figures come from, and whether any fix offered stops them coming back.
questions.correct_explanation: The KRI is only as good as the scan times it reads, and late scans misstate how long boxes sat out of cold storage. The flaw recurs at capture, so the lasting fix is there: the data's owner, who answers for its quality, has staff scan as boxes move. Hand correction is the runner-up: it patches each report, but the true move times are unknown, so corrections are guesses and the flaw returns every period.

wrong_explanations.A: The true move times are unknown, so hand corrections are estimates, and the same flaw returns in every report while its cause is untouched.
wrong_explanations.C: Stating a limit suits a gap that cannot be closed; this flaw can be fixed at capture, and flagging it each time leaves the KRI unreliable.
wrong_explanations.D: Suspending the KRI leaves the risk unwatched while nothing fixes the data; the cause still needs fixing at capture.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps reporting a known flaw that could be fixed, and D leaves the risk unwatched while no one fixes the data.
Final two: B beats A because a recurring flaw is fixed where data is captured, by its owner; hand corrections guess at unknown times in every report.
Exam cue: fix a one-off data error before reporting, but when the same flaw recurs, have the data's owner fix it at capture; cleaning each report treats the symptom.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. No loss history anywhere
questions.question: A toll road operator's risk analyst records an emerging risk: drivers spoofing its new connected-vehicle toll tags, with no losses seen anywhere. Which of the following BEST informs its first scenario?

options.A: Loss figures from the toll-evasion cases that the operator handles today
options.B: The tag maker's assurance that its tags resist spoofing
options.C: A workshop of tag engineers, outside experts and the risk owner
options.D: Penetration test results for the operator's billing website

questions.key_concept: With no loss history anywhere, an emerging risk's first scenario comes from structured judgment by people who know the technology and the objectives.
questions.pre_read: Ask which source actually knows something about this new attack, given that nobody has lost money to it yet.
questions.correct_explanation: Nobody has lost money to tag spoofing yet, so there is no data to rate it from. A structured workshop brings engineers who know the tags, outside experts who know the attacks and the risk owner who knows the objectives at stake, and they can frame how spoofing would work and its effects as ranges. Current evasion figures are the runner-up: they are real data, but they record a different attack.

wrong_explanations.A: Evasion cases are real data on unpaid tolls, not on how spoofing works or spreads; used alone, they rate the new attack as the old one.
wrong_explanations.B: The maker's own claim is not independent and says nothing about attackers' methods or the operator's exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: Billing-website tests cover a different system; they say nothing about whether the new tags can be spoofed.

tips: Eliminate: B rests on the tag maker's own claim, and D tests a different system from the tags at risk.
Final two: C beats A because, with no losses anywhere, structured judgment from engineers, outside experts and the risk owner frames the new attack; evasion records describe a different one.
Exam cue: when an emerging risk has no loss history, build its first scenario in a structured workshop of people who know the technology and the objectives, stated as ranges.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. AI coding errors closed one by one
questions.question: A market research firm's issues log holds 14 cases of its AI tool miscoding open survey answers; each was closed once analysts fixed that client's report. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Track them as one finding with its cause and an agreed plan
options.B: Escalate the 14 cases to the AI vendor's account owner
options.C: Close each new case once the report's owner signs it off
options.D: Stop using the AI tool to code open survey answers

questions.key_concept: Repeated issues closed one at a time hide their cause; one finding for them lets the cause be analyzed and fixed under an agreed plan.
questions.pre_read: Look at how the log has closed these cases so far, and ask what that way of closing them cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: Fourteen miscodings closed one at a time hide a pattern: each fix repairs one report while the cause stays. One finding lets the firm analyze why the tool miscodes and agree a plan with the tool's owner, tracked to validated closure. Escalating to the vendor is the runner-up: the vendor may help, but the cause is not yet known and may lie in the firm's own coding frames.

wrong_explanations.B: The vendor may be part of the fix, but sending it the cases before the cause is known skips the firm's own analysis, owner and plan.
wrong_explanations.C: An owner's sign-off is a statement, not evidence, and closing each case on its own keeps hiding the repeated pattern and its cause.
wrong_explanations.D: Dropping the tool gives up its benefit before anyone knows why it miscodes; the cause may be fixable at modest cost.

tips: Eliminate: C closes each case on an owner's sign-off, a statement rather than evidence, and D drops the tool before anyone knows why it miscodes.
Final two: A beats B because repeats of one issue become one finding, with the cause analyzed and an agreed plan; escalating to the vendor picks a fix before the cause is known.
Exam cue: when the same issue keeps being logged and closed, look for the option that treats the repeats as one problem with a cause, an owner and a plan, not another one-off fix.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator green through the losses
questions.question: A car-sharing service's KRI for app outages, peak server load, stayed green all year while four outages stranded members, none of them load-related. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Lower the red threshold on the server-load KRI
options.B: Add a second KRI that counts each outage members report
options.C: Report the KRI's green year to the risk owner as stable
options.D: Replace the KRI with one that moved before the outages

questions.key_concept: A KRI that stays green through losses with other causes is off their path; replace it, since retuning its threshold cannot see them.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether this measure could ever have changed before these particular outages.
questions.correct_explanation: A KRI earns its place by moving before the loss. Server load stayed green because none of the four outages came from load, so the measure never sat on their path. Replace it with one that would have moved first, tested against the four outages' causes. Lowering the threshold is the runner-up: it makes the same measure noisier, but it still cannot see outages that load does not cause.

wrong_explanations.A: A lower threshold flags more busy periods, but none of the outages came from load, so the measure still misses their causes.
wrong_explanations.B: A count of outages members report is lagging: it records the harm after it happens and gives no early warning.
wrong_explanations.C: Green all year beside four outages shows the KRI is blind to their causes, not that the risk is stable.

tips: Eliminate: B counts outages after members report them, a lagging measure, and C reads a green KRI as a stable risk despite the four outages it missed.
Final two: D beats A because the measure never sat on the outages' path; a lower threshold makes it noisier, not predictive of outages that load does not cause.
Exam cue: when a KRI stays green while its risk occurs, ask whether the losses ran through what it measures; if not, replace it rather than retune its threshold.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Self-ratings an audit contradicted
questions.question: A garden center chain's store managers self-assess their stores' IT controls; all 30 rated till logins effective, weeks before an audit found shared logins at nine stores. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Train store managers on the self-assessment's rating criteria
options.B: Have control owners attach records behind their self-ratings
options.C: Move the self-assessment to the risk team for every store
options.D: Track the share of stores returning self-assessments on time

questions.key_concept: Control self-assessment ratings are claims; asking control owners to attach evidence lets the risk function challenge them.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the self-ratings said with what the audit found, and ask what the ratings were missing.
questions.correct_explanation: Self-assessment builds ownership, but a rating with nothing behind it is a claim: all 30 stores rated logins effective while nine shared them. Asking the store managers, as control owners, to attach evidence for each rating, such as user lists, turns claims into something the risk team can challenge and spot-check. Training on the criteria is the runner-up: it helps managers rate consistently, but their ratings would still rest on their word.

wrong_explanations.A: Training helps managers apply the criteria, but the ratings would still be unsupported claims that the risk team cannot check.
wrong_explanations.C: The risk team facilitates and challenges self-assessment; rating the stores' controls itself takes over the first line's work and weakens ownership.
wrong_explanations.D: A return rate shows managers filled in the form, not that their ratings are right; all 30 returned ratings, and nine were wrong.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the first line's self-assessment to the risk team, and D measures whether forms come back, not whether the ratings are true.
Final two: B beats A because evidence lets each rating be checked; training improves how managers rate but leaves the ratings as unsupported claims.
Exam cue: self-assessment results are claims until evidence backs them; prefer the option that makes ratings checkable over one that improves how people rate but leaves nothing to check.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (control risk self-assessment); NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5 Section 2.4.2 (Assessment Methods: examine, interview and test, with depth and coverage)

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Cheaper tool that needs new staff
questions.question: A bicycle maker's risk owner favors a $30,000 tool over a $70,000-a-year managed service, each bringing design-file theft within appetite; the tool needs two new analysts to run. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Fund both options to leave the least possible residual risk
options.B: Choose the managed service yourself, on the business's behalf
options.C: Give the risk owner both options' full costs, staff included
options.D: Support the risk owner's choice of the cheaper $30,000 tool

questions.key_concept: Responses are compared on their full cost over their life, staffing included; the practitioner gives the owner those figures and the owner decides.
questions.pre_read: Add up what each option costs once it is running, beyond the day it is bought.
questions.correct_explanation: Cost-benefit counts what an option costs to buy and to run. The tool looks cheaper, but two new analysts may cost more each year than the whole service, and that changes which option meets appetite at the lower total cost. The analyst sets out both full costs; the owner still decides. Supporting the owner's choice is the runner-up: the owner does decide, but on figures that leave out the tool's largest cost.

wrong_explanations.A: Either option alone brings the risk within appetite; funding both adds reduction the business does not need at the full cost of the second option.
wrong_explanations.B: The analyst advises; choosing for the business takes the risk owner's decision, even when the service may be the better buy.
wrong_explanations.D: The owner decides, but backing a choice made on purchase price leaves out the analysts' running cost.

tips: Eliminate: A pays for two options when either meets appetite, and B has the analyst choose the response, a decision that belongs to the risk owner.
Final two: C beats D because a cost-benefit choice needs each option's full cost, staff included; backing the owner's choice on purchase price leaves out the tool's biggest cost.
Exam cue: compare responses on what they cost to buy and to run, then let the risk owner choose; a low purchase price can hide the larger cost of staffing.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Office baseline for plant-floor panels
questions.question: A bottling plant plans to apply its office IT baseline, including sign-in lockout, to filling-line operator panels. Which of the following should the risk analyst recommend as the BEST basis for their controls?

options.A: An operational technology overlay tailored to the filling lines
options.B: The office baseline with sign-in lockout removed from the panels
options.C: The office IT baseline, applied to the panels as written
options.D: The security settings the panel vendor ships as defaults

questions.key_concept: A control baseline for operational technology starts from an overlay tailored to that environment, then is tailored further, not from office settings.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each basis was designed for, and whether that matches a production line.
questions.correct_explanation: Plant-floor systems put safety and continuous operation first, so office settings can harm them: an operator locked out during a fault could stop a line. An OT overlay, such as the one in NIST SP 800-82, tailors the whole baseline for that environment, keeping each control's intent where possible, and the plant tailors it further. Removing lockout alone is the runner-up: it fixes the one problem seen and leaves the rest unchecked.

wrong_explanations.B: Dropping lockout fixes one known clash, but other office settings, such as automatic updates, may also disrupt the line; an overlay tailors them all.
wrong_explanations.C: Office settings assume office priorities; on a line, lockout or automatic updates can halt production or delay operators during a fault.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor defaults are set for easy setup, not from the plant's risk, and can leave default passwords in place.

tips: Eliminate: C applies office settings as written to a line where lockout can stop operators, and D relies on vendor defaults that are not set from the plant's risk.
Final two: A beats B because an overlay tailors every control for the plant floor; removing lockout fixes the one clash seen and leaves the rest unchecked.
Exam cue: when a control catalog meets a different environment, such as plant-floor OT, start from an overlay built for it and tailor further, rather than fixing settings one at a time.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 4.3.3 (Select: overlays such as the OT overlay in Appendix F give tailored baselines that are starting specifications for OT and reduce ad hoc tailoring); NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Appendix F (OT Overlay: for AC-7, operators of continuously running systems stay logged on, so logon-attempt limits apply to accounts not needed for continuous operation)

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. New control after one run
questions.question: A nursing home operator's new monthly access review passed its design walkthrough and has run once, with no failure or change. What is the risk analyst's BEST next step on its operating effectiveness?

options.A: Test its operation now, sampling the one run completed so far
options.B: Credit its operation on the strength of the walkthrough
options.C: Have the control owner certify that the review operates
options.D: Test its operation at the scheduled point, after more runs

questions.key_concept: Operating effectiveness needs enough runs to sample; a new control is credited for design, then tested for operation at its scheduled point.
questions.pre_read: Count how many times this control has actually run, and ask what that many runs can show.
questions.correct_explanation: Operating effectiveness means a control works consistently over a period, so it needs enough runs to sample. A monthly review that has run once has shown its design, and one clean run proves little; with no failure or change to act on, the operating test belongs at its scheduled point, once several runs exist. Testing the one run now is the runner-up: it is evidence, but a sample of one cannot show consistent operation.

wrong_explanations.A: One run is evidence, but a sample of one cannot show the review works consistently; crediting operation on it overstates the control.
wrong_explanations.B: A walkthrough shows design and implementation; it says nothing about whether the review keeps running correctly month after month.
wrong_explanations.C: A control owner's statement is not test evidence; an owner certifying their own control gives no independent basis for credit.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a design walkthrough as proof of operation, and C rests credit on the control owner's own statement rather than test evidence.
Final two: D beats A because operating effectiveness needs runs over a period to sample; one clean run cannot show consistency, and nothing has failed that calls for testing early.
Exam cue: a new control shows its design at once and its operation over time; with no failure or trigger, its operating test waits for its scheduled point.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. High pass rate, top risk exposed
questions.question: A microfinance lender's risk committee report says 94% of tested controls passed; the failures include both controls over its top-rated risk, mobile loan fraud. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST change?

options.A: Report the pass rate for each business unit too
options.B: List each failed control with its owner and fix date
options.C: Show the failures against the risks they leave exposed
options.D: Exclude failed controls that their owners are already fixing

questions.key_concept: Control test results are reported against the risks they protect, so a high overall pass rate cannot hide failures behind a top risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the committee can decide from a pass rate, and what that figure cannot show it.
questions.correct_explanation: A 94% pass rate tells the committee little when the failures sit on the controls behind its top risk. Showing failures against the risks they leave exposed lets members see that mobile loan fraud has lost both its controls and decide what to do. Listing each failure with its owner and fix date is the runner-up: owners need that action list, but it does not show the committee which risks are exposed.

wrong_explanations.A: Splitting the pass rate by unit still averages over controls; the two failures behind the top risk stay hidden in the figures.
wrong_explanations.B: Owners need the action list, but the committee decides on risk; a list of failed controls does not show which risks lost protection.
wrong_explanations.D: Failures being fixed still leave their risks exposed until the fixes work; dropping them hides the top risk's lost controls from the committee.

tips: Eliminate: A is still an aggregate rate across many controls, split by unit, and D drops failures already being fixed, hiding exposure that stays until the fixes work.
Final two: C beats B because the committee needs failures shown by the risks they expose; an owner-and-date list suits the owners managing the fixes.
Exam cue: an overall pass rate averages away failures that cluster on one risk; set results against the risks they protect so a concentrated gap stands out.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Plan signed by the team doing the work
questions.question: A pet food maker's IT manager drafted and signed off the action plan for the recipe-system tampering risk, which the production director owns; work starts Monday. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Sign the plan as owner of the risk management process
options.B: Have the risk owner approve the plan before work starts
options.C: Get each action owner to sign the plan as well
options.D: Track the plan's actions against their due dates from Monday

questions.key_concept: A risk action plan is approved by the risk owner before work starts; those who draft or run it cannot approve it for them.
questions.pre_read: Note each person named in the stem and what each one has authority over.
questions.correct_explanation: The production director owns the tampering risk, so they decide whether the plan's target, cost and dates are acceptable; the IT manager runs the work but cannot approve treatment of a risk they do not own. The analyst gets the owner's approval before work starts. Tracking from Monday is the runner-up: tracking matters, but it would monitor a plan nobody with authority over the risk has agreed.

wrong_explanations.A: Owning the risk process does not give the analyst authority to approve how a business risk is treated; that belongs to the risk owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Action owners commit to their actions, but their signatures do not approve the plan's target, cost or dates for the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tracking is the analyst's job once the plan is agreed; starting it now monitors a plan the risk owner has not approved.

tips: Eliminate: A has the analyst approve a business risk's treatment, and C adds action owners' signatures, which commit to tasks but do not approve the plan.
Final two: B beats D because a plan needs the risk owner's approval before work starts; tracking a plan signed by IT alone monitors work nobody with authority has agreed.
Exam cue: a risk action plan is approved by the owner of the risk it treats; the people who draft or run the work cannot approve it on that owner's behalf.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Owners silent after being named
questions.question: A driving school chain's senior management named owners for 30 new register risks a month ago; none of the owners has opened or confirmed their entries. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the 30 owners to confirm they accept the role
options.B: Train the 30 owners on the duties of a risk owner
options.C: Record the risk team as interim owner of the 30 risks
options.D: Report the 30 unconfirmed risks to the board

questions.key_concept: Ownership takes hold when the named owner confirms the role; the risk analyst checks this with the owners before training or escalating.
questions.pre_read: Note what the owners have and have not done since they were named.
questions.correct_explanation: Senior management named the owners, but ownership is confirmed when each named person accepts it, and a month of silence suggests some may not know or agree. Asking them to confirm is the first validation step, and it surfaces anyone who disputes the assignment so it can go back to senior management. Training is the runner-up: it helps owners act later, but it does not show that any of them has accepted the role.

wrong_explanations.B: Training explains the duties but gets nobody to take them on; until the owners confirm, the register still shows names, not accountable owners.
wrong_explanations.C: The risk team supports owners but should not own business risks, even for a while; doing so hides the ownership gap instead of closing it.
wrong_explanations.D: Going to the board skips the owners and the senior managers who named them; the owners are asked to confirm first.

tips: Eliminate: C has the risk team own business risks, and D takes an ownership gap to the board before the owners or senior management have dealt with it.
Final two: A beats B because ownership is validated by the named owner's own confirmation; training helps owners act but does not show anyone has accepted the role.
Exam cue: when named owners have not responded, confirm the role with each before training, relying on them or escalating; owners who respond but misread the role need teaching.
