questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Processing moved after the report period
questions.question: A commodity broker's settlement vendor moved processing to a new data center three months after its clean SOC 2 Type 2 report's period ended. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the business owner rely on the report's clean result
options.B: Get the vendor's written statement on controls at the new data center
options.C: Take out insurance cover approved by the risk owner
options.D: Ask the vendor for independent assurance on the new data center

questions.key_concept: An assurance report covers only the locations and period it tested; a later move outside them needs new independent evidence.
questions.pre_read: Compare when and where the report's testing took place with what the vendor has changed since.
questions.correct_explanation: An assurance report counts only for the locations and period it tested, so a clean report on the old site does not show controls working at the new one. The analyst recommends obtaining independent assurance covering the new data center through the vendor's relationship owner. The vendor's written statement is the runner-up: it is quick and on record, but it is the vendor vouching for itself, not tested evidence.

wrong_explanations.A: The report tested the old site before the move, so its clean result does not cover processing at the new data center.
wrong_explanations.B: A vendor's letter can bridge a short gap when nothing has changed, but this site is new; the vendor vouching for its own untested controls cannot show they work.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance may cover some losses, but it gives no evidence about the new site's controls and leaves accountability with the broker.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a report that tested a site the vendor has left, and C buys insurance, which shifts some cost but shows nothing about controls.
Final two: D beats B because independent assurance tests the new site's controls; the vendor's own statement about the site is unverified and cannot show its controls work.
Exam cue: read an assurance report for the sites and dates it tested; a vendor change outside them needs fresh independent evidence, not the old report or a promise.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Product chosen before the risk
questions.question: An avionics maker's engineering director wants to buy a $400,000 data-loss prevention suite after a vendor demonstration; the register has no entry for design theft. Which of the following should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Get the risk owner's budget approval for the suite
options.B: Analyze the risk to the designs and its main causes
options.C: Analyze the suite's features against two rival suites
options.D: Pilot the suite on the design servers to judge it

questions.key_concept: Controls are selected from an analyzed risk and its causes; a product is weighed only once the risk it should treat is understood.
questions.pre_read: Ask what has to be known before any control, bought or built, can be chosen.
questions.correct_explanation: Control selection starts from an analyzed risk: how designs could be stolen, how likely and damaging that is, and what drives it. Only then can the analyst judge whether a data-loss suite, or something cheaper, treats those causes in proportion to the risk. Comparing the suite with rivals is the runner-up: it looks methodical, but it assumes a data-loss suite is the answer before anyone knows what the risk needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Approving the budget commits $400,000 to a control before anyone knows whether it addresses how designs are actually at risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Comparing products picks the best suite, not whether a suite is the right response; it starts from the tool instead of the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: A pilot implements the control before the risk is analyzed, so there is nothing to judge its fit against.

tips: Eliminate: A commits the budget before the risk is known, and D pilots the control, implementing it before any analysis.
Final two: B beats C because controls are chosen from the analyzed risk and its causes; comparing suites assumes a suite is the answer before the risk shows what is needed.
Exam cue: when a product is proposed before the risk is in the register, analyze the risk and its causes first; product comparisons come after.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Tracing report figures
questions.question: Which of the following BEST lets a label-printing firm's risk analyst trace any figure in its risk report back to where it came from?

options.A: Copies of past risk reports kept on file
options.B: Sample checks of the report's figures against their source records
options.C: A data dictionary of the figures' sources, formulas and owners
options.D: Sign-off of the report by the risk owners it covers

questions.key_concept: A data dictionary records each figure's source, formula and data owner, so any reported number can be traced back.
questions.pre_read: Separate options that record where data comes from from those that check or approve it.
questions.correct_explanation: Tracing a reported figure needs a standing record of where each one comes from: its source system, how it is calculated and who supplies the data. A data dictionary gives that for the whole report, so anyone can follow a number back. Sample checks are the runner-up: they test whether some figures match their sources, but they rely on knowing those sources and cover only the figures sampled.

wrong_explanations.A: Old reports show what was reported before, not which system or calculation produced a figure.
wrong_explanations.B: Sampling checks the accuracy of a few figures; it cannot trace figures outside the sample and needs the sources recorded first.
wrong_explanations.D: Owners' sign-off shows they read the report, not where its figures came from or how they were calculated.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps old reports, which show history rather than origin, and D records the owners' sign-off, which shows review, not where figures came from.
Final two: C beats B because a data dictionary documents the source and formula of every figure; sampling tests a few figures against sources it must already know.
Exam cue: traceability comes from documenting each measure's source, formula and data owner; validation checks then test figures against that record.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Admin-rights indicator as staff grow
questions.question: A data center's admin-rights misuse KRI, the share of accounts with admin rights, fell from 4% to 3% while admin accounts rose from 20 to 30. Which KRI should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Number of accounts holding admin rights
options.B: Share of accounts with admin rights, shown by site
options.C: Breaches traced to misused admin rights
options.D: Admin-rights requests approved by system owners

questions.key_concept: When each item is its own path to harm, count the items; a share of a growing base can fall while the exposure rises.
questions.pre_read: Work out whether the risk grows with the number of items or with their share of a total.
questions.correct_explanation: Each admin account is a path to misuse, so exposure grows with how many there are, not with their share of all accounts. Here the share fell only because staff numbers grew, while admin accounts rose by half; a count shows that rise. The share by site is the runner-up: it adds detail, but each site's figure still shrinks as headcount grows, even while admin accounts multiply.

wrong_explanations.B: Splitting the share by site still divides admin accounts by headcount, so staff growth keeps hiding growth in admin rights.
wrong_explanations.C: Breaches are counted after misuse has happened; a KRI should warn while the exposure is building.
wrong_explanations.D: Approvals measure how busy the request process is, not how many admin accounts exist or whether they are still needed.

tips: Eliminate: C counts breaches after the misuse, a lagging measure, and D counts approvals, an activity of the request process rather than the exposure.
Final two: A beats B because exposure here grows with each admin account; a share divided by headcount falls as staff grow, even while admin accounts multiply.
Exam cue: for an exposure KRI, count items that are each a path to the risk event, as a share can fall while the base grows; use a rate when exposure scales with volume.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Rising overrides of an AI model
questions.question: A gas utility's field supervisors override 22% of its AI model's leak-survey rankings, up from 5% six months ago; the data science lead wants to retrain the model. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Report the overrides to the board as a model failure
options.B: Test the model's accuracy on its original test data
options.C: Investigate why overrides rose, with the model's owner
options.D: Schedule retraining of the model on recent survey data

questions.key_concept: A rising rate of people overruling an AI model is a signal to analyze with its owner before a fix such as retraining is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the trend proves for certain and what it leaves unexplained.
questions.correct_explanation: A rising override rate shows supervisors disagree with the model more often, but not who is right: the model may have drifted, or supervisors may be overriding out of habit or for reasons the model cannot see. Investigating the rise with the model's owner finds the cause and lets the owner choose the response. Retraining now is the runner-up: it may prove necessary, but it fixes the model before anyone knows it is at fault.

wrong_explanations.A: A rising override rate shows more disagreement, not that the model has failed; reporting it to the board as a failure overstates it and bypasses the model's owner.
wrong_explanations.B: Old test data shows how the model performed when it was built, not why supervisors reject its rankings today.
wrong_explanations.D: Retraining assumes drift is the cause; if supervisors are overriding for other reasons, a retrained model leaves the real cause in place.

tips: Eliminate: A reports the overrides to the board as a model failure, overstating a monitoring signal and bypassing the owner, and B tests the model on old data that cannot explain today's overrides.
Final two: C beats D because the override trend must be explained before a fix is chosen; retraining assumes the model, not the supervisors' practice, is what changed.
Exam cue: a rising rate of people overruling an AI tool is a monitoring signal to explain with its owner, not proof that the model or the people are wrong.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Early research before a board decision
questions.question: A snack maker's board decides next week on buying packaging lines their maker manages remotely; the risk analyst's scan found lab research on attacks via such remote access. What is the analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Rate the attacks as a high risk for the plant's risk owner
options.B: Drop the research as too early to bear on the board's decision
options.C: Have the lines' business owner add remote-access terms to the contract
options.D: Add the research, and what remains unknown, to the board's decision paper

questions.key_concept: An emerging risk that bears on a pending decision is reported to the decision makers before they commit, with its uncertainty stated.
questions.pre_read: Note who is about to decide what, and when.
questions.correct_explanation: An emerging risk matters most while a choice is still open: the board decides next week, so it needs the research and its uncertainty in front of it. It can then ask for contract terms, tests or a staged rollout. Adding remote-access terms is the runner-up: they may well be wise, but setting them before the board has weighed the risk chooses a response for the decision makers.

wrong_explanations.A: Lab research shows an attack is possible, not how likely it is here; rating it high treats an uncertain risk as certain.
wrong_explanations.B: Early signals are what horizon scanning is for; dropping this one leaves the board deciding without a risk the scan has found.
wrong_explanations.C: Contract terms may help, but setting them before the board sees the risk chooses a response on the decision makers' behalf.

tips: Eliminate: A rates lab research as a known high risk, overstating it, and B drops the research, so the scan's finding never reaches the decision.
Final two: D beats C because the board is about to commit and needs the uncertain risk in front of it; contract terms are one response it may then choose.
Exam cue: when an emerging risk bears on a pending decision, report it to the decision makers before they commit, saying what is known and what is not.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Control owner sent the board summary
questions.question: A hospice operator's IT manager owns the backup and access controls over patient records but receives only the board's quarterly risk summary, which rates both controls amber. What is the risk analyst's BEST change?

options.A: Add the board's appetite statement to the risk summary
options.B: Send the IT manager the test results and remediation tasks
options.C: Copy the board's risk summary to the patient-records risk owner
options.D: Show both controls as red in every report to the board

questions.key_concept: Control owners need test results and remediation tasks for their controls; a board summary rating tells them something is wrong, not what to fix.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the person in the stem has to do and what that job needs to know.
questions.correct_explanation: Each report should carry what its reader must act on. The IT manager owns the controls and fixes them, so they need the test results behind the amber ratings and the remediation tasks, not a board summary that only says amber. Copying the summary to the risk owner is the runner-up: the risk owner should see the risk, but the same summary still gives nobody the detail needed to fix the controls.

wrong_explanations.A: Appetite statements help the board judge its profile; they give the control owner nothing to fix.
wrong_explanations.C: The risk owner should see the risk, but the summary still lacks the test details the control owner needs to act.
wrong_explanations.D: Changing a rating without new evidence misreports the controls and still shows the control owner nothing to fix.

tips: Eliminate: A adds board-level content the control owner cannot act on, and D changes ratings with no new evidence.
Final two: B beats C because the control owner needs the test results and tasks to fix the controls; sending the risk owner the same summary still gives nobody the detail.
Exam cue: a control owner fixes controls, so their report carries the test results and open remediation; a summary rating says something is wrong but not what.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Card payments moved to a group team
questions.question: A chocolate maker's online shop moved card payments to the group's payments team under an internal agreement with penalty charges, then recorded its card breach risk as transferred. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep the risk in the register, rated on the payments team's controls
options.B: Count the internal penalty charges as the share of the loss transferred
options.C: Record the card risk as transferred out of the shop's register
options.D: Get the risk owner to insure the online shop's card breach risk

questions.key_concept: Transfer assigns risk to another enterprise; moving work to a team in the same group keeps the risk in-house, rated on the controls now running.
questions.pre_read: Trace where a breach's costs would finally land once the work has moved.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk transfer assigns risk to another enterprise, such as an insurer. The payments team belongs to the same group, so a card breach still costs the group; the move may lower the risk, so it stays in the register, rated on the controls the payments team runs. Counting the penalty charges is the runner-up: they look like cover to the shop, but they move money between units and leave the group's loss unchanged.

wrong_explanations.B: Penalty charges shift cost between the shop and the payments team; the group still pays the whole breach, so no loss leaves the enterprise.
wrong_explanations.C: A team in the same group is not another enterprise, so nothing is transferred; ownership may move inside the group, but the risk stays on the enterprise's books.
wrong_explanations.D: Insurance could later cover part of the loss, but buying it now treats a risk that has not been rated since the work moved.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a team inside the group as another enterprise, and D buys insurance for a risk nobody has rated since the work moved.
Final two: A beats B because penalty charges move money between units of one group; the group's loss is unchanged, so the risk stays in the register, rated on the new controls.
Exam cue: when work moves to another unit of the same group, nothing is transferred; rate the risk on the controls that now run it.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. More data sent than the vendor was vetted for
questions.question: A vineyard gave a marketing vendor, vetted as low risk at onboarding, its subscribers' names and emails; it now also sends their birth dates and purchase histories. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Add data protection terms to the vineyard's contract with the vendor
options.B: Take the vendor's privacy certificate as cover for the new data
options.C: Get the risk owner to repeat the vendor's due diligence
options.D: Re-tier the vendor by the vineyard's spend with it

questions.key_concept: Due diligence depth follows the data a vendor holds; when the business sends it more sensitive data, the vendor is vetted again at that depth.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the vendor was vetted for with what it now receives.
questions.correct_explanation: Due diligence is scaled to what a vendor holds, and this vendor was vetted only for names and emails. Birth dates and purchase histories put it in a higher tier, so the risk owner, who answers for the vendor risk, has its due diligence repeated at that depth. Contract terms are the runner-up: they will likely be needed, but which terms, and whether the vendor can meet them, depend on that review.

wrong_explanations.A: Data protection terms are likely needed, but writing them before the review means choosing terms without knowing what the vendor can protect.
wrong_explanations.B: A certificate covers the scope its auditor tested, which may leave out this service and data; it does not replace due diligence at the new tier.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendors are tiered mainly by the data they hold and the processes they support; spend says little here, as a cheap vendor can hold the most sensitive data.

tips: Eliminate: B lets a general certificate stand in for due diligence on this data, and D tiers the vendor by spend instead of by the data it holds.
Final two: C beats A because the vendor was vetted for less data than it now holds; repeated due diligence shows which terms are needed and whether the vendor can meet them.
Exam cue: when the business sends a vendor more sensitive data than it was vetted for, vet the vendor again at the new tier before choosing fixes.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Issue re-rated by its action owner
questions.question: A sign maker's action owner re-rated an open issue from high to medium in the tracker, recording no reason, which moved its due date out by 90 days. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Restore the issue's high rating and its original due date
options.B: Notify the board that issue ratings are being changed
options.C: Keep the medium rating the action owner entered in the tracker
options.D: Review the change with the risk owner against the criteria

questions.key_concept: An issue's rating follows the enterprise's rating criteria; an unexplained change is checked against them with the risk owner before it stands or is reversed.
questions.pre_read: Note who changed the rating, what the change did and what basis came with it.
questions.correct_explanation: Issue ratings follow the enterprise's criteria, not the view of whoever holds the issue, and this change gave the fix 90 more days with no reason recorded. Reviewing it against the criteria with the risk owner, who agrees any due-date extension, shows whether something such as an interim control lowered the risk. Restoring the old rating is the runner-up: it follows if no basis holds, but doing it first assumes the change was wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: Restoring the rating is right if the change has no basis, but doing it first skips checking whether something really lowered the risk.
wrong_explanations.B: One unexplained re-rating is not yet a board matter; it is checked with the risk owner first, and escalation follows the policy's set points.
wrong_explanations.C: Accepting the new rating lets the person whose fix is due decide its deadline; ratings follow the enterprise's criteria, not the issue holder.

tips: Eliminate: B takes one unexplained re-rating to the board, and C lets the person whose fix is due set its own deadline.
Final two: D beats A because a rating change is tested against the criteria before it is kept or reversed; restoring it first assumes the change had no basis.
Exam cue: when an issue's rating drops with no recorded reason, check it against the rating criteria with the risk owner before keeping or reversing it.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Automatic rollback of an AI pricing model
questions.question: A perfume retailer's AI pricing service reverts automatically to the last approved model version when a release's price errors exceed their limit. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST classification of this rollback?

options.A: A preventive control that stops a faulty release going live
options.B: A corrective control that restores a known good version
options.C: A detective control that finds a release's price errors
options.D: A compensating control that stands in for release testing

questions.key_concept: A control that restores a known good state after a fault is corrective; the check that spots the fault is the detective part.
questions.pre_read: Ask when the rollback acts: before the release, as errors are found, or after.
questions.correct_explanation: A corrective control fixes errors once they are detected. The rollback acts after a faulty release is live, restoring the last approved version so wrong prices stop spreading; the error limit that triggers it is the detective part. Detective is the runner-up: the rollback depends on that check, but finding the errors is not what the rollback itself does; it acts on what the check found.

wrong_explanations.A: The faulty release is already live when the rollback fires, so it cannot stop the release going out; testing before release would be preventive.
wrong_explanations.C: The error limit check detects the fault, but the rollback is the step that acts on it; each part is classified by what it does.
wrong_explanations.D: A compensating control stands in for a missing or weak control; the rollback adds recovery and replaces nothing.

tips: Eliminate: A acts after the release is live, so it cannot stop it going out, and D replaces no missing control, so it does not compensate.
Final two: B beats C because the rollback restores the approved version after the fault; the limit check that triggers it is the detective part.
Exam cue: when an AI or automated service reverts itself to a known good version after a fault, the reversal is corrective; the check that triggers it detects.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Refunds split under the approval limit
questions.question: A boiler servicing firm's agents need a manager's approval for refunds over $500, but some pay one customer several $450 to $499 refunds in one day. Which change should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add a control owner review of refunds close to the approval limit
options.B: Train agents to pay just one refund per complaint
options.C: Apply the approval limit to a customer's combined refunds
options.D: Report refunds near the limit to the risk owner as a trend

questions.key_concept: A limit checked one payment at a time can be dodged by splitting; that design gap closes when the check acts on the combined amount.
questions.pre_read: Compare how the refunds were paid with what the approval rule actually checks.
questions.correct_explanation: The rule checks each refund on its own, so one large refund split into several under $500 never needs approval: a design gap. Applying the limit to a customer's combined refunds over a set period closes it at the cause, so split refunds still need approval before payment. A control owner review near the limit is the runner-up: it would catch some splits, but only after the money is paid, and agents could split lower.

wrong_explanations.A: A review near the limit finds some splits after payment, and agents can split further below it; the gap in the rule stays open.
wrong_explanations.B: Training sets an expectation but cannot stop agents who split refunds on purpose; the rule itself still lets them through.
wrong_explanations.D: A trend report tells the risk owner the rule is being dodged but changes nothing about the rule; it watches the gap rather than closing it.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on training where the rule itself lets split refunds through, and D reports the pattern to the risk owner without changing the rule.
Final two: C beats A because applying the limit to combined refunds stops split refunds before payment; a review near the limit finds some afterward and misses splits further below it.
Exam cue: when a per-payment limit is dodged by splitting, the gap is in the design; redesign the check to act on the combined amount.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Automated check that has flagged nothing
questions.question: A shipping agent's new automated check has flagged no unapproved customs entries over $10,000 since going live; the risk analyst plans to rely on it instead of sample tests. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Run entries known to lack approval through the new check
options.B: Compare the check's results with a manual sample of entries
options.C: Get the control owner's confirmation the check covers every entry
options.D: Treat the check's clean results as passed control tests

questions.key_concept: A check that has flagged nothing is proven by putting through cases it should catch; clean results alone cannot show it works.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the check's results so far can and cannot show about whether it works.
questions.correct_explanation: A check that has flagged nothing may be working, or may be unable to see the problem. Running entries known to lack approval through it shows whether it flags them, which the analyst needs before it replaces sample tests. Comparing it with a manual sample is the runner-up: running both side by side is sound practice, but if both find no exceptions, their agreement says nothing about what the check would miss.

wrong_explanations.B: Parallel running is sound practice, but a manual sample that also finds no unapproved entries cannot show whether the check would flag one.
wrong_explanations.C: The control owner's confirmation is inquiry; it does not show that the check flags an unapproved entry, which is what reliance needs.
wrong_explanations.D: Clean results are also what a broken check would report; treating them as passed tests credits the check before it is shown to work.

tips: Eliminate: C rests on the control owner's word, which is inquiry, and D credits clean results that a broken check would also produce.
Final two: A beats B because known failing entries show whether the check catches them; a manual sample that also finds none cannot show what the check misses.
Exam cue: before a new automated check that has flagged nothing replaces sample tests, put through cases it should catch and see it flag them.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Three teams each report their action done
questions.question: A petrol station chain's anti-skimming plan had operations fit pump seals, IT add tamper alerts and managers add daily checks; each team showed its part done. Which of the following BEST validates the response?

options.A: The teams' evidence that their own actions are complete
options.B: The risk owner's sign-off that the plan is finished
options.C: A re-rating of the skimming risk at target by its owner
options.D: A joint test of seals, alerts and checks at sampled stations

questions.key_concept: When a plan's actions sit with different teams and depend on each other, validation tests them working together, not only each part done.
questions.pre_read: Note how the three actions depend on one another to stop skimming.
questions.correct_explanation: The response works only if its parts work together: a broken seal must raise an alert that someone acts on, and the checks must catch what the alerts miss. A joint test at sampled stations shows whether skimming would be stopped. The teams' evidence is the runner-up: validation usually starts there, but it shows three parts done, not that they work as one response.

wrong_explanations.A: Each team's evidence shows its own action was done, which validation needs, but not that seals, alerts and checks work together to stop skimming.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk owner signs off a plan once it is validated; a sign-off is a decision, not evidence that the response works.
wrong_explanations.C: Re-rating at target credits the result the plan promised before anyone has shown the combined response reduces skimming.

tips: Eliminate: B treats the risk owner's sign-off as evidence, and C re-rates the risk at target before the response is shown to work.
Final two: D beats A because the response depends on its parts working together; each team's evidence proves its own action, not the combined effect.
Exam cue: when a plan's actions sit with different teams and depend on each other, validate them working together, not only part by part.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Branch counts to different cut-offs
questions.question: A locksmith firm's monthly KRI for lost master keys adds branch figures; three of 12 branches report counts to the 15th, when their old system closes its month. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Exclude the three branches from the KRI total
options.B: Ask the three branches for counts to the month-end cut-off
options.C: Have the risk owner agree to add the branches' counts as reported
options.D: Show the KRI as the share of branches reporting a loss

questions.key_concept: Figures added into one KRI must cover the same period; a cut-off mismatch that can be fixed at source is fixed before adding them.
questions.pre_read: Check whether every branch's count covers the same days before they are added.
questions.correct_explanation: Counts to the 15th cover different days from the rest, so the total mixes two periods and misstates the month. Asking the three branches for counts to the month-end cut-off comes first, as the figure may be fixable at source. Having the risk owner agree to the counts as reported is the runner-up: each still covers a month, and steady offsets are sometimes tolerated, but late-month losses would land in the next report.

wrong_explanations.A: Leaving out three branches makes the total incomplete, and keys lost there would vanish from the KRI instead of being counted.
wrong_explanations.C: A steady offset is sometimes tolerated, but agreeing to it leaves losses after the 15th in next month's figure; nobody has yet asked whether these branches can count to month-end.
wrong_explanations.D: A share of branches with a loss still mixes counts from different periods and hides how many keys were lost; it changes the measure, not the data.

tips: Eliminate: A drops three branches from the KRI, and D changes the measure while still mixing counts from different periods.
Final two: B beats C because nobody has yet asked whether the branches can count to month-end; agreeing to the offset leaves their losses after the 15th in next month's KRI.
Exam cue: when sources feeding one KRI close their periods on different dates, get figures to one common cut-off before adding; a stated mismatch is for sources that cannot be fixed in time.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. A ban on USB copying
questions.question: A watchmaker's design director bans copying design files to USB drives and records the design-leak risk as avoided, though designers' PCs still accept USB drives. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Recommend a block on USB ports for the designers' PCs
options.B: Record the ban as a detective control in the register
options.C: Re-rate the risk with the ban as a mitigating control
options.D: Name the designers bound by the ban as the risk's owners

questions.key_concept: Avoidance removes the activity or exposure behind a risk; a ban that people can still break is a mitigating control, rated for its effect.
questions.pre_read: Read what the response changes in practice, not what the register calls it.
questions.correct_explanation: Avoidance removes the activity or exposure that creates a risk. Designers still handle the files on PCs that accept USB drives, so the exposure remains; the ban is a mitigating control that lowers likelihood only as far as people obey it. Re-rating the risk with the ban as a control comes first. Recommending a USB block is the runner-up: it may follow, but until the risk is rated, nobody knows whether it is needed.

wrong_explanations.A: A USB block may well be the right next step, but recommending it before the risk is re-rated skips the analysis that shows whether more treatment is needed.
wrong_explanations.B: A ban tells designers what not to do and detects nothing; calling it detective misstates how it works, so the rating would credit it for the wrong effect.
wrong_explanations.D: A risk is owned by one manager with authority over its treatment; staff bound by a rule follow it but do not own the risk it addresses.

tips: Eliminate: B files a ban, which detects nothing, as a detective control, and D makes rule-bound staff the owners, though one manager with authority over treatment owns a risk.
Final two: C beats A because the register calls a live risk avoided; rating it with the ban as a control shows whether a USB block is needed at all.
Exam cue: avoidance removes the activity or exposure itself; a rule telling people not to do something is a mitigating control, rated on how well it works.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Coordinator named as owner
questions.question: A property manager's facilities unit names its risk coordinator, a non-manager who compiles monthly updates, as owner of all 14 unit risks. Which of the following should concern the risk analyst MOST?

options.A: An owner who cannot fund or accept the risk
options.B: A coordinator who is not on the risk committee
options.C: One owner named on 14 different unit risks
options.D: A coordinator without technical knowledge of the risks

questions.key_concept: A risk owner holds the authority and accountability to fund treatment and accept risk; a coordinator who compiles updates facilitates but cannot own.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against what a risk owner must be able to do.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk owner needs the authority to fund treatment and accept residual risk, as well as accountability for the outcome. A non-manager who compiles updates facilitates the process but cannot make those decisions, so the 14 risks have no one able to act on them. One owner named on many risks is the runner-up: it can be fine when that person holds authority over all of them, as a unit head often does.

wrong_explanations.B: Risk committee membership is not a condition of ownership; owners are named for their authority over the affected objectives, not for a committee seat.
wrong_explanations.C: One manager can own many risks when they hold authority over them, as a unit head often does; the number matters less than who holds them.
wrong_explanations.D: Owners draw on experts for technical detail; ownership rests on authority and accountability for the outcome, not on technical knowledge.

tips: Eliminate: B makes a committee seat a condition of ownership, and D asks for technical knowledge, though owners draw on experts and need authority instead.
Final two: A beats C because one person can own many risks within their authority; a non-manager who compiles updates holds none, so no one can act on these risks.
Exam cue: a risk owner is marked by authority to fund treatment and accept risk; a coordinator who gathers updates facilitates the process but cannot own the risks.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Exception tied to a replacement
questions.question: A pasta maker's approved exception lets its old packing-line PCs skip the endpoint protection standard until the line is replaced; the replacement is unfunded and unscheduled. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Track the start date of the replacement project in the register
options.B: Ask the risk owner to give the exception a fixed expiry date
options.C: Convert the exception into an exemption the risk owner reviews
options.D: Tell senior management the exception is a breach

questions.key_concept: An exception needs a fixed expiry date and a plan to comply; one tied to an unscheduled event can run on without a fresh decision.
questions.pre_read: Check each option against what makes an exception temporary.
questions.correct_explanation: An exception is a temporary, approved deviation, so it needs a date when it ends or is decided again. Ending it when the line is replaced ties it to an event with no funding or schedule, so in practice it never ends and is never reconsidered. Asking the risk owner to set a fixed expiry date restores that decision point. Tracking the replacement's start date is the runner-up: useful, but the exception stays open-ended.

wrong_explanations.A: Watching the replacement project is useful, but with no funding or schedule it may never start, so the exception still has no end and no point of fresh decision.
wrong_explanations.C: An exemption fits a requirement that cannot apply; endpoint protection can apply once the line is replaced, so the gap stays a time-limited exception.
wrong_explanations.D: The deviation was approved and recorded, so it is not a breach; the problem is its missing end date, not a missing approval.

tips: Eliminate: C uses an exemption, meant for a requirement that cannot apply, and D calls an approved, recorded deviation a breach.
Final two: B beats A because the replacement has no funding or date; tracking it leaves the exception without an end, while a fixed expiry forces a fresh decision.
Exam cue: an exception needs a fixed expiry date and a plan to comply, so the owner decides again; one tied only to an unfunded, unscheduled project is open-ended in practice.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. ML fraud model as a detective control
questions.question: A builders merchant credits an ML model that flags fraudulent trade-account applications as a detective control; its training data ends in March. Which of the following BEST shows the risk analyst that it works?

options.A: The vendor's accuracy on pre-April cases held back from training
options.B: A walkthrough of how staff clear the model's flags
options.C: The share of applications the model has flagged
options.D: Fraud cases confirmed since April, run through the model

questions.key_concept: An ML model credited as a detective control is tested on confirmed cases from after its training data, in the period it is relied on.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask what it proves about the model catching fraud.
questions.correct_explanation: A detective control is credited on whether it catches what it targets in the period it is relied on. Fraud confirmed since April, including cases found without a flag, comes after the training data ends, so running it through the model shows whether it detects fraud newer than its training. The vendor's pre-April held-back results are the runner-up: those cases come from the training period, so they show fit to older patterns, not detection now.

wrong_explanations.A: Held-back cases share the training period's patterns, so strong results on them can overstate how well the model catches fraud that has changed since March.
wrong_explanations.B: A walkthrough shows how staff handle flags, a design point; it does not show whether the model flags the fraudulent applications at all.
wrong_explanations.C: A flag count shows activity, not accuracy; the model could flag many genuine applications and still miss the fraud.

tips: Eliminate: B shows how staff handle flags, a design point, and C counts flags without showing whether any were fraud or fraud was missed.
Final two: D beats A because the held-back cases come from the training period; only fraud confirmed since April tests the model on patterns newer than its training data.
Exam cue: test an ML detective control on confirmed cases from after its training data ends; results on data from its training period can overstate it.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Sources for cold-store KRIs
questions.question: A fish processor's risk analyst is choosing KRIs for the scenario of a cold-store control system outage spoiling stock, after four such outages in two years. What is the BEST source of candidate KRIs?

options.A: Metrics the cold-store system's owner already reports
options.B: The root causes behind the past cold-store outages
options.C: A published library of KRIs for food processors
options.D: Repair times the control owner logs for past outages

questions.key_concept: Candidate KRIs come from the drivers of the scenario, found in the causes of its past events, before generic lists or data already collected.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a KRI must track before judging where to look for one.
questions.correct_explanation: A KRI earns its place by tracking a driver of its scenario that moves before the loss. The causes behind the four past outages show which conditions built up before each failure, so they point to leading indicators for this cold store. A published KRI library is the runner-up: it is a useful prompt, but its measures fit other firms' systems and may miss what caused these outages.

wrong_explanations.A: Metrics already reported were chosen for other purposes and are easy to collect; they may say nothing about the conditions that build up before an outage.
wrong_explanations.C: A library suggests measures written for other firms' systems; it helps once this cold store's own causes are known, not as the starting point.
wrong_explanations.D: Repair times measure the repair process after an outage, a lagging performance measure, not an early warning of the next one.

tips: Eliminate: A starts from data already collected rather than what drives outages, and D uses repair times, a lagging measure of the fix after each outage.
Final two: B beats C because a KRI must track this scenario's own drivers; the four outages show what built up before each failure, while a library reflects other firms' systems.
Exam cue: when a scenario has a history of events, draw candidate KRIs from their causes, then test each for measurability; generic lists and existing reports help after that.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Outage inside the rated range
questions.question: A vending machine operator rates card-reader outage risk on about six outages a year costing up to $3,000 each; the year's fifth, costing $1,800, came in November. What is the risk analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Reassess the outage risk's likelihood after the new outage
options.B: Escalate the outage to the risk owner as a tolerance breach
options.C: Log the outage against the risk for its scheduled review
options.D: Add backup connections to the fleet's card readers

questions.key_concept: An event inside the frequency and size a rating assumed is consistent with it; it is logged for the scheduled review, not reassessed at once.
questions.pre_read: Compare the new event with what the rating already assumed.
questions.correct_explanation: The rating already expects about six outages a year costing up to $3,000 each; a fifth costing $1,800 in November falls inside that, so it fits the rating rather than challenging it. Logging it against the risk keeps the event history for the scheduled review. Reassessing likelihood now is the runner-up: outages are evidence, but this one adds nothing the rating did not assume; one outside that range would call for it.

wrong_explanations.A: An outage is evidence, but this one sits inside the frequency and size the rating assumed, so reassessing now would re-rate a risk that nothing has changed.
wrong_explanations.B: An outage inside the rated range breaches no tolerance; calling it a breach misuses escalation and spends the owner's time on an expected event.
wrong_explanations.D: Backup connections are a treatment choice for the risk owner on an analyzed risk; one outage the rating expected gives no reason to change the response.

tips: Eliminate: B calls an expected outage a tolerance breach, and D jumps to new treatment, the risk owner's choice on an analyzed risk, after one expected outage.
Final two: C beats A because the fifth outage, costing $1,800, sits inside the six a year of up to $3,000 the rating assumed; it fits the rating, so it waits for the scheduled review.
Exam cue: an event inside the frequency and size a rating assumed fits that rating; log it for the scheduled review, and reassess when events run outside that range.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 3.6.1 (Continuous Risk Monitoring: monitoring that shows a risk approaching its tolerance level triggers a review of the risk); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk: compliance, response effectiveness and risk-impacting changes)

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Flaw details in a wide report
questions.question: A tax adviser firm's monthly risk dashboard lists unpatched client-portal flaws with server names and goes by email to 40 managers, most with no part in remediation. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Mark the dashboard confidential before it goes to managers
options.B: Add the flaws' CVSS scores to the managers' dashboard
options.C: Report just the patched flaws in the managers' dashboard
options.D: Move flaw details to a restricted report for the patching team

questions.key_concept: Reports carry the detail each audience needs; exploitable technical detail goes to the people who fix it, not to a wide management list.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each reader of the report needs in order to act.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk reports are built for what each audience must decide or do, and exploitable detail is kept to the people who need it. Managers with no part in fixing the flaws need the risk's position and trend, not server names an attacker could use; that detail belongs in a restricted report for the people patching. Marking the dashboard confidential is the runner-up: it signals care, but 40 readers still hold detail they do not need.

wrong_explanations.A: A confidential label asks readers to take care, but it still sends server names and flaw details to 40 managers, most of whom do not act on them.
wrong_explanations.B: CVSS scores add technical detail for an audience that does not fix the flaws; managers need the risk in business terms, not more scanner data.
wrong_explanations.C: Listing just the patched flaws drops the open exposure the managers' dashboard exists to show; the fix is less detail, not less risk.

tips: Eliminate: B adds technical scores for an audience that does not fix the flaws, and C drops the open exposure the dashboard exists to report.
Final two: D beats A because most managers play no part in fixing the flaws; a label leaves the server names with them, while a restricted report keeps them with the patching team.
Exam cue: match each report's detail to its readers' roles; exploitable technical detail goes to the people who act on it, and others get the risk's position and trend.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Study budget for nine signals
questions.question: An armored cash transport firm's horizon review lists nine emerging risks, each with a proposed owner, but the budget funds deeper study of only three. Who is MOST appropriate to decide which three are studied?

options.A: Senior management, from the analyst's ranked shortlist
options.B: The risk analyst, on the likelihood scores they assign
options.C: Each emerging risk's proposed owner, for their own risk
options.D: The security team, as the main source of the signals

questions.key_concept: Senior management decides which emerging risks to study or prepare for when they compete for limited funds; the analyst ranks and proposes.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the decision covers before matching it to a role.
questions.correct_explanation: Choosing which emerging risks get scarce study money is a decision across the enterprise's priorities, so senior management makes it; the risk analyst ranks the nine by relevance to objectives and proposes. Each proposed owner deciding for their own risk is the runner-up: owners decide how to prepare for their own emerging risk, but nine owners cannot each settle a share of one budget that funds three studies.

wrong_explanations.B: The analyst ranks and proposes, but choosing where scarce money goes is a management decision; a practitioner who settles it takes the business's choice.
wrong_explanations.C: Owners decide how to prepare for their own emerging risk, but nine owners cannot each settle a share of one budget that funds three studies.
wrong_explanations.D: The security team supplies many of the signals but answers for no business objective; where study money goes is a management decision.

tips: Eliminate: B has the analyst choose where money goes, a management decision, and D gives the choice to a source of signals that answers for no business objective.
Final two: A beats C because one budget funds three of nine studies; owners decide how to prepare for their own risk, but choosing among risks sits with senior management.
Exam cue: when emerging risks compete for limited study funds, senior management decides from the analyst's ranked shortlist; each owner then decides how to prepare for their own.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Supplier risks held by procurement
questions.question: A waste collector's register names its procurement manager as owner of the risks from all 45 suppliers, including the vendor of the route-planning software its crews depend on. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep procurement as owner, with service heads consulted
options.B: Name the suppliers' own account managers as the risks' owners
options.C: Move supplier risks to the heads of the services using them
options.D: Take the supplier risks into the risk team's own portfolio

questions.key_concept: Vendor risk is owned by the business manager whose service depends on the vendor, not by procurement, the vendor or the risk team.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose objectives would suffer if each supplier failed.
questions.correct_explanation: A supplier risk belongs with the manager whose service depends on that supplier: their objectives suffer when it fails, and they decide how to treat it. Procurement runs buying and contracts. Moving the supplier risks to the heads of the services using them puts the decision where the impact falls. Keeping procurement as owner with service heads consulted is the runner-up: it sounds joined up, but those who carry the impact still cannot decide.

wrong_explanations.A: Procurement manages contracts and due diligence, but route planning failing hurts the crews' service, not procurement's; consulting service heads leaves the decision away from the impact.
wrong_explanations.B: A supplier's account manager works for the supplier; outsourcing moves the work, not accountability for the risk, which stays with a manager inside the waste collector.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk team facilitates, analyzes and reports; holding business risks itself would leave no business manager accountable for treating or accepting them.

tips: Eliminate: B hands the risks to the suppliers' own staff, though accountability for the risk stays in-house, and D gives them to the risk team, which facilitates and reports rather than owns.
Final two: C beats A because the service heads' objectives suffer when a supplier fails; procurement runs the contract, so ownership there keeps the decision away from the impact.
Exam cue: vendor risk sits with the business manager whose service relies on the vendor; procurement, IT and the risk team support that owner rather than replace them.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Using a right to audit
questions.question: A vendor's SOC 2 report excludes the settlement module built for a clearing house, whose contract grants audit rights. Which of the following should the risk analyst propose as the BEST party to use them?

options.A: The vendor's own internal audit team, sharing its results
options.B: The clearing house's internal audit function, under the contract
options.C: The settlement service's business owner, using a checklist
options.D: The clearing house's IT operations team that runs the module

questions.key_concept: A right to audit is used by the customer's own auditors, such as internal audit, so the evidence answers to the customer, not the vendor.
questions.pre_read: Ask whom each candidate reports to and what role it plays.
questions.correct_explanation: A right to audit lets the clearing house gather its own evidence where the vendor's SOC 2 report stops. Its internal audit function works for the clearing house, so the evidence it gathers under the contract answers to the clearing house. The vendor's own internal audit team is the runner-up: it knows the module, but it answers to the vendor's management, so its results are the vendor's account of itself.

wrong_explanations.A: The vendor's internal auditors report to the vendor's management; sharing their results gives the clearing house the vendor's view of itself, which the right to audit exists to go beyond.
wrong_explanations.C: The business owner accepts the vendor risk, arranges assurance for the gap and acts on the results; running a checklist review personally is a first-line check, not an audit.
wrong_explanations.D: The team that runs the module relies on it day to day; checking its own service's supplier is first-line work and not an audit of the vendor's controls.

tips: Eliminate: C has the business owner, who accepts the risk, run a checklist, and D has the team that runs the module check it; neither is an assurance role.
Final two: B beats A because the right to audit gives the clearing house its own evidence; the vendor's internal auditors answer to the vendor's management, not to the clearing house.
Exam cue: when a contract gives a right to audit a vendor, look to the customer's own internal audit, or auditors it engages, to use it; a vendor's internal auditors answer to its management.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. An AI control catalog of its own
questions.question: A bookseller's data science lead, adopting the NIST AI RMF, plans an AI control catalog drawn from its subcategories and kept apart from the enterprise control library. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Evaluate the AI tools against the subcategories as a checklist
options.B: Name the data science lead as the AI catalog's owner
options.C: Add an AI section to the library listing the subcategories
options.D: Map the AI RMF outcomes onto the existing control library

questions.key_concept: AI RMF outcomes are mapped into the existing control library, with AI-specific controls added for the gaps, not run as a parallel AI catalog.
questions.pre_read: Notice whether the framework in the stem sets outcomes or lists controls.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF sets outcomes, not controls, and expects AI risk management to sit inside enterprise risk management. Mapping its outcomes onto the existing library shows which current controls, such as change and access management, already meet them, and where AI-specific controls such as drift checks must be added. Adding an AI section that lists the subcategories is the runner-up: it shares the library but treats outcomes as controls and repeats ones that exist.

wrong_explanations.A: The AI RMF says its actions are not a checklist; running the tools against the subcategories ignores tailoring and still leaves AI outside the existing library.
wrong_explanations.B: Naming an owner settles who runs the separate catalog, but it keeps a second control set beside the library, with its own duplicated tests.
wrong_explanations.C: A section listing the subcategories puts AI in the library but treats outcomes as controls and repeats controls it already holds, such as access reviews.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the AI RMF as a checklist, which it says it is not, and B only names an owner for a parallel catalog that duplicates the library.
Final two: D beats C because the subcategories are outcomes; mapping them to existing controls shows which are met and where AI controls are needed, while listing them copies outcomes in as controls.
Exam cue: when a new framework arrives, such as one for AI, map its outcomes into the existing control library and add controls for the gaps, rather than running a second catalog.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Repair invoices outside the match
questions.question: A shopping center landlord's system pays invoices only once they match a purchase order, but emergency repair invoices, a quarter of spend, bypass it unchecked. Which change should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Budget owner approval of emergency invoices ahead of payment
options.B: A later review of paid emergency invoices against repair records
options.C: Share of spend paid outside the invoice match
options.D: Sign-off of emergency invoices by the contractor's own supervisor

questions.key_concept: A control covers only the transactions that pass through it; a route around it, such as emergency payments, needs its own check before the loss.
questions.pre_read: Trace which transactions pass through the control and which do not.
questions.correct_explanation: A control protects only what passes through it, so control analysis follows every route around it. A quarter of spend skips the match, so that route needs a check of its own. Approval by the budget owner before each emergency invoice is paid stops wrong payments without slowing urgent repairs. A later review against repair records is the runner-up: it finds false or duplicate invoices only after the money has gone.

wrong_explanations.B: A later review is detective: it finds false or duplicate repair invoices after payment, when recovering money is harder, while an approval before payment stops them.
wrong_explanations.C: Measuring the spend outside the match shows how big the gap is, but it puts no check on the invoices paid outside it.
wrong_explanations.D: The contractor's supervisor works for the firm being paid; a party approving its own invoices cannot show whether the charges are genuine.

tips: Eliminate: C measures the unchecked spend without checking any of it, and D lets the firm being paid approve its own invoices, which segregation of duties rules out.
Final two: A beats B because a quarter of spend leaves with no check; an approval before payment stops a bad invoice, while a later review finds it once the money is gone.
Exam cue: when analyzing a control, look for routes around it; a route that skips the check needs its own control, placed before the loss where it can be.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. A long plan with only an end date
questions.question: A plastics molder's funded 15-month plan to replace shared logins has interim controls but only an end date; its lead, the action owner, reports 'on track' monthly. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Collect evidence of the work done so far from the action owner
options.B: Split delivery of the plan between the IT and operations teams
options.C: Ask the plan's lead to set dated milestones for the rollout
options.D: Re-rate the risk whenever the lead reports progress

questions.key_concept: Long risk action plans need dated milestones, so progress reports can be checked and slippage shows early, not at the end date.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a progress report in the stem could be checked against.
questions.correct_explanation: A plan needs milestones so slippage shows while there is still time to act; with only an end date, 'on track' has no dated point to be checked against before the 15 months are up. Asking the lead to set dated milestones gives each report those points. Collecting evidence of work done is the runner-up: it shows what has been done, but without milestones nobody can tell whether that is enough by now.

wrong_explanations.A: Evidence of work done shows activity, but with only an end date there is no point to compare it with, so slippage stays hidden until the end.
wrong_explanations.B: Splitting delivery across two teams blurs who answers for each action; a plan needs one owner per action, and this does nothing for tracking progress.
wrong_explanations.D: A rating changes when actions are validated as working, not each time someone reports; re-rating unchanged facts gives no view of slippage.

tips: Eliminate: B splits delivery across two teams, blurring the one owner each action needs, and D re-rates a risk whose facts have not changed instead of tracking the work.
Final two: C beats A because the plan has only an end date; evidence of work done cannot show whether progress is on schedule until there are dated points to measure it against.
Exam cue: a long action plan needs dated milestones as well as an end date, so reports can be checked and slippage shows while there is time to act.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. A sensor feed gone silent
questions.question: A fruit packer's KRI showed no cold-store temperature breaches at one packhouse for five weeks because its sensor feed had silently stopped. Which control should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: A sample check of the feed's figures against sensor logs
options.B: An attestation from the sensor system's owner that it still works
options.C: Estimates for silent weeks from other packhouses' averages
options.D: An automatic alert to the feed's data owner when records stop

questions.key_concept: Completeness is checked as data arrives: a feed that stops should raise an alert, so silence is not reported as zero risk events.
questions.pre_read: Ask how each option would tell a true zero from missing data.
questions.correct_explanation: A silent feed reads as zero, and zero looks like good news, so completeness has to be checked as data arrives. An automatic alert to the feed's data owner when records stop flags the gap at once, so the KRI is marked incomplete before reporting. A sample check against the sensor logs is the runner-up: it tests the figures, but only when the next check runs, and its sample may skip the silent packhouse.

wrong_explanations.A: Sample checks test accuracy, but they find a silent feed only when the next check runs and only if the sample includes that packhouse.
wrong_explanations.B: An attestation is the owner's own claim that the system works; it would not have shown that the feed had stopped sending data.
wrong_explanations.C: Estimating the missing weeks fills the gap with guesses and hides the outage; the fault is missing data, which needs detecting, not filling in.

tips: Eliminate: B rests on the owner's own claim rather than the data, and C fills the silent weeks with guesses, hiding the outage instead of detecting it.
Final two: D beats A because the feed sat silent for five weeks; an alert when records stop flags it at once, while a sample check catches it only if run on that packhouse.
Exam cue: when no data can pass for good news, check completeness as data arrives; an automatic alert on a silent feed beats a later sample check.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for an archive filling up
questions.question: A bookkeeping firm's document archive grows unevenly from month to month, and adding storage takes ten weeks. Which of the following should the risk analyst propose as the BEST KRI for the archive filling up?

options.A: Time left until the archive fills at the recent growth rate
options.B: Share of the archive's storage space already in use
options.C: Client uploads the archive rejected for lack of space
options.D: Time taken to approve and fit new storage

questions.key_concept: A KRI should warn early enough for the response to take effect, so it is best set against the time that response needs.
questions.pre_read: Note any fact in the stem about how long the response takes.
questions.correct_explanation: A KRI must warn early enough for the response to work, and here the response, adding storage, takes ten weeks. Time left until the archive fills at the recent growth rate can be set against that lead time and moves as growth changes. The share of storage in use is the runner-up: it rises toward the limit, but with uneven growth a fixed percentage can mean months of headroom one time and days the next.

wrong_explanations.B: With uneven growth, the same share in use can leave months or days before the archive fills, so a fixed percentage gives no steady warning time.
wrong_explanations.C: Rejected uploads show the archive is already full; a lagging measure like this confirms the harm rather than warning before it.
wrong_explanations.D: This tracks how fast purchasing and fitting work, a performance measure; it says nothing about how close the archive is to filling.

tips: Eliminate: C counts uploads already rejected, a lagging sign of harm, and D measures the purchasing process, a KPI rather than an indicator of exposure.
Final two: A beats B because growth is uneven and new storage takes ten weeks; time left at the recent rate sets directly against that lead time, while a fixed share does not.
Exam cue: a KRI should warn earlier than the response takes to work; prefer one expressed in terms that can be set against that lead time.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. A scan that forwards only likely signals
questions.question: A national mapping agency's horizon scan forwards only signals analysts judge likely; this year it dropped three high-impact ones, including solar storms disrupting satellite positioning. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Forward every signal, likely or not, to senior management
options.B: Screen signals on potential impact as well as likelihood
options.C: Rate just the solar storm risk on the agency's usual scale
options.D: Review the three dropped high-impact signals with the analysts

questions.key_concept: Horizon signals are screened on potential impact as well as likelihood, because emerging risks are often unlikely but severe.
questions.pre_read: Look at the rule the scan uses to decide what goes forward.
questions.correct_explanation: Horizon scanning screens signals for relevance to objectives, and an emerging risk is often unlikely but severe. A screen that forwards only likely signals is built to drop exactly those, which is why three high-impact ones went missing this year. Screening on potential impact as well as likelihood fixes the cause. Reviewing the three dropped signals with the analysts is the runner-up: it learns from these cases but leaves the screen that dropped them unchanged.

wrong_explanations.A: Forwarding everything skips the screening that makes a scan usable; senior management would get every signal with no view of which ones matter to objectives.
wrong_explanations.C: A usual-scale rating treats an uncertain, emerging risk as well understood, and it deals with one signal while the screen keeps dropping others.
wrong_explanations.D: Reviewing the dropped signals learns from three cases, but the rule that dropped them stays in place and will keep filtering out unlikely, severe signals.

tips: Eliminate: A skips the screening that keeps a scan usable, burying senior management in signals, and C rates one uncertain signal on the usual scale as if it were well understood.
Final two: B beats D because the same rule dropped three high-impact signals; changing the screen fixes the cause, while reviewing the three cases leaves it in place.
Exam cue: emerging risks are often unlikely but severe; screen horizon signals on potential impact on objectives as well as likelihood, so rare, damaging ones reach decision makers.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. An AI vendor's indemnity for wrong advice
questions.question: A chamber of commerce's AI assistant gives members export advice; the vendor indemnifies the chamber against members' legal claims over wrong advice. Which of the following register entries should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: The vendor recorded as the owner of the wrong-advice risk
options.B: A lower likelihood of wrong advice reaching members
options.C: A partial transfer, the rest kept by its risk owner
options.D: A note of the indemnity, with the rating left unchanged

questions.key_concept: An AI vendor's indemnity transfers only the legal costs it covers; the harm to customers and trust stays with the risk owner.
questions.pre_read: Ask which parts of the loss the contract would actually pay for.
questions.correct_explanation: An indemnity transfers only what it covers: here, members' legal claims. Wrong advice still harms members, whose goods may be held at a border, and their trust in the chamber, and neither moves to the vendor. A partial transfer credits the covered claim costs and keeps the rest with the risk owner. A note with the rating unchanged is the runner-up: it is cautious, but it ignores the claim costs that really have moved.

wrong_explanations.A: A contract moves some claim costs, not accountability; the chamber's risk owner still answers for the harm wrong advice does to members and to the chamber's standing.
wrong_explanations.B: The indemnity pays once wrong advice has led to a claim; it does nothing to make wrong advice less likely, so the likelihood stays as rated.
wrong_explanations.D: Leaving the rating unchanged ignores the members' legal claims the vendor now pays; the entry should credit that cost while keeping the harm that stays.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the indemnity as handing the risk to the vendor, though accountability stays, and B credits it against likelihood, though it pays only after a claim.
Final two: C beats D because the indemnity does move the cost of members' legal claims; a partial transfer credits that cost and keeps the harm to members and trust with the risk owner.
Exam cue: an AI vendor's indemnity is a partial transfer; credit the costs it covers, and keep the harm it cannot reach, such as lost trust, with the risk owner.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. A risk re-rated beyond its owner's authority
questions.question: A nut processor's allergen-labeling risk, owned by a plant manager who can accept risks up to medium, is re-rated critical after a five-year supermarket contract tripled volume. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the plant manager as owner, referring each decision upward
options.B: Re-rate the risk as medium, counting planned label checks
options.C: Give the risk committee the risk to hold as a group
options.D: Move the risk to an executive with authority for its rating

questions.key_concept: A risk owner needs authority that matches the risk's rating; when a lasting re-rating exceeds it, ownership moves up to someone who can decide.
questions.pre_read: Compare the owner's authority with the risk's new rating.
questions.correct_explanation: Ownership should match a risk's rating: the owner funds the response and accepts what remains. The five-year contract makes the critical rating lasting and beyond the plant manager's authority, so moving the risk to an executive with authority for that rating puts the decisions with someone who can make them. Keeping the plant manager as owner and referring each decision upward is the runner-up: it leaves an owner who can decide nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Referring a decision upward suits a one-off acceptance; with a lasting critical rating, it leaves a named owner who can neither accept the risk nor fund its response.
wrong_explanations.B: Planned checks give a target, not the current rating; re-rating on them to fit the owner's limit shrinks the risk to suit the authority.
wrong_explanations.C: A committee can oversee and challenge, but a risk held by a group often means no one acts; one named executive should own it.

tips: Eliminate: B rates the risk on planned checks to fit the owner's limit, and C hands it to a committee, where shared holding leaves no one accountable.
Final two: D beats A because the five-year contract keeps the rating critical; an owner who must refer every decision upward holds the title while the executive above makes the decisions.
Exam cue: when a risk's rating rises beyond its owner's authority and stays there, move ownership to someone who can accept and fund it; refer one-off decisions upward.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Compensation that misses the flaw
questions.question: A border agency cannot patch a critical, remotely exploitable e-gate flaw until the vendor certifies the fix; the exception request offers daily malware scans as compensation. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Limit network access to the flawed service until patched
options.B: Run the scans hourly, with results sent to the system owner
options.C: Compare the scans' cost with the risk they would reduce
options.D: Install the uncertified patch with the system owner's consent

questions.key_concept: A compensating control for an exception must act on the risk the missing requirement addressed, such as the path to an unpatched flaw.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the missing patch was meant to stop.
questions.correct_explanation: A compensating control must reduce the risk the missing patch leaves: remote exploitation of the flaw. Limiting network access to the flawed service closes that path until the certified patch arrives. Malware scans look for harm after an attacker may already be in. Comparing the scans' cost with the risk they would reduce is the runner-up: cost-benefit matters, but the scans do not act on the flaw, so their cost is not yet the question.

wrong_explanations.B: Hourly scans find an infection sooner but still act after exploitation; the remote path to the flaw, which the patch would have closed, stays open.
wrong_explanations.C: Cost-benefit weighs controls that treat the risk; scans do not block remote exploitation of the flaw, so comparing their cost settles nothing about the exception.
wrong_explanations.D: The patch is held back for certification; installing it uncertified risks e-gate failures at the border, trading one risk for the one the exception exists to avoid.

tips: Eliminate: B runs a detective check more often, still after exploitation, and D installs the uncertified patch the exception exists to avoid, risking e-gate failures.
Final two: A beats C because a compensating control must act on the flaw's remote path; the scans look for malware afterward, so weighing their cost comes too early.
Exam cue: judge an exception's compensating control by whether it acts on the risk the missing requirement covered; a check that finds harm afterward rarely replaces one that prevents it.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Limits the checked can change
questions.question: An actuarial consultancy's valuation system holds back client reports whose results fall outside set limits, but the actuaries whose reports it checks can change those limits. Which change should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Test the hold using results set just outside the limits
options.B: Log limit changes for the chief actuary's monthly review
options.C: Restrict limit changes to a role outside the actuarial teams
options.D: Get each actuary to sign off the limits they set

questions.key_concept: An automated check's settings need protecting from the people it checks; separate who sets its limits from whose work it checks.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can change the check's settings and whose work the check covers.
questions.correct_explanation: A check is only as strong as the protection on its settings. While the actuaries it checks can change its limits, one can widen a limit to pass their own report. Restricting limit changes to a role outside the actuarial teams separates setting the check from being checked. Logging changes for the chief actuary's monthly review is the runner-up: it finds a widened limit only after the reports it passed have gone to clients.

wrong_explanations.A: The hold works as built; a test with out-of-limit results shows it fires, not that the limits it fires on are safe from the actuaries it checks.
wrong_explanations.B: A monthly review of logged changes is detective; a limit widened today lets reports through to clients for weeks before anyone looks at the change.
wrong_explanations.D: Actuaries signing off their own limits is still self-review; it records the choice without separating who sets the check from whose work it checks.

tips: Eliminate: A tests that the hold fires, which is not in doubt, and D has actuaries sign off their own limits, which is self-review rather than separation.
Final two: C beats B because stopping the checked from changing the check prevents a widened limit before any report goes out; a monthly review finds it after clients have the reports.
Exam cue: when analyzing an automated check, ask who can change its settings; if the people it checks can, separate that access rather than rely on reviews after the fact.
