questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. An earlier test after staff changes
questions.question: A shoe maker's ratings credit planners' daily check of production orders against approved materials lists, tested effective in January; half the planners have since been replaced. What is the risk analyst's BEST next step?

options.A: Obtain the control owner's word that it still runs
options.B: Test a sample of checks the new planners have run
options.C: Review the training records of the planners who joined
options.D: Walk through the check's design again with a new planner

questions.key_concept: Earlier test results lose weight when conditions change; after turnover among the people running a control, test its operation since the change.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has changed since the control was last tested.
questions.correct_explanation: January's result was earned by the planners who ran the check then. With half of them replaced, the conditions behind that result have changed, so it no longer shows the check works today. Testing a sample of the checks the new planners have run gives current evidence of operation. Reviewing the new planners' training records is the runner-up: it shows they were taught the check, not that they perform it correctly.

wrong_explanations.A: A statement that the check still runs is inquiry, the weakest evidence on its own, and the owner may not see how new planners perform it.
wrong_explanations.C: Training records show the new planners were taught the check; they do not show it has been performed, or performed correctly, since they started.
wrong_explanations.D: Nothing in the check's design has changed; the people running it have, so a new walkthrough repeats a design test when operation is in question.

tips: Eliminate: A rests on the owner's word alone, the weakest evidence, and D retests a design that has not changed, when the people running it have.
Final two: B beats C because training records show what the new planners were taught; a sample of the checks they ran shows whether the control operates now.
Exam cue: an earlier test result holds only while the conditions behind it hold; after a material change, such as new people running a manual control, test the period since.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicators that skip the top risks
questions.question: A landfill operator's risk committee receives 24 KRIs, all chosen for easy data; none covers its two biggest risks. Which of the following should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Note the two uncovered risks beside the 24 KRIs
options.B: Cut the set to the 12 KRIs with the most reliable data
options.C: Report the share of incidents caused by the two top risks
options.D: Develop leading KRIs that track the two top-rated risks

questions.key_concept: KRIs are chosen for the top risks first and checked for data second; indicators picked for easy data can miss the risks that matter.
questions.pre_read: Check which risks the current indicators actually cover.
questions.correct_explanation: KRIs earn their place by warning of the risks that matter most. A set picked for easy data can be measurable and still blind to the two top-rated risks. Developing leading KRIs that track those risks puts early warning where exposure is greatest. Cutting the set to the 12 KRIs with the most reliable data is the runner-up: a smaller, cleaner set helps, but it still tracks neither of the top risks.

wrong_explanations.A: A note admits the gap but leaves the committee with no early warning on its two highest risks; the set still follows convenience, not exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Reliable data is one test of a KRI, but relevance to the top risks comes first; the 12 most reliable still track neither top-rated risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Incident shares show how often the top risks have already caused harm; they lag the events and warn of nothing before the next one.

tips: Eliminate: A notes the gap without closing it, and C reports past incidents, which lag the events a KRI should warn of.
Final two: D beats B because relevance to the top risks comes before data quality; a cleaner set of the wrong indicators still gives no warning where exposure is greatest.
Exam cue: choose KRIs for the risks that matter most, then test their data and timing; a set built from whatever is easy to measure can be precise and still blind.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (key risk indicator); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 2.4 (Metrics: adopting any available data point can undermine reporting, so a quantitative metric is kept only if it shows a valid control's performance or tracks a material risk to objectives)

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Teams choosing what they self-assess
questions.question: An app developer's nine product teams each choose which of their controls to rate in the yearly control self-assessment, and most pick their strongest. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Swap the self-assessment for risk-team tests of every control
options.B: Base the scope on the key controls over the top risks
options.C: Add last year's failed controls to the list each team chooses
options.D: Train control owners to rate their controls more critically

questions.key_concept: A control self-assessment's scope is set from the key controls over the top risks, not left to teams, who tend to pick their strongest controls.
questions.pre_read: Ask who decided which controls the self-assessment covers.
questions.correct_explanation: A self-assessment is only as useful as its scope. When teams pick which controls to rate, they choose their strongest, and the weak ones stay out of sight. Basing the scope on the key controls over the top risks puts the controls that matter most in front of their owners. Adding last year's failed controls is the runner-up: it catches known failures but still lets teams leave out weak controls nobody has tested.

wrong_explanations.A: Second-line tests of every control are neither risk-based nor practical, and they drop the first line's ownership of its controls that self-assessment builds.
wrong_explanations.C: Last year's failures widen the list, but teams still choose the rest, so weak key controls that never failed a test stay out of scope.
wrong_explanations.D: Training improves how controls are rated, not which controls are rated; teams that choose their own scope can still leave their weakest controls out.

tips: Eliminate: A swaps self-assessment for second-line tests of every control, losing first-line ownership, and D trains people to rate better while they still choose what to rate.
Final two: B beats C because scope should follow the risks; adding past failures to a self-chosen list still leaves untested weak controls out of view.
Exam cue: in a control self-assessment, the risk function sets the scope from the key controls over the top risks; letting each area choose what to rate tends to hide its gaps.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. A report that arrives after the budget
questions.question: An antique dealer's partners set spending each January; the risk analyst's yearly report, sent in April, has shown online fraud above appetite for two years, with no treatment funded. What is the analyst's BEST change?

options.A: Send the report before the partners set spending
options.B: Estimate treatment spending for the April report
options.C: Show the partners the fraud risk a band above its rating
options.D: Send the April report to the shop managers as well

questions.key_concept: Risk reporting is timed to the decisions it informs, such as budget setting, so that risk shapes choices instead of reviewing them afterward.
questions.pre_read: Compare when the report arrives with when the decision is made.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk report serves decisions, and the partners make their spending decision in January. A report arriving in April describes a risk the budget has already passed over, which is why two years of above-appetite ratings funded nothing. Sending the report before the partners set spending puts the risk in front of the decision. Estimating treatment spending for the April report is the runner-up: costs help a decision, but by April the money is allocated.

wrong_explanations.B: Treatment costs make a report more useful for deciding, but in April the year's spending is already set; better content arriving after the decision changes nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: Ratings are reported as assessed; inflating one to draw attention misleads the partners and undermines trust in every other rating in the report.
wrong_explanations.D: Shop managers cannot set the dealer's spending; adding readers without that authority does not bring the risk to the decision that funds treatment.

tips: Eliminate: C inflates a rating to draw attention, which misleads, and D adds readers who cannot set spending, so neither reaches the decision.
Final two: A beats B because the partners decide spending in January; cost estimates help only if they arrive while the money is still unallocated.
Exam cue: a risk report must reach decision makers before the decision it should inform, such as the budget round; content that arrives afterward describes a choice already made.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. A subcontractor the vendor never named
questions.question: At renewal, an interpreting agency's risk analyst finds its platform vendor quietly moved client data to a subcontractor, since reviewed as sound; the contract is silent on subcontractors. What should the analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Log the subcontractor in the business owner's vendor record
options.B: Advise the platform's business owner to switch vendors
options.C: Use the contract's audit right on the subcontractor's site
options.D: Add terms requiring notice and approval of subcontractors

questions.key_concept: A contract silent on subcontractors lets a vendor move data unseen; renewal terms requiring notice and approval of new subcontractors close that gap.
questions.pre_read: Separate the subcontractor found this time from the gap that let it happen.
questions.correct_explanation: The subcontractor was reviewed as sound, so this one is settled. The gap is the contract: silent on subcontractors, it let the vendor move client data without telling the agency and would let it do so again. Terms requiring notice and approval of new subcontractors, added at renewal, close that gap. Logging the subcontractor in the business owner's vendor record is the runner-up: it tracks this fourth party but leaves the next move unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Recording the subcontractor tracks this fourth party, but the contract still lets the vendor add or switch subcontractors without notice, so the next move stays unseen.
wrong_explanations.B: The subcontractor is sound and renewal is the moment to fix the contract; advising a switch over a gap that terms can close is out of proportion.
wrong_explanations.C: The subcontractor has already been reviewed as sound, and a contract silent on subcontractors may give no right over their sites; an audit repeats settled work.

tips: Eliminate: C audits a subcontractor already reviewed as sound, and B moves to a vendor switch when renewal terms can close the gap.
Final two: D beats A because recording this subcontractor tracks one fourth party; terms requiring notice and approval stop the vendor moving data unseen next time.
Exam cue: when a vendor moves data unannounced because the contract is silent, fix the contract at renewal with notice and approval rights; recording one change leaves the next unseen.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Controls over design-file theft
questions.question: A bearing maker's risk analyst is classifying its controls over theft of design files. Which of the following is BEST classified as a deterrent control?

options.A: Blocking of design-file uploads to personal cloud storage
options.B: Alerts on unusual download volumes by a single user
options.C: A sign-in notice that downloads are logged and misuse disciplined
options.D: A legal demand that a departing engineer return copied files

questions.key_concept: A deterrent control discourages an attempt by warning of its consequences; a preventive control stops the act whatever the person intends.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each control stops, finds, fixes or discourages the theft.
questions.correct_explanation: A deterrent control works on intent: it discourages an attempt by warning of consequences, without stopping or finding the act itself. A sign-in notice that downloads are logged and misuse disciplined does exactly that. Blocking uploads to personal cloud storage is the runner-up: it also lowers likelihood, but it is preventive, because it stops the transfer whatever the person intends.

wrong_explanations.A: Blocking uploads stops the transfer itself, whatever the person intends; that makes it preventive, even though, like a deterrent, it mainly lowers likelihood.
wrong_explanations.B: Alerts on unusual downloads find possible theft as it happens or after, so they are detective; they reduce harm only if someone acts on them in time.
wrong_explanations.D: A legal demand to return copied files acts after the theft to limit its harm, which makes it corrective, not a control that discourages the attempt.

tips: Eliminate: B finds unusual downloads once they happen, which is detective, and D acts after the theft to limit harm, which is corrective.
Final two: C beats A because a deterrent works by warning of consequences; a block that stops the upload whatever the intent is preventive, though both mainly lower likelihood.
Exam cue: classify a control by what it does to the event: deterrents discourage by warning, preventive controls stop the act, detective ones find it and corrective ones limit the harm.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. A bought prompt filter for a support chatbot
questions.question: A cloud backup provider's prompt filter, 99% effective on its vendor's public jailbreak benchmark, should stop the support chatbot from revealing customers' account details. Which of the following BEST shows the risk analyst it works?

options.A: Attack tests built from the provider's own support chats
options.B: The vendor's benchmark report, with its prompts and scoring
options.C: Share of support chats the filter has blocked since launch
options.D: Inspection of the filter's settings against the vendor's guide

questions.key_concept: An AI guardrail is tested with attacks drawn from the organization's own use and data, not judged on a vendor's benchmark of generic prompts.
questions.pre_read: Ask where each piece of evidence was produced, and under what conditions.
questions.correct_explanation: A guardrail is tested under the conditions it must work in. Attack tests built from the provider's own support chats try the routes customers and attackers would take to account details, so the results show whether the filter holds here. The vendor's benchmark report is the runner-up: it is real test evidence, but of generic jailbreak prompts, not of attempts on this chatbot's data and conversations.

wrong_explanations.B: A public benchmark shows how the filter handles generic jailbreak prompts; it does not show how it handles requests aimed at this chatbot's account data.
wrong_explanations.C: Blocked chats show the filter acting, not what it missed; a high count can mean frequent attacks or harmless questions being stopped.
wrong_explanations.D: Settings that match the vendor's guide show the filter is set up as designed; they do not show it stops attempts on account details in use.

tips: Eliminate: C counts what the filter blocked, not what got past it, and D checks its setup against the guide, which shows design, not whether it stops attacks.
Final two: A beats B because the benchmark tests generic jailbreaks; attack tests built from the provider's own support chats try the filter where it must hold, on account details.
Exam cue: test an AI guardrail with attacks drawn from the organization's own use and data; a vendor's benchmark shows performance under someone else's conditions.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Due dates that action owners can move
questions.question: A pipeline operator's action owners can move due dates in its risk register; the overdue-actions report has shown none for a year while several plans slipped. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Attestation by action owners that their due dates are realistic
options.B: Slippage reported against the due dates the plans first set
options.C: Review of the plans' status colors by the risk committee
options.D: Automatic reminders sent before due dates arrive

questions.key_concept: Slippage is measured against the due dates first agreed, so dates that action owners move cannot hide delay from the risk owner.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the overdue report measures against, and who can change it.
questions.correct_explanation: When action owners can move due dates freely, a slipping plan simply gets a new date, so the overdue report stays empty while the risk stays above its planned level. Reporting slippage against the dates the plans first set shows the risk owner how far each plan has drifted. Attestation by action owners is the runner-up: it asks the people who moved the dates to vouch for them, and reveals no drift.

wrong_explanations.A: The action owners who moved the dates would attest to them; a statement that dates are realistic does not show how far plans have drifted from what was agreed.
wrong_explanations.C: Status colors rest on the same movable dates and, with dates reset, show green; the committee would see the picture the empty overdue report already gives.
wrong_explanations.D: Reminders help meet dates, but a date that is about to be missed can still be moved unseen, so the overdue report stays empty while plans slip.

tips: Eliminate: C reviews status colors that rest on the same reset dates, and D sends reminders of dates that can still be moved unseen.
Final two: B beats A because measuring against the dates first set exposes drift from the record; attestation asks the owners who moved the dates to vouch for them.
Exam cue: when action owners can reset their own due dates, measure slippage against the dates first agreed; a report built on movable dates will show no delay.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Plants that send their top five risks
questions.question: A cocoa processor's six plants each send the group risk analyst five top-rated risks; a bean supplier's failure, ranked sixth to eighth at four plants, never appears. What should the analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Extend the plants' submissions from five risks to ten
options.B: Compare the plants' top-five lists for risks they share
options.C: Rank group risks from the plants' full registers combined
options.D: Ask the plants to mark register entries they think others share

questions.key_concept: Enterprise risks are ranked after combining units' full registers; a per-unit top-five filter can drop a risk that is large across units.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the ranking happens and what is dropped before it.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk ranked below the cut-off at several plants can be one of the group's largest, yet a top-five filter at each plant drops it before anyone sees the total. Ranking group risks from the plants' full registers combined lets shared exposure, such as the bean supplier's failure, add up and surface. Extending submissions to ten is the runner-up: it catches this risk, but any cut-off still drops one ranked lower at every plant.

wrong_explanations.A: Ten risks per plant would catch this supplier risk, but a cut-off remains: a shared risk ranked lower at every plant would still never reach the group view.
wrong_explanations.B: The supplier risk is in none of the top-five lists, so comparing those lists cannot find it; the filter acts before the comparison.
wrong_explanations.D: A plant sees its own register, not the others', so it cannot tell which risks are shared; the group view of the combined registers can.

tips: Eliminate: B compares lists the supplier risk never entered, and D asks plants to spot sharing they cannot see from their own registers.
Final two: C beats A because any per-plant cut-off drops a risk ranked below it at every plant; ranking after combining full registers lets shared exposure add up.
Exam cue: aggregate before you filter; when each unit forwards its top risks, a risk shared across units can be large in total yet miss the enterprise view.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. A small sample of many changes
questions.question: An outdoor gear retailer's risk team tests 25 of about 3,000 privileged changes a quarter against approved tickets; the change logs and tickets are machine-readable and share IDs. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the control owner automate matching changes to tickets
options.B: Double the sample the risk team draws at random
options.C: Get the control owner's sign-off that changes match their tickets
options.D: Limit privileged changes to a set change window

questions.key_concept: Where control records are high in volume and machine-readable, automated monitoring of the whole population covers far more than periodic sampling.
questions.pre_read: Weigh the sample size against the volume, and note what form the records take.
questions.correct_explanation: With about 3,000 privileged changes a quarter, and logs and tickets that are machine-readable and share IDs, a check can compare every change with its ticket as it happens. Having the control owner automate that match turns a small periodic sample into continuous coverage, with the risk team validating the check and reviewing its exceptions. Doubling the sample is the runner-up: it strengthens the test, but 50 of about 3,000 still leaves most changes unchecked.

wrong_explanations.B: A larger random sample tests the control more reliably, but 50 of about 3,000 changes still leaves most unchecked when the records allow checking every one.
wrong_explanations.C: A sign-off is the owner's statement that changes match tickets, which is inquiry; it adds no evidence and checks no change against its ticket.
wrong_explanations.D: A change window controls when privileged changes happen, not whether each was approved; changes made inside the window still need matching to tickets.

tips: Eliminate: C rests on the owner's word, which checks nothing, and D limits when changes happen, not whether they were approved.
Final two: A beats B because the logs and tickets are machine-readable and share IDs, so automation can check the whole population; a bigger sample still leaves most unseen.

Exam cue: when a control's records are high in volume and machine-readable, automated checks of the whole population beat larger samples; the control owner runs them, the risk team validates them and reviews exceptions.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. A pass rate from part of the controls
questions.question: A professional body's risk committee report says 96% of key controls are effective; the risk analyst finds the figure covers the 48 of 110 tested this year. What is the BEST change to the report?

options.A: Map the result onto the committee's heat-map color bands
options.B: Estimate results for the untested key controls from the tested ones
options.C: Show the result's trend against earlier reports
options.D: Report the number of key controls tested beside the result

questions.key_concept: A control pass rate is reported with the number of controls tested, so untested controls are not read as working.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the percentage is a share of.
questions.correct_explanation: A pass rate means little without its coverage: 96% of the 48 controls tested says nothing about the 62 not tested, yet the committee may read it as 96% of all key controls working. Reporting the number of key controls tested beside the result states that limit plainly. Showing the trend against earlier reports is the runner-up: trend helps, but a trend in a figure whose coverage is unstated keeps the gap hidden.

wrong_explanations.A: Heat-map colors restyle the 96% without saying how many controls it covers; the committee would still read it as a result for the whole set.
wrong_explanations.B: Untested controls give no evidence; estimating their results from the tested ones assumes they work, which is the very gap the report should show.
wrong_explanations.C: Trend adds direction, but a trend in a pass rate covering 48 of 110 key controls still hides that most key controls were not tested.

tips: Eliminate: A recolors the result without stating what it covers, and B credits untested controls with results no test produced.
Final two: D beats C because the committee cannot weigh 96% without knowing it covers 48 of 110 key controls; a trend in that figure keeps the gap hidden.
Exam cue: report control results with their coverage; a pass rate on the controls tested says nothing about those not tested, so state how much of the population it covers.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. A data source under consultation
questions.question: A meteorological office's forecasts depend on free satellite data from a foreign agency, which is consulting on keeping it free, charging for it or ending access. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: A single scenario built on the most likely outcome
options.B: Scenarios for the three outcomes, agreed with the risk owner
options.C: A rating based on the worst outcome, the agency ending access
options.D: Commercial satellite data under contract as a backup

questions.key_concept: An emerging risk with several distinct possible outcomes is analyzed as alternative scenarios agreed with its owner, not rated on one outcome.
questions.pre_read: Count the possible outcomes and ask whether they need the same response.
questions.correct_explanation: The consultation has three distinct outcomes, and they would hit forecasting differently: charging needs budget, ending access needs another data source, and keeping it free needs nothing. Scenarios for the three outcomes, agreed with the risk owner, show the effect of each and the options to prepare. A rating based on the worst outcome is the runner-up: it is prudent, but it sizes one future and prepares nothing for the charging outcome.

wrong_explanations.A: Planning on the most likely outcome leaves the office unready if the consultation goes another way, and while the decision is open no outcome is known.
wrong_explanations.C: Rating on the worst case sizes one future; charging for the data would need a different response, which a single worst-case rating does not prepare.
wrong_explanations.D: Signing for commercial data commits spending before the outcome is known; if the data stay free, the money is wasted, and scenarios would show when a backup is needed.

tips: Eliminate: A plans on one outcome while the decision is open, and D commits spending on a backup before anyone knows whether it will be needed.
Final two: B beats C because the three outcomes need different responses; a worst-case rating sizes one of them, while scenarios agreed with the risk owner prepare for each.
Exam cue: when an emerging risk could resolve in several distinct ways, build a scenario for each with the risk owner, not a rating of one outcome, then prepare options to match.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Many small card-fraud losses
questions.question: A bookstore chain's online store has about 600 card-fraud chargebacks a year, averaging $300, and their yearly total is above appetite; the finance director proposes insurance. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Buy an insurance policy that covers chargeback losses
options.B: Stop taking card payments in the online store
options.C: Run fraud checks on online orders before dispatch
options.D: Budget for the losses like other trading costs

questions.key_concept: Insurance suits rare, severe losses; many small, predictable losses above appetite are better cut at their cause, as cover is priced on expected claims.
questions.pre_read: Note how often the losses happen and how large each one is.
questions.correct_explanation: The losses are many, small and predictable, and together above appetite. Fraud checks on orders before dispatch act on the cause and cut how often the losses happen. Insurance covering chargebacks is the runner-up: transfer is a real response, but cover for losses this regular is priced on the claims the insurer expects, plus its own costs, so the chain pays for its fraud through premiums while the fraud carries on.

wrong_explanations.A: Cover for losses this frequent is priced on the claims the insurer expects, plus its costs; it moves money without reducing the fraud behind the losses.
wrong_explanations.B: Card payments are how the online store sells; ending them gives up that revenue to remove a risk that a control at the cause could reduce.
wrong_explanations.D: The yearly total is above appetite, so budgeting for the losses like other costs keeps a level of risk the appetite does not allow; acceptance fits risks within it.

tips: Eliminate: B gives up the store's card sales when a control could cut the risk, and D budgets for losses above appetite like other costs.
Final two: C beats A because the losses are many and small; checks cut them at the cause, while cover for such regular losses is priced on the claims it repays.
Exam cue: insurance fits rare, severe losses the business cannot absorb; when many small losses add up above appetite, reduce them at the cause.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.4.1 (Risk Response Cost: the cost of a response is compared with the risk exposure to support a cost-benefit analysis); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 Task 3-2 (Evaluation of Alternatives: effectiveness, feasibility and cost)

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Patient data in a booking app
questions.question: A physiotherapy clinic chain needs an owner for the risk of patient data leaking from its new online booking app. Which of the following should the risk analyst propose as the MOST appropriate owner?

options.A: The operations director who runs patient bookings
options.B: The project manager who led the app's build
options.C: The IT manager whose team hosts the app
options.D: The data protection officer for the chain

questions.key_concept: A risk is owned by the manager who runs the affected service and can fund its controls; a data protection officer advises and monitors instead.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each role does for the app once it is in use.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk belongs with the manager who runs the service it affects and has the authority and budget to treat it: the operations director who runs patient bookings. The data protection officer is the runner-up: the role advises on and monitors how patient data is handled, but it does not run bookings or fund their controls, and owning the risk would leave it overseeing its own decisions.

wrong_explanations.B: The project manager answers for delivering the app; the project role ends once the app is in use, which would leave the live risk with nobody.
wrong_explanations.C: IT hosts the app and may own technical controls on it, but the harm of leaked patient data falls on the bookings service, which IT does not run.
wrong_explanations.D: The data protection officer advises on and monitors patient-data handling; owning the risk would mean overseeing its own decisions, without authority over bookings.

tips: Eliminate: B's project role ends once the app is in use, and C hosts the app without running the service whose patients would be harmed.
Final two: A beats D because the operations director runs bookings and can fund their controls; the data protection officer advises and monitors, which owning the risk would compromise.
Exam cue: a risk to personal data is owned by the manager who runs the service using it; builders, hosts and advisory roles such as a data protection officer support that owner.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk owner); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. An outside rating falls
questions.question: An accreditation body subscribes to a service that rates vendors' security from their internet-facing systems; the score of the vendor hosting its online exams has dropped sharply. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Start moving the exams to another hosting vendor
options.B: Re-rate the vendor's risk using the new score
options.C: Report the score's drop to the board's risk committee
options.D: Seek the vendor's explanation of the score's drop

questions.key_concept: An outside security rating is a signal; when a vendor's score drops, get the cause and its evidence from the vendor before re-rating its risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the rating service can see, and what it cannot.
questions.correct_explanation: The service rates the vendor from what it sees online, so the drop is a signal with no known cause: a real weakness, a minor issue or systems wrongly linked to the vendor. Seeking the vendor's explanation through its relationship owner, with evidence, gives the facts to reassess on. Re-rating the vendor's risk using the new score is the runner-up: a reassessment is due, but resting it on the score alone may misstate the risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Moving the exams is costly and disruptive, and the drop has no known cause; acting before learning it may answer a problem that does not exist.
wrong_explanations.B: The score comes from an outside view and can misread systems or weigh minor issues; re-rating on it before learning the cause may misstate the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Taking an unexplained score to the risk committee asks leaders to weigh a signal nobody has checked; the cause should be known first.

tips: Eliminate: A starts a costly vendor move on an unexplained signal, and C takes an unchecked score to the risk committee.
Final two: D beats B because the score is an outside view of the vendor's systems; the vendor's explanation, with evidence, gives the reassessment facts, while the score alone may misstate the risk.
Exam cue: when an outside rating of a vendor drops with no known event behind it, ask the vendor for the cause and its evidence first, then reassess on what that shows.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-07 (the risks posed by a supplier, their products and services and other third parties are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to and monitored); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SR-6 (Supplier Assessments and Reviews)

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Red-team findings on an AI tool
questions.question: An ad tech firm's red team found nine weaknesses in its unreleased AI ad writer, such as leaking other clients' briefs; its developers queued them in their backlog. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep the ad writer out of client campaigns
options.B: Enter the findings in the issue log with owners and ratings
options.C: Keep the findings in the developers' backlog, ranked by severity
options.D: Add an output filter that hides other clients' details from its ads

questions.key_concept: Red-team findings on an AI tool are issues: logged, rated by the risk they affect and owned; the builders' backlog schedules the fixes.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can see the weaknesses, and on what scale, once they sit in the backlog.
questions.correct_explanation: Red-team findings are weaknesses like audit findings. In the issue log, they are rated by the risk they affect, given owners and due dates, escalated when late and closed on evidence. Keeping them in the developers' backlog, ranked by severity, is the runner-up: the backlog can still schedule the fixes, but its severity scale says nothing about business risk, and the risk owner never sees a leak of clients' briefs.

wrong_explanations.A: Holding the ad writer back from client campaigns comes before anyone has rated the weaknesses; the response should follow the rated risk, and the findings still need tracking.
wrong_explanations.C: The backlog schedules fixes, but outside the issue log the weaknesses have no risk rating or accountable owner, so the risk owner cannot see or escalate them.
wrong_explanations.D: An output filter may treat one weakness, but it is a fix chosen before the nine are rated, and the other weaknesses stay untracked.

tips: Eliminate: A holds the tool back before anyone has rated the weaknesses, and D picks one fix before the nine are rated and leaves the rest untracked.
Final two: B beats C because the backlog gives the findings a technical severity and no accountable owner; in the issue log they are rated by risk, owned and tracked.
Exam cue: when a red team finds weaknesses in an AI tool, log them in the issue log with owners and risk ratings; the builders' backlog schedules fixes but does not show the risk.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Travel claims within the limits
questions.question: A review found members' travel claims at a parliamentary office were within allowed amounts but covered private trips; the office handles about 400 claims a month. Which control should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: A claims officer's check of trips against official agendas
options.B: Rules that flag claims above set amounts for review
options.C: Signed statements from members that their trips were official
options.D: Publication of members' names alongside their claim totals

questions.key_concept: A control should test the condition that failed, here a trip's purpose, against records the claimant does not keep, at a volume people can check.
questions.pre_read: Ask which condition the private trips broke and which control actually tests it.
questions.correct_explanation: The claims passed because nobody checked what the trips were for. A claims officer comparing trips with the office's official agendas tests that purpose against records the claimant does not keep, and at about 400 claims a month a person can do it. Signed statements from members are the runner-up: they may deter, but they ask the people who made the private claims to vouch for their own trips.

wrong_explanations.B: The private trips were within the allowed amounts, so a rule on amounts would pass them; it tests the condition that held, not the purpose that failed.
wrong_explanations.C: A signed statement relies on the members who made the private claims to judge their own trips; it may deter, but it adds no independent check of purpose.
wrong_explanations.D: Publishing names and totals shows how much members claim, not what the trips were for; claims within the allowed amounts would look normal.

tips: Eliminate: B tests amounts, which the private trips already met, and D publishes totals that say nothing about what a trip was for.
Final two: A beats C because a statement from the claimant is not an independent check; an officer comparing trips with official agendas tests purpose against records the claimant does not keep.
Exam cue: when a control passes items that meet its rule but fail its purpose, choose a check of that purpose against independent evidence, not the claimant's word.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. A shop closed to avoid a risk
questions.question: A cereal maker closed its web shop to avoid a breach of the card details it stored; the action owner reports the plan done with the site offline. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Record the card breach risk as avoided in the register
options.B: Put the plan's closure to the risk owner for sign-off
options.C: Confirm the stored card details have been deleted
options.D: Record the plan as complete in the risk report

questions.key_concept: An avoidance plan is complete when the exposure is gone, such as stored card details deleted, not when the visible activity stops.
questions.pre_read: Separate the activity that stopped from the exposure the risk describes.
questions.correct_explanation: Avoidance removes the exposure behind a risk. Taking the site offline stops new orders, but the risk is a breach of the card details the shop stored, which may still sit in its database. Confirming they have been deleted, backups included, shows the exposure is gone. Putting the plan's closure to the risk owner for sign-off is the runner-up: the owner signs once evidence shows it worked, and an offline site is not that evidence.

wrong_explanations.A: Recording the risk as avoided rests on the action owner's report; the stored card details, the exposure itself, may still exist.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk owner signs closure on evidence that the plan worked; asking now puts an unchecked claim in front of them.
wrong_explanations.D: Reporting the plan complete passes the action owner's unchecked claim to readers, while the stored card details may still exist.

tips: Eliminate: A records the risk as avoided on the action owner's word, and D reports the plan complete on the same unchecked claim.
Final two: C beats B because the risk owner signs closure on evidence; an offline site stops new orders but says nothing about the card details already stored.
Exam cue: when an avoidance plan is reported done, confirm the exposure itself is gone, such as stored data deleted, before anyone signs or reports it closed.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. More orders riding on one system
questions.question: A trucking firm's dispatch system fails as often as ever, but more orders carry same-day delivery promises. Which of the following should the risk analyst propose as the BEST KRI for its outage risk?

options.A: Dispatch outages the system owner has logged
options.B: Orders now booked for same-day delivery slots
options.C: Share of dispatch servers missing current patches
options.D: Same-day deliveries the risk owner's team logged as missed in outages

questions.key_concept: KRIs can track drivers of impact: when more business rides on a system, a KRI of that exposure shows an outage would cost more.
questions.pre_read: Ask which part of the risk the stem says is changing.
questions.correct_explanation: The outages happen as often as before, so the risk is growing through its impact: more orders carry same-day promises that an outage would break. A KRI of orders booked for same-day delivery tracks that exposure and moves before the next outage costs more. Missed same-day deliveries are the runner-up: they also measure impact, but they rise after an outage has broken promises, not ahead of the next one.

wrong_explanations.A: Logged outages are past events, and the stem says they come no more often; a count of them cannot show that the next one would cost more.
wrong_explanations.C: Patch gaps drive how often the system fails, but the outages come as often as ever; the growth is in what an outage would break.
wrong_explanations.D: Missed deliveries logged in outages count harm already done; they rise after an outage breaks promises, not as more orders come to carry them.

tips: Eliminate: A counts outages and C tracks patch gaps that drive them; both measure how often the system fails, which the stem says has not changed.
Final two: B beats D because D counts missed deliveries after an outage strikes; B rises with same-day bookings before the next outage costs more.
Exam cue: when a risk grows through what an event would cost, such as more business riding on one system, choose a KRI of that exposure, not of how often it fails.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. A scan that misses the supply regions
questions.question: A rubber goods maker's horizon scan watches technology and regulation, yet most of its natural rubber comes from plantations in two regions. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Hire more analysts to read the current sources
options.B: Score signals on likelihood before they are reported
options.C: Send questionnaires to its rubber suppliers on their risks
options.D: Widen the scan to conditions in both growing regions

questions.key_concept: A horizon scan's sources should follow what the enterprise depends on, such as the regions its key raw material comes from.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the scan watches with what the business depends on.
questions.correct_explanation: The scan watches technology and regulation, but the business depends on rubber from two regions, where crop disease, weather or export rules could cut supply. Widening the scan to conditions there catches those changes early. Questionnaires to the rubber suppliers are the runner-up: they assess each supplier's current controls, as reported by the supplier, but they do not watch for changes across a region that no single supplier controls.

wrong_explanations.A: More analysts reading the same sources cover the same ground; the gap is what the scan watches, not how many people read it.
wrong_explanations.B: Emerging risks are often unlikely but severe, so screening on likelihood drops signals that matter; it also leaves the supply regions unwatched.
wrong_explanations.C: Supplier questionnaires report each supplier's current controls in its own words; they do not watch for regional changes, such as disease or export rules, that no supplier controls.

tips: Eliminate: A adds readers to the same sources, and B screens signals on likelihood alone, which drops unlikely but severe ones.
Final two: D beats C because the gap is the scan's coverage of the two regions; supplier questionnaires assess current controls, not regional changes no single supplier controls.
Exam cue: when a horizon scan's sources miss something the business depends on, such as where a key material comes from, widen the scan to cover it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286A Rev. 1 Section 2.2.5 (Recording Identified Risks: developing or emerging risks are yet to be fully defined but might disrupt enterprise objectives in the future); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-03 (internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded)

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Owners who left or moved
questions.question: Twice this year, a soft drink maker's register named risk owners who had left or changed jobs, leaving risks undecided for months. Which of the following should the risk analyst recommend as the BEST fix?

options.A: Job-change notices from HR routed to the risk team
options.B: A reminder for managers to report their own job changes
options.C: Departments named as risk owners in the register
options.D: Deputies named as second owners of the risks

questions.key_concept: Ownership stays current when HR's job-change notices reach the risk team, so a departure or move prompts reassignment as it happens.
questions.pre_read: Pin down what went wrong twice before judging the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Owners left or moved without the register showing it, so ownership checks need a trigger where those changes are first recorded. Job-change notices from HR, routed to the risk team, flag each departure or move as it happens, so the risk can be reassigned. A reminder for managers is the runner-up: it relies on each manager remembering to report a move while leaving or starting a new role, so some still go unreported.

wrong_explanations.B: Self-reporting depends on each manager remembering to tell the risk team while leaving or starting a new role, so moves can still go unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.C: A department cannot be held to account or accept a risk; ownership needs one named person with authority, so the risks would still have nobody to decide them.
wrong_explanations.D: Two owners per risk blur who must decide, and a deputy can leave or move unnoticed too; it adds names without catching the changes.

tips: Eliminate: C hands risks to departments, which cannot be held to account, and D adds second owners, which blurs who decides and still misses moves.
Final two: A beats B because HR records each job change where it happens; a reminder relies on every manager remembering to report a move, so some slip through.
Exam cue: when named owners leave or move without the register noticing, tie ownership checks to HR's job-change records, not to people reporting their own moves.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. A vendor's four-hour recovery promise
questions.question: A medicines regulator's case-management SaaS vendor promises in its contract to recover the service within four hours, matching the regulator's RTO. What should the risk analyst ask the vendor for as the BEST assurance?

options.A: A written recovery plan for the service
options.B: Penalty terms for late recovery of the service
options.C: The latest recovery test results for the service
options.D: Uptime figures the vendor reports for the service

questions.key_concept: A vendor's promised recovery time is backed by its recovery test results; a plan, uptime figures or penalty terms cannot show the promise holds.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the vendor says from what it has shown.
questions.correct_explanation: A contract promise and a plan say what the vendor intends; a test shows whether the service actually comes back within four hours. The latest recovery test results give the regulator evidence that its RTO can be met, and show any gaps to raise with the vendor. A written recovery plan is the runner-up: it shows how recovery is meant to work, but until it is tested nobody knows whether it does.

wrong_explanations.A: A plan shows how the vendor means to recover, which is design; without test results it cannot show the service returns within four hours.
wrong_explanations.B: Penalty terms pay the regulator something when recovery is late; they shift some cost but neither show nor improve the vendor's ability to recover in time.
wrong_explanations.D: Uptime shows how rarely the service has failed, not how fast it returns when it does; a strong record says nothing about the four-hour promise.

tips: Eliminate: B prices a late recovery without showing the promise can be met, and D measures how rarely the service fails, not how fast it recovers.
Final two: C beats A because test results show recovery working in practice; a written plan shows how the vendor intends to recover, not that it can.
Exam cue: when the business relies on a vendor's promised recovery time, seek results of the vendor's recovery tests; plans, uptime and penalties do not prove the promise.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. A login that cannot be named
questions.question: A pathology lab network's analyzers run maker-validated software with one built-in administrator login that cannot be split into named accounts. Which control should the risk analyst recommend as the BEST compensating control?

options.A: A paper log of setting changes kept beside the analyzers
options.B: Access to the shared login through a vault logging its users
options.C: Password changes for the login after staff leave
options.D: Review of setting changes by the lab supervisor

questions.key_concept: A compensating control covers the weakness it stands in for; when a shared login cannot be split, a vault that records each checkout restores accountability.
questions.pre_read: Name the weakness first, then ask which option covers it.
questions.correct_explanation: The weakness is that one shared login hides who made each change. A vault that hands the login to named staff, records each checkout and changes the password after use restores that link, compensating for the missing named accounts. A paper log kept beside the analyzers is the runner-up: it aims at the same gap, but depends on staff writing in it, so a change made without an entry stays untraceable.

wrong_explanations.A: A paper log targets the right gap, but it depends on people writing in it; a change made without an entry still cannot be traced to anyone.
wrong_explanations.C: Changing the password after leavers shuts out former staff, but current staff still share one login, so no change can be tied to a person.
wrong_explanations.D: A supervisor's review finds setting changes after they happen, but the shared login still hides who made them, which is the gap to cover.

tips: Eliminate: C shuts out leavers while current staff still share the login, and D spots setting changes without showing who made them.
Final two: B beats A because the vault records each user as it hands out the login; a paper log depends on staff choosing to write in it.
Exam cue: a compensating control must cover the weakness it stands in for; when a login cannot be split into named accounts, pick the option that ties each use to a person.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Evidence of capability level 4
questions.question: A locomotive overhaul works set COBIT 2019 capability level 4 as the target for its change management process. Which of the following BEST shows the risk analyst the process has reached it?

options.A: A documented change process that the teams follow
options.B: Records showing changes were approved before release
options.C: Experienced staff who run changes without written steps
options.D: Quantitative measures kept of how the process performs

questions.key_concept: On COBIT 2019's capability scale, level 4 adds quantitative measurement of performance to a well-defined process; a followed procedure shows level 3.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each capability level adds to the one below it.
questions.correct_explanation: On COBIT 2019's scale, level 4 means the process achieves its purpose, is well defined and has its performance quantitatively measured. Quantitative measures kept of how the process performs are the evidence that sets level 4 apart. A documented change process that the teams follow is the runner-up: it shows a well-defined process, which is level 3, but without measurement it cannot show level 4.

wrong_explanations.A: A defined process that the teams follow marks level 3; level 4 also needs the process's performance measured, which a procedure does not show.
wrong_explanations.B: Approval records show a basic, complete set of activities being performed, about level 2; they show neither a defined process nor measurement.
wrong_explanations.C: Staff working from experience with no written steps show an intuitive way of working, not a defined process; level 4 needs a defined process with measured performance.

tips: Eliminate: C describes an intuitive process with nothing written down, and B shows approvals being performed; both sit well below a measured process.
Final two: D beats A because level 4 adds quantitative measurement to a well-defined process; a procedure that the teams follow shows level 3.
Exam cue: on COBIT 2019's capability scale, look for performed activities at level 2, a defined process at 3, quantitative measurement at 4 and continuous improvement at 5.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Industry News 18 March 2019 (Defining Target Capability Levels in COBIT 2019: level 4 means a process achieves its purpose, is well defined and its performance is quantitatively measured); ISACA Glossary (maturity)

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Bias testing reported done at licensing
questions.question: HR reports a lumber yard chain's plan to add bias testing to its AI applicant screener as done, because the testing tool is now licensed. What should the risk analyst request FIRST?

options.A: Confirmation of the license for the bias-testing tool
options.B: Confirmation that the testing tool is linked to the screener
options.C: Bias test results from the screener's recent decisions
options.D: The risk owner's sign-off that the plan is complete

questions.key_concept: An action plan adding AI bias testing is complete once tests run on live decisions and results reach the risk owner, not at licensing.
questions.pre_read: Separate buying a tool from the work the plan promised.
questions.correct_explanation: A licensed tool is a purchase, not a control at work. The plan is complete when bias tests actually run on the screener's decisions and their results reach the risk owner, so results from recent screening are the evidence to request first. Confirmation that the tool is linked to the screener is the runner-up: it shows the tool is installed, but not that any test has run or what it found.

wrong_explanations.A: A license shows the tool was bought; it says nothing about whether any bias test has run on the screener's decisions.
wrong_explanations.B: A link shows the tool is installed and can reach the screener; installed is not operating, and there are still no results for anyone to act on.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk owner approves closing the plan, but signing off an unchecked claim adds no evidence; the sign-off follows the test results, not before them.

tips: Eliminate: A proves a purchase, not a test, and D asks the risk owner to sign off a claim before any evidence backs it.
Final two: C beats B because results show bias tests running on real screening decisions; a link to the screener shows the tool is installed, not used.
Exam cue: an action that adds a check is done when the check runs and its results reach the owner; a bought or installed tool is not yet a working control.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Plants logging losses from different amounts
questions.question: Two of a faucet maker's four plants log every loss over $1,000; the other two log only losses over $25,000. To rank the plants by this quarter's losses, what should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Use losses over $25,000 from the four plants
options.B: Require the two plants to log losses over $1,000
options.C: Rank the four plants' totals, thresholds noted alongside
options.D: Estimate losses under $25,000 at the two plants

questions.key_concept: Unit figures logged above different amounts are not comparable; compare units on the highest amount they all record before ranking or adding them.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the four plants' figures measure the same thing.
questions.correct_explanation: The plants record losses above different amounts, so their totals do not compare: the two logging from $1,000 look worse simply because they record more. Using losses over $25,000 from the four plants puts them on one basis before ranking. Ranking the totals with the thresholds noted alongside is the runner-up: stating a limitation suits a gap that cannot be closed, but this one can, and a note leaves the ranking itself skewed.

wrong_explanations.B: One $1,000 threshold suits future quarters, but two plants hold no records of this quarter's smaller losses, so it cannot fix this ranking.
wrong_explanations.C: A note states the flaw but leaves it in the ranking; the plants logging from $1,000 still look worse, though a common basis is available now.
wrong_explanations.D: Estimating losses nobody recorded adds guessed figures to the ranking, when recorded losses above a shared amount already give a fair comparison.

tips: Eliminate: B changes future logging but cannot recover this quarter's small losses, and D fills the gap with estimates nobody measured.
Final two: A beats C because the gap can be closed now by ranking on losses over $25,000 at every plant; a note leaves the skewed ranking in place.
Exam cue: before ranking or adding units' figures, put them on one basis, such as the same recording threshold; state as a limitation a gap that cannot be closed.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. A surveillance rule above every limit
questions.question: An energy trading firm's limit-breach monitor flags trades over $50 million and flagged none this year; traders' approved limits run from $5 million to $20 million. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: One $20 million threshold for the firm's trades
options.B: The clean year taken as evidence the traders' approved limits hold
options.C: Confirmation from the vendor that the monitor runs correctly
options.D: Trade thresholds tied to the traders' approved limits

questions.key_concept: A monitoring rule is set from the limits it polices; a threshold above every limit stays silent while breaches pass.
questions.pre_read: Compare the monitor's setting with the limits it is supposed to watch.
questions.correct_explanation: The monitor flags what its rule asks for, and a $50 million threshold sits above every trader's limit, so a breach can pass unflagged and a silent year proves nothing. Trade thresholds tied to the traders' approved limits make the rule test what the limits forbid. One $20 million threshold is the runner-up: it matches the largest limit, but a trader with a $5 million limit could exceed it by $15 million unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: One threshold at the largest limit still lets traders with $5 million limits trade up to $20 million unflagged; the rule has to follow the limits.
wrong_explanations.B: A rule set above every limit cannot flag a breach, so its silence is no evidence that traders keep to their limits.
wrong_explanations.C: The monitor may run exactly as built; the gap is the rule's setting, which sits above the limits it is meant to police.

tips: Eliminate: B takes the rule's silence as proof, and C checks that the monitor runs when the gap is its setting, which sits above every limit.
Final two: D beats A because thresholds tied to the approved limits flag a breach at any size; one $20 million threshold misses traders with smaller limits.
Exam cue: when monitoring stays silent, ask what its rule could ever flag; set alert rules from the limits or tolerances they police, not a round figure.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Accepted risks past their review dates
questions.question: A password manager vendor's monthly reports to risk owners list their risks, KRIs and open actions, yet four accepted risks passed their review dates unnoticed. What should the risk analyst add as BEST?

options.A: Share of accepted risks past their review dates
options.B: The upcoming review dates of their accepted risks
options.C: Board reports listing accepted risks once a year
options.D: Board dashboards marking lapsed acceptances in red

questions.key_concept: Reports to risk owners show their accepted risks coming up for review, with the dates, so owners decide again before an acceptance lapses.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an owner needs to see before a date passes.
questions.correct_explanation: The reviews lapsed because owners did not see the dates coming, so their own reports should show them in time. The upcoming review dates of their accepted risks let each owner decide again, renew, change or end the acceptance, before it lapses. Share of accepted risks past their review dates is the runner-up: it measures the problem, but counts lapses after they happen and does not tell an owner which risk to review next.

wrong_explanations.A: A share of lapsed reviews shows the problem after dates have passed; it does not point an owner to the acceptance falling due next.
wrong_explanations.C: The board does need accepted risks in view, but a yearly report reaches the board, not the owners, and too late to prompt a review before its date.
wrong_explanations.D: Marking lapses red shows them after the dates have passed, and on a board dashboard, not in the reports read by the owners who must act.

tips: Eliminate: C reports accepted risks to the board once a year, not to the owners, and D flags acceptances once they have already lapsed.
Final two: B beats A because upcoming dates prompt each owner before a review falls due; a share of lapsed reviews counts the failures after they happen.
Exam cue: when acceptances lapse because owners did not see their review dates coming, show each owner the dates falling due; a share of past lapses counts failures after the fact.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. A bug bounty within appetite
questions.question: A cybersecurity firm's public bug bounty program finds flaws its testers miss; its analyzed risk, legal exposure included, is within appetite, but counsel wants it closed. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Record the risk owner's acceptance of the program's risk
options.B: Replace the program with more testing by in-house staff
options.C: Replace public entry with researchers invited under contract
options.D: Have the risk owner buy cover for researchers' testing damage

questions.key_concept: Risk within appetite from a beneficial activity is accepted on record by its risk owner and monitored; closing or narrowing it would forfeit that benefit.
questions.pre_read: Place the analyzed risk against appetite before weighing any change to the program.
questions.correct_explanation: The program's analyzed risk is within appetite, and the program serves the firm by finding flaws its own testers miss, so the risk owner accepts the risk on record and it stays monitored. Replacing public entry with invited researchers is the runner-up: it cuts the risk further, but gives up much of the outside testing that finds those flaws, to reduce a risk the firm can already carry.

wrong_explanations.B: Ending the program avoids a risk already within appetite and gives up its benefit, flaws found that the firm's own testers miss.
wrong_explanations.C: Limiting the program to invited researchers reduces a risk that already fits appetite and loses much of the outside testing that finds missed flaws.
wrong_explanations.D: Insurance moves part of the cost of a risk the firm can already carry within appetite, so it adds cost without need.

tips: Eliminate: B ends a program that finds flaws in-house testers miss, and D buys cover for a risk already within appetite; both spend benefit or money without need.
Final two: A beats C because the risk already fits appetite; inviting researchers cuts the outside testing that finds missed flaws, while the risk owner's acceptance keeps it running and monitored.

Exam cue: when a beneficial activity's risk is within appetite, the risk owner accepts it on record, with monitoring; closing, narrowing or insuring it spends benefit or money on a risk the firm can carry.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. An exception up for renewal
questions.question: A care home operator's exception, due for renewal, lets its nurse-call system skip the encryption standard; compensating log reviews cost $60,000 a year, and a fix $40,000. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Renewal by the risk owner with the same log reviews
options.B: An exemption for the nurse-call system from the standard
options.C: A funded upgrade that brings the system into compliance
options.D: Spot checks of a sample of the nurse-call system's logs

questions.key_concept: At an exception's renewal, compare the yearly cost of its compensating controls with the cost of complying; when complying costs less, recommend the fix.
questions.pre_read: Compare what keeping the exception costs each year with what ending it would cost.
questions.correct_explanation: An exception is a temporary deviation with a plan to comply. Here the compensating log reviews cost $60,000 every year, while a fix costs $40,000, so a funded upgrade removes both the gap and its running cost; the risk owner decides on that recommendation. Renewal by the risk owner with the same reviews is the runner-up: it follows the approval route but keeps paying more each year for a gap the fix would close.

wrong_explanations.A: Renewal follows the approval route, but it keeps paying $60,000 a year to compensate for a gap that a $40,000 fix would close.
wrong_explanations.B: An exemption suits a requirement that cannot apply; this system can be brought into line with the standard, so it needs a plan to comply.
wrong_explanations.D: Thinning the compensating reviews saves money by weakening the control that covers the gap, without weighing the risk it then leaves.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a requirement the system can meet as one that cannot apply, and D thins the compensating control to save money without weighing the risk left.
Final two: C beats A because the reviews cost $60,000 every year against a $40,000 fix; renewal follows the process but keeps paying more for a gap the upgrade closes.
Exam cue: at an exception's renewal, set what keeping it costs, compensating controls included, against what complying costs; when complying is cheaper, recommend the fix over another renewal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked); NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.4.1 (Risk Response Cost: the cost of a response is compared with the risk exposure to support a cost-benefit analysis)

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Baselines for a grants system
questions.question: A research council applying NIST SP 800-53B chose the moderate baseline for its grants system, which holds applicants' personal data. Which of the following is the BEST addition for the risk analyst to recommend?

options.A: A move to the high security baseline for the system
options.B: Controls copied from a peer council's grants system
options.C: Controls mapped from CSF 2.0's Protect outcomes
options.D: The privacy control baseline, tailored to the system

questions.key_concept: SP 800-53B pairs security baselines chosen by impact level with a privacy baseline for systems that process personal data, applied whatever the impact level.
questions.pre_read: Notice what kind of data the system holds, then ask which baseline covers that kind of risk.
questions.correct_explanation: SP 800-53B gives three security baselines, chosen by a system's impact level, and a privacy baseline applied irrespective of impact level to manage the privacy risks of processing personal data. The grants system holds applicants' data, so the privacy baseline, tailored to it, is the addition. The high security baseline is the runner-up: it adds protection against loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability, not the controls for how personal data is processed.

wrong_explanations.A: A higher security baseline adds protection against loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability; privacy risks from processing personal data are addressed by the privacy baseline.
wrong_explanations.B: Another council's controls reflect its own systems and risks; SP 800-53B baselines are a starting point tailored to this system.
wrong_explanations.C: CSF 2.0's Protect outcomes concern cybersecurity; mapped to controls, they point to security controls like the baseline's, not to how personal data is processed.

tips: Eliminate: B copies another council's controls instead of tailoring a baseline to this system, and C maps CSF Protect outcomes, which point to security controls, not to how personal data is processed.

Final two: D beats A because security baselines follow the impact level and cover loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability; privacy risks from processing personal data have their own baseline.

Exam cue: SP 800-53B gives security baselines by impact level and a separate privacy baseline; when a system processes personal data, add the privacy baseline and tailor it, whatever the security baseline.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Access approvals from a list of names
questions.question: A stevedoring firm's managers approve access requests to its terminal operating system from lists giving names but not the rights requested; audits keep finding excess access. Which change should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: A second manager's approval of each access request
options.B: IT's request forms showing approvers the rights sought
options.C: Later reviews of the access rights users now hold
options.D: Policy training for the managers who approve access requests

questions.key_concept: An approval works only if the approver can see what is being approved; fix that design gap before adding approvers, training or later reviews.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the approving managers can actually see when they approve.
questions.correct_explanation: An approval can stop excess access only if the approver sees what is being granted; these lists show names, not rights, so the design gap sits in the approval itself. IT, which runs the access tool, can change its request forms to show approvers the rights sought. Later reviews of the access rights users hold are the runner-up: worth keeping, but they find excess access after it is granted and used.

wrong_explanations.A: A second approver sees the same list of names without the rights requested, so excess access still passes, now with two approvals.
wrong_explanations.C: Reviews of access already held find excess rights after they are granted and used; the approval still cannot see what it grants.
wrong_explanations.D: Training explains the access policy, but managers still cannot apply it to rights the request lists do not show them.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a second approver who sees the same names without the rights, and D trains managers on a policy they cannot apply to rights they cannot see.
Final two: B beats C because the gap is at the approval, which cannot see the rights it grants; later reviews find the excess access only after it is granted and used.

Exam cue: when a check keeps passing what it should stop, ask whether the person checking can see what they are judging; give the check that information before adding reviewers, training or later reviews.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Counts kept by the managers they judge
questions.question: A mineral water producer's site managers count their own sites' unapproved control-setting changes for a group KRI that is one of their bonus targets. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Spot checks of the reported counts at a few sites
options.B: Signed statements from each site manager on their count
options.C: Counts collected by a team independent of the sites
options.D: A KRI threshold set from the sites' average count

questions.key_concept: Where possible, KRI data is collected independently of the people whose bonus depends on it; later checks leave the conflict at the source.
questions.pre_read: Ask who gathers the figure and what they gain or lose by it.
questions.correct_explanation: The site managers count their own unapproved changes while the count is one of their bonus targets, so the figure carries a conflict of interest wherever it is checked later. Counts collected by a team independent of the sites remove that conflict where the data is gathered. Spot checks of the reported counts are the runner-up: they can catch some misreporting, but most counts still come from the people the figure judges.

wrong_explanations.A: Spot checks test a few reports after the fact; the counts still come from managers whose bonus depends on them.
wrong_explanations.B: A signed statement comes from the same managers whose bonus depends on the count, so it adds a signature, not independence.
wrong_explanations.D: A threshold built from self-reported counts inherits their bias, and thresholds are set from tolerance, not from the data's average.

tips: Eliminate: B asks the managers to vouch for the counts their bonus depends on, and D sets a threshold from the same self-reported figures, not from tolerance.
Final two: C beats A because spot checks catch some misreporting after the fact while managers still count what their bonus depends on; independent collection removes the conflict.
Exam cue: when people whose bonus or rating depends on a KRI collect its data, have someone independent of them collect it; later checks leave the conflicted source in place.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.1 (Measures Documentation: when possible, the information collector is a different individual or organizational unit from the information owner, to avoid a conflict of interest); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.4 (Data Quality: a validation process checks the integrity, accuracy and structure of data before any analysis is done)

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. An index that stayed green
questions.question: A zinc smelter's board tracks one control-system security index blending 12 measures; it stayed green for two months while one, failed furnace-controller backups, was red. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Breaches in single measures shown apart from the index
options.B: A heavier weight for the backup measure within the index
options.C: A trend line plotting the index's past values
options.D: A narrower green band for the overall index

questions.key_concept: A composite index can stay green while a measure inside it breaches; show such breaches on their own, keeping the index as a summary.
questions.pre_read: Ask what one blended score can hide about the measures inside it.
questions.correct_explanation: A blended index averages 12 measures, so one red measure can sit inside a green score, as failed controller backups did for two months. Showing breaches in single measures apart from the index keeps each measure's threshold working while the index stays a summary. A heavier weight for the backup measure is the runner-up: it would have shown this failure, but the next measure to breach can hide the same way.

wrong_explanations.B: Re-weighting fixes the measure that failed this time; another of the 12 measures can still breach inside a green index.
wrong_explanations.C: A trend of the blended index follows the very figure that stayed green, so it cannot show a breach the blend hid.
wrong_explanations.D: Retuning suits a single indicator set too loose; in a blend of 12 measures, one can still breach badly while the index stays inside a narrower band.

tips: Eliminate: C trends the blended figure that hid the breach, and D tightens the index's band, which a single breaching measure can still sit inside.
Final two: A beats B because re-weighting fixes the measure that failed this time; reporting breaches of any measure on their own catches the next one too.
Exam cue: a composite index can stay green while one measure inside it breaches; keep each measure's own threshold visible and use the index as a summary, not the only signal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286C Rev. 1 Section 2.3 (Analysis of Cybersecurity Risk Registers: aggregated summarization should not impede managers' review of specific risk decisions); NIST IR 8286C Rev. 1 Section 5.2 (Monitoring Risks: KRIs are observed for trends such as rising likelihood or failing controls)
